“In 53 years of supporting United this is the most depressing time. Worse, even, than the pre-Fergie years. The club is completely broken. The owners don’t really care about anything other than money. It’s a matter of public record that they see winning as nice to have [but] not the core objective of an elite football club … I feel deep sympathy for Carrick. His lack of experience was clear when appointed as interim. He did a great job and they rushed to appoint him permanently. It was predictable that the financial constraints of the club would mean he would fail and fail quickly. Our first team squad is completely below average quality and Carrick was completely undermined before the season started by an appallingly negligent transfer window. Every supporter knew where our problems would be and every one of us has been proved right. Why couldn’t Wilcox, Berrada et al see the same as us? It doesn’t matter who the manager is. With this squad and these owners the cycle will just continue” – Robert

“I have supported United for over 70 years through thick and thin but no more, to support United means supporting the Glazers. And I just wonder would a fans’ boycott get rid of them. An empty Old Trafford might do it” – Paul

“I am 62. I have followed Manchester United since the age of four (I found a picture of George Best, and told my mum I liked him). I stood on the Stretford End in my teens and took my son during the 90s. The fanbase needs to wrest control. The only way this will change is for the fanbase to boycott games. Stop going, stop providing matchday revenue. If the Glazers are only interested in the money, stop providing them with an income” – Bob

“Carrick delivered United back to the Champions League and have the team and the fans hope. He did more than I dared hope. But a one-front war is not a four-front war. He should never have been given a new mandate. A manager experienced at dealing with a totally new and different challenge, with Premier League experience, was always the need. Carrick is just another in a long list of managers who has a hands tied by the club. I’ve nothing but admiration for his effort and conduct” – Ben

Sports.title: John McGinn double saves Scotland’s blushes against North Macedonia
Sports.content:
A special occasion for Andy Robertson saw Scotland flirt with embarrassment. Collection of his 102nd cap moves him level with Kenny Dalglish in the all-time Scottish list. Robertson will soon be a record holder. This was, however, John McGinn’s night. A double from McGinn, the second a penalty, spared Scottish blushes against a North Macedonia team who threatened to administer red faces to those in navy blue.

This proved an almighty struggle for Scotland. Questions – and plenty of them – surround whether or not Sébastien Pocognoli can build on the excellent work of his predecessor Steve Clarke. For now, Scotland are a tough watch. Pocognoli looks tactically inflexible and this is not the new dawn many predicted.

“At times it wasn’t pretty,” admitted McGinn. The 32-year-old compared this Scotland process to a club team starting a new season. The rationale is fair enough, were this a remotely forgiving environment.

It was Robertson who led the dressing room inquest in the immediate aftermath of last month’s defeat to Slovenia. It is not in the Tottenham full-back’s make-up to personalise scenarios but shortcomings in the last international window, Pocognoli’s first as the Scotland manager, added to the sense that the bigger picture was important here. North Macedonia looked favourable visitors, having not scored a goal in eight outings.

Pocognoli could call upon Kieran Tierney, Scott McTominay and Ché Adams for the first time and deployed all three from the outset. It already appears the Belgian coach will not deviate from a back three. Ben Gannon-Doak took his place at right wingback, as is feasible against such weak opposition. Scotland’s approach will inevitably change for Monday’s meeting with Switzerland.

View image in fullscreen Andy Robertson, the Scotland captain, equalled Kenny Dalglish’s record of 102 caps. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Scotland had been ponderous until McTominay came within an excellent Stole Dimitrievski save of properly announcing his international return. The midfielder swivelled and struck, with Dimitrievski equal to the Napoli man’s effort.

Robertson was denied the opportunity to mark his special night with a goal by an errant whistle. The referee hauled play back for a Scotland free kick – McTominay had been upended – when the playing of advantage would have seen Robertson collect a Billy Gilmour pass in a scoring position. The Hampden crowd mumped and moaned, which rather summed up recent attitudes around this Scotland team. It feels as if the public are not yet fully engaged with Pocognoli’s project. Adams sought to lift the mood, the striker stooping for a header that took a deflection before Dimitrievski batted away.

In backing up their statistical position, North Macedonia were providing nothing by way of attacking threat. Their enjoyment came from frustrating the Scots. McTominay, who has previous for acrobatic excellence in this arena, tried a 34th minute bicycle kick that flew over the crossbar and Scotland’s most lively player tried again with a low shot which Dimitrievski blocked with his midriff. This lack of cutting edge was a Scottish concern long before Pocognoli entered the dugout. The boos that met the half-time whistle, seconds after North Macedonia had created their first chance of the evening, depicted a supporter base who remained unconvinced.

Less than a minute of the second half had been played when Gilmour produced one of the worst misses ever witnessed at this famous old venue. Calamity in the North Macedonia defence allowed Adams to steal in. The Torino striker laid the ball back to Gilmour six yards out and, with an open goal, he blazed his shot wildly over the bar. It was a genuine, utter howler.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Billy Gilmour reacts after shooting over from six yards against North Macedonia. Photograph: Russell Cheyne/Reuters

Route one broke the deadlock for Scotland. Ryan Porteous’s looping header from the halfway line caused panic in the North Macedonia defence. Adams capitalised, his pass to the advancing McGinn setting up the Aston Villa midfielder’s 23rd goal for his country. Relief was as obvious as celebration.

Although a North Macedonia response was not in the script, the equaliser epitomised Scottish slackness. A near post run from Elmin Rastoder saw him meet a menacing Enis Bardhi corner from the left. Angus Gunn in the home goal was helpless as Rastoder flicked home.

North Macedonia clearly now sensed Scottish vulnerability. While Pocognoli’s men continued to dominate the ball, North Macedonia’s counterattacking threat had increased. Officialdom, and sharp footwork from Gannon-Doak, were soon to come to Scotland’s rescue.

Gannon-Doak was instantly convinced of the foul by Dimitrievski after the Bournemouth man tried to skip past the goalkeeper. It took the VAR to inform the referee that the incident was worthy of further inspection. Intriguingly, it was not Oli McBurnie – still awaiting his maiden Scotland goal and on in place of Adams – who took the spot-kick. Up stepped McGinn, who made no mistake. While Gannon-Doak is due credit for winning the penalty, this appearance once more raised serious questions about his decision making.

That of the Scottish FA in hiring Pocognoli would be open to question had North Macedonia delivered a shock. That they did not do so spared Scotland ignominy. “It was not always perfect,” said Pocognoli. You aren’t kidding, Sébastien.

Sports.title: Jesús Owono given 12-match ban for tackle that resulted in Jesús de Miguel’s death
Sports.content:
The FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono was suspended for 12 matches by the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee on Friday after his challenge on Jesús de Miguel resulted in the death of the Tenerife striker last week.

Owono, an Equatorial Guinea international, was sent off in the second division match on 2 November after racing into midfield and colliding with De Miguel while trying to clear an aerial ball. After the collision, De Miguel, 30, was placed in intensive care in hospital and the Spanish forward died on 3 November.

“The assessment of the conduct under consideration in these proceedings must be based on the facts expressly recorded in the referee’s report, which states that the player was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play,’” said the committee in a statement.

“The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesús de Miguel, is public knowledge. In view of the nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances … the maximum sanction, 12 matches of suspension, is justified.”

Spanish police sources said last week that an investigation into what happened had been opened under judicial supervision.

Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after De Miguel’s death. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words, and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club last week.

“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesús. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesús and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesús.”

The FC Andorra head coach, Carles Manso, said on Thursday it would be Owono who decides if and when he returns to football after the tragic incident.

Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including the Spain head coach, Luis de la Fuente, and the Real Madrid president, Florentino Pérez.

Sports.title: Tuchel to remind England players of anti-racism protocols before game in Spain
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel will remind his ­England players of the anti-racism protocols as they prepare to play Spain in Madrid for the first time since the notorious meeting between the countries in 2004. Spain won 1-0 at the Bernabéu but the occasion was ruined by racist abuse directed at England’s black players from the stands.

England have since played three games in Spain, although they refused to return to Madrid for the first of them in 2009. The match was moved to Seville. There were no ­problems in any of the three; the second was in Alicante in 2015, the third back in Seville in 2018.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The Spanish federation was fined £44,750 in the wake of the 2004 fixture when Ashley Cole, Rio ­Ferdinand, Shaun Wright-Phillips, Jermaine Jenas and Jermain Defoe were targeted. England face Spain in the Nations League at Madrid’s other major stadium – the Metropolitano.

Spain were last month fined £15,000 and ordered to play their next friendly with a partial stadium closure after supporters sang a discriminatory chant about Muslims during a match against Egypt in Barcelona in March.

Tuchel said: “We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September of last year]. There is a protocol in place. Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]. It’s important that the players know about the protocol. And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch.”

England’s head coach made it clear he did not anticipate any problems at the Metropolitano. “It’s unacceptable,” he said. “In any stadium, not even in stadiums … we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone. That’s just not who we are. I expect, of course, full support from the Spanish crowd for the Spanish team. But we will not expect anything [untoward].”

Sports.title: Branding it like Beckham: how Jude Bellingham is future-proofing his fame
Sports.content:
This Sunday, Jude Bellingham will line up with his England teammates for a match against Spain. But the footballer has been hitting the headlines way beyond the pitch recently – thanks to fronting a Calvin Klein underwear ad released this month, and becoming the first footballer to appear solo on the cover of British Vogue.

It’s a savvy move for the 23-year-old, future-proofing himself as a power player both on and off the pitch. This is a roadmap carved out by David Beckham, who since retiring in 2013 has become a brand and personality that transcends sport. Beckham – together with his wife, Victoria – became a billionaire this year.

The Calvin Klein ads, which feature Bellingham in underwear, sometimes in his signature Christ the Redeemer pose, have caused a stir since appearing in London and New York, with passersby stopping to take selfies. The popularity of a billboard in Soho, New York also cements his celebrity status in the US after this summer’s World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham on the cover of British Vogue. Photograph: Alasdair McLellan/British Vogue

Of course Bellingham is a bona fide star on the pitch. Mark Borkowski, a public relations consultant, says this factor is pivotal to the footballer’s crossover appeal. “Bellingham is an exceptional sporting talent, and his brand value is understandably enormous,” he says. “But fashion doesn’t create that value, football does. Fashion merely provides another means of exploiting it.”

This buzz is working out well for Calvin Klein. The fashion data firm Launchmetrics said in 48 hours the Calvin Klein campaign generated $35.8m (£27m) in media impact value, the metric that works out the monetary value of social media posts. The fashion platform Lyst reports that searches for Calvin Klein underwear have risen by 25% since the campaign was released.

Bellingham has a savvy team around him, with his mother, Denise, a former HR executive, working as his personal manager. Some are wondering if his 21-year-old brother, Jobe – in the England squad for the first time this month – might do similar campaigns, increasing the rise of the Bellingham brand.

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham poses for Calvin Klein’s cotton stretch underwear campaign. Photograph: Oliver Hadlee Pearch

So far Bellingham – and his management team – have been strategic with his brand choices. As well as Calvin Klein, Bellingham works with Adidas, Kim Kardashian’s underwear brand Skims and Louis Vuitton.

Daniel-Yaw Miller, in his influential SportsVerse newsletter, compared him to Beckham. “It’s very intentional,” he says. “What [Bellingham is] doing is aimed at the higher tier of the market but at the same time, a big part of his personality is very relatable.”

Bellingham is also a heart-throb, with looks that, in another life, could belong to a boyband. Vogue have amped up this factor: the magazine comes with a pull-out poster. “It helps that he’s incredibly good-looking,” says Miller.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Fashion Statement Style, with substance: what's really trending this week, a roundup of the best fashion journalism and your wardrobe dilemmas solved Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Bellingham is not the only male footballer to work with the fashion industry. Bukayo Saka and Son Heung-min were in Burberry’s autumn campaign, Kylian Mbappé worked with Christian Dior, and Declan Rice is on the cover of GQ this month. “The earnings that they can get during their football career are obviously huge,” says Miller. “But what sets them up for life beyond that is being brands and businesses in their own right. It’s not only just a money thing. It’s about cementing a legacy and securing their profile in the game long term, commercially and culturally.”

View image in fullscreen Jude Bellingham posing for British Vogue in its December 2026 issue. Photograph: Alasdair McLellan/British Vogue

Not everyone is impressed by Bellingham’s foray into fashion. Felicia Pennant, the editor of the football and fashion magazine Season, says if he is following Beckham’s business model, the older footballer pushed the boundaries more, appearing in edgy photoshoots covered in (fake) blood for The Face magazine in 2001, and in artwork by Sam Taylor-Johnson. “Beckham was the subject of art and he was the art rather than selling the art,” she says. “I think what Jude’s doing feels quite transactional … there’s nothing that directional about anything he’s done so far.”

Borkowski sounds a note of caution going forward. “Fame surrounds exceptional young athletes with people whose livelihoods depend on telling them how wonderful they are. That can become a very dangerous echo chamber,” he says. “The football makes the myth. The business can preserve it. But hubris can destroy both.”

Sports.title: Why Chelsea and Manchester City’s WSL clash is not as season-defining as you think
Sports.content:
There was a time when the games between the top three – traditionally Chelsea, Manchester City and Arsenal – were title-deciders. Where every point taken off a title rival was key. Such was the gap in investment and quality between those teams and the rest of the Women’s Super League, it was extremely rare that points would be dropped to teams outside that elite clique.

As the WSL has grown in investment, profile and size, that narrative has started to shift a little. The investment gap is still large from the top to the bottom of the league. But increased investment among the best of the rest and even among those teams further down the table, as well as an increase in high-quality coaches with the tactical and technical vision to get more from players, is having an impact.

That’s a roundabout way of saying that when Chelsea welcome the title holders and current league leaders to Stamford Bridge on Saturday lunchtime, counterintuitively, the three points isn’t the most important takeaway. Instead, based on the state of play, it’s the momentum, confidence, belief and bragging rights that are critical.

Naturally, should Chelsea win and thus leapfrog Manchester City, then the title race will be considered wide open. If Andrée Jeglertz’s City extend their lead over Chelsea from two points to five, even at this early stage, they will be considered favourites for the title in May, but it will be said with a little less confidence than it might have been in previous years.

The WSL is more and more competitive year on year. There have been only two occasions, in the 15 years since the first WSL season was played (after it was launched to replace the FA Women’s Premier League National Division), when the title winners have lost more than two games in a season. Both of those have come in the last three years, with Chelsea the first to do so in 2023-24 and then Manchester City last season.

You could say that because wins are less consequential in the games between title rivals, those games are less thrilling, but the reality is that the growing unpredictability of almost every match across the WSL means that every game becomes a must-watch.

At Stamford Bridge on Saturday, the remaining two unbeaten teams have the opportunity to inflict a first defeat. Neither side has looked infallible this season. City have kept just two clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions, while Chelsea stuttered last weekend, with their second draw of the season allowing City to move above them.

View image in fullscreen Manchester City leapfrogged Chelsea at the top of the WSL after beating West Ham last weekend. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

Arguably, there has been a momentum shift between Sonia Bompastor’s and Jeglertz’s teams, with the former having dropped points against Everton before a 0-0 draw with the Swedish side Häcken in the Champions League while City earned a 5-0 win over West Ham and picked up a first win in Europe, after three draws, with a 4-1 defeat of Inter.

Jeglertz said that moving top had changed nothing before this clash. “We’re still early in the season. We want to win all games. That’s our focus this weekend,” he said. “Nothing has changed from that point of view and I don’t think it will have for them either.”

Chelsea have been defensively strong, and are the only WSL team to still be in single figures for goals conceded, on five to City’s 10, and they have kept nine clean sheets in their 13 games in all competitions (not including Champions League qualifying).

However, the key to the west London side’s ambition of drawing first blood between the two teams this season will probably centre around how well they cope without Lauren James.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

They may lead the way in goals scored too, 28 to City’s 27, but against Everton the absence of the England forward’s creativity was keenly felt and Chelsea’s attack looked a little predictable. Everton nullified the impact of the wide players Ellie Carpenter and Sandy Baltimore and Chelsea struggled to find another way through.

“My job is to make sure I find solutions when some players are not available and not playing for the team,” Bompastor said last week.

While Chelsea have to cope with the absence of James, who has a hamstring injury that Bompastor says means they “won’t see her until the end of this block” – up until at least the international break at the end of the month – City have players returning.

Rebecca Knaak is fine after a knock to the head against Inter and Vivianne Miedema, Beth Mead and Niamh Charles are on their way back. “All three of them, actually, were in the session today and I hope that they will be available for Saturday,” said Jeglertz. Advantage City then, just.

In a way, that it is unlikely that this result decides either team’s season makes it a more interesting and exciting contest, because players are free to play uninhibited by the pressure of how catastrophic a loss could be and, with the two dominant teams going head to head, we’re in for a show.

Sports.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
Sports.content:
It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

Reader, it did not. But it did set a precedent that is being enthusiastically revived. It’s even possible that, after several decades of hurt, the world’s favourite sport may finally be getting its artistic due. There have been three iterations of the Football Art Prize in the past 20 years, and the latest arrives at the National Football Museum this month (from the Sheffield Millennium Gallery) with a breadth of entries that demonstrate how resonant the subject can be.

View image in fullscreen Felix Higham’s Newcastle 2 Barcelona 7, one of many exhibits that focus on football culture rather than the game itself. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Meticulous still lives – of battered balls, or boots mid-clean – ache with memory. There’s haunting photo-documentary: Bangladeshi youths playing a pickup game in the middle of a rubbish dump, pitches affected by climate change. “You see the whole gamut of footballing experience on display,” says the museum’s exhibitions director, Pip Diment. Her assumptions – she initially imagined herself hanging portraits of famous moments and iconic players – were overturned. “Pretty much every one of the artists is expressing how football matters to them, but they’re responding and reacting in such different ways.”

There are a few famous faces nevertheless. One artist worked in charcoals to create a hyper-realist bust of N’Golo Kanté. Roy Keane appears twice, once proffering a plate of prawn sandwiches to his viewer, another time in a diptych with Micah Richards. The latter is the work of Conor Rogers, whose satirical series of paintings on abandoned betting slips took second prize. They include a poignant image of Sheffield United’s manager, Chris Wilder, head in hands, next to a repurposed bookmaker’s logo asking: “Lad r u ok?”

Diment says football and art are still perceived as almost entirely separate spheres, so it’s interesting that this year’s winning work – a video by Alina Akbar – explores the connection between “high” and “popular” culture. In Footwork, the multimedia artist segues between keepy-uppy skills and the choreographed movements of Kathak, an Indian classical dance style. The combined rhythms and sounds create a mesmerising meditation on identity, related to the northern South Asian community in which she grew up.

View image in fullscreen Kyle King-Jagger ‘s Roy’s Rolls riffs on Roy Keane’s famous ‘prawn sandwich brigade’ comment. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

Football, she says, is a post-migration culture whose value is sometimes overlooked by the very people who adopted it. “Whenever I went to my great-grandparents’ house, football was on TV all the time and I’d be on their street, trying out tricks,” says Akbar. “My grandad and his brothers were really excited when I started playing, because they’d gone through the more racist era of the 70s, and they never went to games.”

For all its social themes, Akbar’s work still expresses the balletic movement and poise that Picasso once pursued in the flowing form of his ceramic sculpture Footballeur. It’s interesting how so much of the art in the show reflects football culture rather than the game itself – watching from the sofa, in the pub, on the touchline of a recreational game. Perhaps it’s hard for artists to compete with the volume of visual content that the games already provide. And we have moved a long way from a classically inspired fascination with athletes’ physiques (for comparison, check out the leaping goalkeeper in Cecil Beaton’s mid-20th-century painting Footballers, with his unashamedly pert buttocks).

Tim Marlow, the director of the Design Museum and chair of the judging panel, points out that “artists today have unashamedly adopted the position of the spectator or the fan” and that it’s rare to find works that try to get inside the experience of the footballer themselves. One of his favourite exceptions is the 2006 film, Zidane: A 21st Century Portrait, which he calls “a great piece of conceptual art”. “It’s a really intimate study of the game, which in the current era, when you’ve got referees with head cams, might feel old hat, but nothing like it had been done before.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Keith Bird’s Full-time at Maine Road depicts Manchester City’s former home. Photograph: Courtesy of the National Football Museum

And then there’s Tottenham’s stadium gallery, OOF, where exhibitions of football-related work have ranged from Roger Mayne’s 1950s street photography to AC Larsen’s polemic on the FA’s trans ban. This month brought the opening of Trackie McLeod’s celebration of Wag culture. Historic football art, meanwhile, is rocketing in value. Four years ago Lowry’s Going To The Match went for £7.8m at auction, a record price for the Salford artist’s work, and in 2022 one of Nicholas de Staël’s Parc des Princes 1952 abstract series – based on a friendly he watched between France and Sweden – became the most expensive football artwork when it sold for £16.7m.

Money has always been a key element in the art world, and there are notable collectors within the footballing world today, from billionaire club owners to cultured former players. Fabio Capello has a well documented passion for Kandinsky; David Beckham’s collection is said to include Andy Warhol, Banksy and Yayoi Kusama; Michael Ballack is spotted at major art fairs around the world. The whimsically named J St John, who organised Football and Fine Arts, told the Liverpool Daily Post 70 years ago that art needed a new form of patronage, to help people appreciate the painted canvas in the same they understood the artistry of Joe Mercer, Ferenc Puskas and Stanley Matthews. Could his dream finally be coming to pass?

Sports.title: Max Dowman creates England Under-21 history as he breaks Jude Bellingham record
Sports.content:
Max Dowman has become the youngest-ever player to represent the England national Under-21 team.

The Arsenal starlet made his debut for the side in a 1-0 friendly defeat to Portugal on Friday night at Ashton Gate as a substitute in the second half.



2 Dowman made history for the England U21 team when he came off the bench in their friendly defeat to Portgual Credit: Getty

Before the match, Jude Bellingham held the record of youngest-ever England U21 player.

The Real Madrid superstar featured for the first time at the age of 17 years, two months and six days against Kosovo in September 2020.

However, Dowman has now taken the title off him by playing for the team aged 16 years, ten months and 13 days old.



France are their next opponents on Monday night, and the Gunners academy graduate Dowman could be in line for a start under Lee Carsley.

His appearance on Friday has only increased his list of individual feats for club and country.



In England colours, he is their youngest-ever player and scorer at U17 and U19 level.

For Arsenal, Dowman is the club's youngest starter and scorer, as well as their youngest Champions League player.



The winger also holds the youngest accolade for their starter, scorer and champion in the Premier League.

Dowman continues his rise

Now in his second senior season at Arsenal, Dowman has featured six times in all competitions and scored two goals.

Both of those came in the 4-2 Carabao Cup third round win away at Ipswich Town.

2 Bellingham was youngest England U21 player before Friday, and now the crown belongs to Dowman Credit: Getty



However, Dowman was shown a straight red card in the shock defeat to Fleetwood Town for kicking out after a strong challenge.

Mikel Arteta cut a furious figure when he walked past him and down the tunnel as Arsenal crashed out against the League Two side.

He has made just two outings in the Premier League, with both being as a substitute.

However, Dowman has now upgraded from an England U19 star to U21 hopeful in record-breaking circumstances.



Next on the pathway at international level is a senior appearance, but this is by no means guaranteed to happen soon.

Wayne Rooney holds the record for being the youngest player to don an England shirt aged 17 years and 156 days having featured against Australia in 2003.

Sports.title: Antonio Nusa speaks on possible Arsenal transfer as Norway boss advises against move
Sports.content:
All recommendations within this article are informed by expert editorial opinion. If you click on a link in this story we will earn affiliate revenue.

Antonio Nusa speaks on possible Arsenal transfer as Norway boss advises against move

Antonio Nusa is distancing himself away from transfer speculation as Arsenal sustain interest in the RB Leipzig winger.

Nusa has been directly involved in 11 goals [four goals, seven assists] in the Bundesliga so far this season - the joint-highest combined tally with Bayern Munich star Harry Kane.

2 Nusa is one of the leading forwards in the Bundesliga and on the radar of English champions Arsenal Credit: Getty

The 21-year-old, dubbed the 'Norwegian Neymar', is reported to be a target for English clubs.

One of those is Premier League holders Arsenal who, as per BILD, are a persistent suitor of the forward.

They are also said to have sent a delegation to watch Nusa in action for Leipzig in their 3-2 Champions League loss to Manchester City.

However, whilst the Gunners may be an attractive proposition, Nusa is choosing not to get distracted by rumours on his future.

"I try to take a step back from that," he told TV2. "There's a lot going on at the same time now. I try not to open my phone too often, because there's always something going on there, he says, laughing."

On what appears on his phone, Nusa added: "I see everything, then! Whatever comes. I'm not blind, so I get it.

"That's why I try to take a step back. I have good people around me. There's no stress. I just try to enjoy the everyday life I have in Leipzig. It's a fantastic team with a fantastic coach (Martin Demichelis).

"Next to that I have an agent who works with all the other parts and just lets me focus on the football. That's the most important thing for me."

Nusa told to avoid Arsenal transfer

The January transfer window is just weeks away and offers clubs the chance to strengthen for the rest of the season.

Arsenal may look to do so for their Premier League title defence and Champions League push, but Nusa has been told to stay in Leipzig.

2 Nusa is not reading into the speculation too much, and his Norway boss Solbakken has advised against a January exit from Leipzig Credit: AFP

Norway boss Stale Solbakken said: "I think it's a good idea for him to play there this season, and get a good Bundesliga season where he can mature a little more before he takes the final step.

"If he then leaves after a season instead of in the middle of a season, you also get a long pre-season and get to know the coaches and players in a summer where there is no European Championship or World Cup."

Nusa has won 34 caps for the Norwegian national team and scored nine goals with ten assists.

One of his strikes came during the 2026 World Cup when they were 2-1 winners against Ivory Coast in the last 32.

He could make his 35th international appearance on Saturday in the Nations League clash against Wales.

Norway have to win to stand a chance of reaching the quarter-finals as they currently sit bottom of Group A4.

Sports.title: Manchester United star sent home from international duty to hand Mauricio Pochettino instant blow
Sports.content:
Manchester United star sent home from international duty to hand Mauricio Pochettino instant blow

Patrick Dorgu has been sent back to England by Denmark due to a lack of fitness having linked up for international duty.

The versatile full-back, who can also operate as a winger, only just returned to action for Manchester United following his recovery from a hamstring injury.



3 Dorgu is not fit enough to play for Denmark during the international break, despite joining the squad two days ago Credit: Getty

Dorgu injured himself during Denmark's 2-0 Nations League win over Wales in September, and was substituted with 30 minutes played.

Despite not initially being picked by Brian Riemer for this international break, the 22-year-old joined his nation's squad on Wednesday.

This was three days after he came off the bench for United to score their late equaliser in the 4-4 Premier League draw with Aston Villa.



However, although he trained with the rest of the Denmark players, Dorgu will not play in their matches against Portugal and Norway.

Denmark statement on Dorgu

A statement from Denmark's doctor Morten Boesen read: "We have carried out a series of tests on Dorgu, and he has not performed well enough to be ready to play in the two matches.



"He needs further recovery time after his injury.

"So we are sending him home for additional rehabilitation.”

Head coach Riemer had held a positive outlook on his ability to play a role in the international break before the news of his fitness.

“There are still some lingering issues with the major muscle injury he suffered," he said, via United's website.



"We need to make sure it doesn’t flare up again. We're optimistic, and we also believe things will go well."

3 Dorgu picked up a hamstring knock during the October international break Credit: AFP

But Riemer also stressed that if Dorgu was fit to play, he would likely only be used as a substitute against Norway on Tuesday.

The Dane's lack of fitness will come as a blow to United and their new head coach Mauricio Pochettino.



Pochettino has signed a two-and-a-half year deal and will join from his United States men's national team role next week.

With United 18th and in the Premier League relegation zone, he faces a difficult battle to guide them towards European qualification.

Left-back has become a position of concern for them this season as Luke Shaw is sidelined with a muscle issue.

Diogo Dalot, a natural right-back, has been the go-to replacement for him in the role, but has struggled.



3 Pochettino already faces a fitness concern at left-back as the new United head coach with Dorgu's withdrawal Credit: Getty

Dorgu has played at left-back for United, as well as left-wing back and on the wing.

Pochettino will hope he can return to full fitness in time for his first match as head coach against Liverpool on November 22.

Sports.title: ‘Average player, failed coach, weak link’ – Gabby Agbonlahor fires back at The Overlap
Sports.content:
Gabby Agbonlahor has hit back at Jamie Carragher, Gary Neville and Roy Keane as he returned fire towards the Premier League legends.

The talkSPORT pundit was mocked by three of The Overlap pundits for, in their view, caring more about Aston Villa now than he did when he played for his boyhood club.

2 Agbonlahor didn't take the criticism lying down...

The trio were discussing a message that Carragher sent to Gabby on social media around the Sky Sports pundit's recent spat with Aston Villa that saw him threatened with legal action.

And they suggested that talkSPORT's very own Gabby cares more about the Villans now than he did during his 391 appearances for the club between 2005-2018.

Speaking on air with Sam Matterface and Scott Minto, he quipped: "I don't understand where they are going with it, Carragher said that I didn't used to run.

"If you look at my social media, I posted a video of me winning a header against Carragher and Chris Sutton plays me through on goal.

"I don't know what Carragher was towing when he was trying to catch me, I did that to Carragher every time I played against him - Neville as well.

"Neville had a fantastic career, didn't he? But whenever I played against him, he was one of the ones I targeted.

"Roy Keane, fantastic player - terrible coach. Walked out of Villa like he walked out of Republic of Ireland, so he can't say anything.

"It is tongue in cheek with Carragher, but come on, I know you won the Champions League, but average player (said with a smirk)."

What did Carragher, Neville and Keane say about Agbonlahor?

It started with Neville, who was speaking to Carragher in Thursday's episode of The Overlap, and said: "His line to Agbonlahor on his Instagram.

"You put, 'I am always more worried about someone who is more passionate about their club when they're a pundit than when they were when they played for them.'"

Keane added: "Brilliant shout. I love that."

Carragher then said: "I see these people, and I watched you play - you didn't even run."

Keane jumped in: "I see ex-players who say they love the club, and you are thinking that when they played, it didn't seem they loved it that much.

"It is really key that when you play for a club, you love it, aterwards, you can be chilled out. Great shout, Jamie."

2 Agbonlahor was Villa's top Premier League goalscorer before being surpassed by Ollie Watkins Credit: Getty

Final word

This all stems from Carragher saying that Unai Emery would absolutely take the Manchester United job, which he didn't.

Instead, he's set sign a new deal to remain at Villa Park beyond 2029.

But at the time, Carragher told Villa fans to 'shut the f*** up' about Emery not leaving.

In the end, the legal action was withdrawn, and Carragher apologised.

Gabby has defended his club throughout, and former Chelsea left-back Minto also refuted any doubts about him as well.

He stated: "I don't think anyone can tell Gabby that he didn't care about Aston Villa."

To round off the conversation, Gabby said: "I made loads of mistakes as a player, but to say I didn't love that football club...

"Carragher came for my football club and apologised."

Sports.title: England don’t need to leave Wembley – they just need a restraining order against Croatia
Sports.content:
England don’t need to leave Wembley – they just need a restraining order against Croatia

England fans are bored of playing Croatia - that was the sole reason for the flat Wembley atmosphere on Thursday night.

That's the view of legendary talkSPORT broadcaster Adrian Durham, who has commented on the Three Lions' 2-1 victory in the Nations League.

4 Harry Kane's penalty clinch another three points at Wembley on Thursday Credit: Getty

Despite the cold weather conditions, 80,000 fans turned out at Wembley for the fixture - a month after England's 7-0 win over Croatia in Rijeka.

But the atmosphere at Wembley left a lot to be desired which once again sparked discussion about whether the FA should schedule fixtures around the country rather than at their spiritual home.

Durham, who was at the Home of Football on Thursday for talkSPORT, has poured cold water on the suggestion and says the match itself was the cause of the diluted atmosphere.

“I think it was more the performance than the atmosphere that we were talking about,” Durham said.

“But in terms of the atmosphere, I hear people saying, take it around the country and all that but listen, there’s 80,000 at Wembley last night.

“A game as flat as that is not going to get a bigger atmosphere anywhere else and a bigger crowd anywhere else.”

What has Durham said about Croatia fixture?

Durham also believes that repetitive fixtures against Croatia has made the fixture less appealing to fans.

The two nations have met three times in the last five months alone including England’s 4-2 win at the World Cup in June.

“Playing Croatia so many times in recent memory is a massive problem,” Durham added.

“We need to get a restraining order against Croatia that they don’t come within a 100 miles of Wembley Stadium!

4 80,000 fans packed into Wembley for the Nations league fixture Credit: Getty

“And no disrespect to them because they probably deserved something from the game to be honest.

“We’ve played them so many times it's hard to get excited about it.

“The other thing I’d say is the Atlanta failure at the end of that [World Cup] semi-final is still fresh in the memory.

“I think it's right that the fans are sitting there waiting for the players to deliver something to those fans who have paid a lot of money to watch England.

“I don’t think prices for tickets were exorbitant last night, but in the current climate, everything is pretty much expensive.

“I’d also say as well, we’ve just won 7-0 away to Croatia [in October] so let’s cut these players a little bit of slack.

4 England lined up against their familiar opponents for the third time in 2026 Credit: Getty

“The atmosphere wasn’t great, the game wasn’t great and I think that was the big problem.”

Higher demands

Durham’s broadcast colleague Stuart Pearce was less critical of England’s performance claiming he saw ‘nice things’ from the Three Lions.

However, Durham believes that although Thomas Tuchel's side were able to pick up the three points, England should be held to higher standards.

“If you’d imagined ten years ago that we’d be moaning about a 2-1 victory at home… times have changed so much,” he remarked.

“Expectations have changed and that’s got to be a good thing because England are in a far better place than what they were.”

Responding to Pearce’s claim, Durham added: “Well that’s OK and that’s a positive and certainly not a negative, but it needs to be exciting, it needs to be decisive rather than nice.

4 England picked up a win in their final game of the year at Wembley Credit: Getty

“I think we’ve moved beyond nice now so I think it’s right to hold England to standards.

“Thomas Tuchel is holding Cole Palmer to certain standards like he held Jude Bellingham to standards before that.

“And it’s right that the England fans hold the teams to standards too.”

Sports.title: Two Manchester United players can thrive under Mauricio Pochettino – look what he did with Dele Alli
Sports.content:
Two Manchester United players can thrive under Mauricio Pochettino – look what he did with Dele Alli

Mauricio Pochettino has been tipped to get the best out of Marcus Rashford and Kobbie Mainoo at Manchester United.

The new Red Devils boss will officially take charge at Old Trafford next week after being announced as Michael Carrick's successor.



4 Rashford and Mainoo have struggled for consistency so far this season - but that could soon change Credit: Getty

Pochettino, who will leave after USA's upcoming fixtures against Haiti, has signed a two-and-a-half year deal with the club as he looks to turn around their fortunes.

United are currently winless in their last eight Premier League matches, a run of form which resulted in Carrick's sacking on Thursday.

As a result, the Red Devils find themselves 18th in the table ahead of Pochettino's first match in charge against Liverpool on November 22.



Amongst those struggling for form is Rashford, who has yet to score or assist in eight appearances across all competitions this term.

Rashford and Mainoo tipped to 'thrive'

According to former Premier League goalkeeper and USA icon Brad Friedel, the forward can thrive under Pochettino this season.



The Argentinian has also been backed to take Mainoo to a new level thanks to his history of working with high potential players.

Speaking to Sam Matterface, Gabby Agbonlahor and Scott Minto live on talkSPORT, Friedel explained: "I think as opposed to trying to get a senior player on board, I think he’ll put his arm around some of the younger players that have incredible potential.



"Somebody like Marcus Rashford could really thrive under him if that’s one of the players that Mauricio pinpoints, Mainoo as well, players like that.

"If you look at what he did with Dele Alli at Spurs when he came in, kind of a similar situation.

"He’s very good at making players that he wants in his system, in his culture at the club, making them feel a million bucks.

4 Pochettino's success with Alli should give United's young stars confidence, says Friedel Credit: Getty



"He’s excellent at that and his whole staff is very good at that, being compassionate and making you feel wanted, making you feel possibly better than you are while making sure that you’re working hard.

"We’ve watched many Manchester United games and some of the games we’ve actually watched and we’ve come away saying, 'They’re just getting outworked at times,' you can’t have that.

"That’s one part of the game he won’t tolerate at all and it really has no meaning to him what your name is on the back of the shirt at all."

Pochettino signed Dele Alli for Tottenham Hotspur back in 2015 when the midfielder was aged just 18.



He would go on to score 55 goals and provide 48 assists in 194 appearances for Spurs under Pochettino.

Alli was also named PFA Young Player of the Year for the 2015/16 and 2016/17 seasons.

4 Here is how Pochettino compares to former United candidates Emery and Howe

Those campaigns also saw him included in the PFA Team of the Year as recognition for his performances.



During his time as Spurs boss, Pochettino secured a second place in the Premier League as well as two third place finishes and a run to the club's first-ever Champions League final.

Fernandes' future under Pochettino

Friedel was also questioned on whether Pochettino will want to keep Bruno Fernandes around the first-team squad.

The United captain has rejected a second new contract offer, with his current deal set to expire at the end of the season.

He added: "I think he’ll want his talent at the football club, but he won’t tolerate it if he does have an ego.



"I don’t know Bruno personally at all. I think Mauricio’s not a fool. He’ll want the best players on the pitch, but he’ll want them fully committed.

4 Fernandes' future will be an early hurdle for Pochettino to overcome Credit: Getty

"If they’re not he will work very quickly to get them out the door. I would imagine he will try to work with him at first and if he doesn’t think he’s going to fit then I don’t think it’ll be an issue for him to change him.

"He is a top quality player, we all know that. Mauricio builds a culture at the club. If he’s not going to buy into that then you’ll be out the door."

Sports.title: Manchester United handed perfect Bruno Fernandes replacement for Mauricio Pochettino to sign
Sports.content:
Nico Paz could be the signing to kickstart the Mauricio Pochettino era at Manchester United - if they move on from Bruno Fernandes.

That's the view of talkSPORT's Gabby Agbonlahor, who has named the Como starlet as a potential solution to one of the first dilemmas facing Pochettino following his appointment as Red Devils boss.

4 Como starlet Paz has been tipped to become Lionel Messi's long-term heir for Argentina Credit: Getty

After days of speculation, Pochettino was confirmed as Man United's new manager on Friday following Michael Carrick's sacking.

But with his new side sitting 18th in the Premier League, the ex-Tottenham and Chelsea boss inherits a less than ideal set of circumstances - made worse by recent news surrounding captain Fernandes.

The United talisman, whose current contract runs out at the end of the season, turned down a second offer from the club.

As it stands, Fernandes is free to negotiate with foreign clubs regarding a free transfer from January.

While United do have the option to trigger an automatic 12-month extension, the 32-year-old's latest decision makes it increasingly likely the club could consider moving him on next summer.

Having been inspirational since his arrival at Old Trafford in 2019 - scoring 113 goals and providing 111 assists for United - Fernandes' departure would leave a gaping hole at the club.

However, former Aston Villa hero Agbonlahor believes Pochettino could look to rebuild his team with a face United are familiar with.

Is Paz the solution?

Discussing Pochettino's possible response to Fernandes' contract saga, Agbonlahor tipped him to consider signing Como sensation Paz - who starred with two stunning goals in his side 4-1 thrashing of United in October.

He told talkSPORT: “Maybe Pochettino comes in and says, ‘You know what? I don't like his attitude. I don’t like the way he throws his arms up at his teammates, the way he threw Michael Carrick under the bus. Can I go and get my own players?’

“Nico Paz - how good has he been? He's the next star for Argentina.

4 Bruno Fernandes is at a crossroads in his Man United career Credit: Getty

4 Pochettino arrives at Old Trafford with plenty to sort, including Fernandes' future at the club Credit: AFP

“Does he say, ‘You know what? I want him next summer from Como, make it happen’. Save the money on wages that maybe Bruno Fernandes wants.

“So he might have his own ideas to get all these players out that maybe have been a little bit of a problem [like], 'I want to refresh the whole squad.'”

Paz would certainly be a popular arrival at Old Trafford, given how he put United to the sword recently in the Champions League.

The 21-year-old is widely regarded as one of the most promising young talents in Europe after impressing in Italy.

A Real Madrid youth product, the Argentina international has starred under Cesc Fabregas at Como since his arrival in 2024, and boasts six goals and eight assists in 14 games altogether this term.

His exploits include three Champions League goals, firing the Italian side to three wins out of their first four European games.

4 Paz has earned 14 senior caps for Argentina, where he has been tipped for a bright future Credit: Getty

This follows a strong 2025/26 campaign, where Paz's 12 goals and seven assists in Serie A helped his team qualify for the Champions League for the first time in their history.

And the youngster is so highly thought of that he has even been touted as the eventual heir to Lionel Messi with his national team.

With Paz into the final 18 months of his Como contract, he won't be short of offers as he weighs up his next move.

And United could certainly prove a tempting option, with the appointment of fellow Argentine Pochettino meaning he would have a clear connection if he did move to Manchester.

Sports.title: New Man United boss Mauricio Pochettino breaks down in tears over ‘most difficult decision of his career’
Sports.content:
New Man United boss Mauricio Pochettino breaks down in tears over ‘most difficult decision of his career’

Mauricio Pochettino broke down in tears during his first press conference since being named Manchester United manager.

The Argentinian has been announced as Michael Carrick's successor on a two-and-a-half year deal.

4 Pochettino broke down in tears as he reflected on leaving his USA role Credit: YouTube/U.S. Soccer

Carrick was sacked on Thursday following an eight-match winless run in the Premier League.

Pochettino will officially begin his United tenure on November 19 following the USA's upcoming fixtures.

As a result, his first match as manager will be away against Liverpool on Sunday, November 22.

Ahead of taking charge at Old Trafford, he will oversee the USA's matches against Haiti before stepping down as head coach.

The national team boss spoke to reporters on Friday prior to their CONCACAF Nations League quarter-final first leg.

Emotional Pochettino on USA exit

A visibly emotional Pochettino wiped away tears as he admitted the decision to leave his role for the United job was 'one of the most difficult' of his career.

Discussing his exit, he joked: "Normally it's the opposite. You're sacked and you cry because you want to stay.

"For this case it's the opposite. It's a really tough decision, but at the same time I'm excited for that step."

Pochettino added: "The staff and the players, I want to say thank you so much for the last two years.

"You made me feel really happy sharing an amazing project. It's difficult now for me to finish.

4 Pochettino's decision to leave the USA was 'one of the most difficult' of his career Credit: AFP

4 Pochettino's record compared to fellow United contenders Unai Emery and Eddie Howe

"We were very excited to share a project which we really believe in and are evolving together, it makes the decision harder.

"It's a sad decision but we are professionals, and we need to try to find the next step to make your dreams come true."

As he continued, Pochettino was in tears whilst admitting: "We increased the federation and around the world too.

"I didn't prepare a speech; I am talking from the heart. We recovered our motivation and the capacity to dig deep.

"I want to recognise the value from us and me. Big thank you. You respect your work. You never lie to us. That is a difficult decision but we need to move forward."

The 54-year-old was first appointed as USA boss in September 2024, signing a deal through to this summer's World Cup.

4 Pochettino guided the USA to the last 16 of this summer's World Cup Credit: AFP

Following the Stars and Stripes' run to the last 16, he was handed a four-year extension until the end of the 2030 finals.

Prior to facing Haiti this week, Pochettino has won 22 of his 35 matches in charge.

Sports.title: Arsenal star Max Dowman smashes Jude Bellingham's record - but a less-familiar name should catch Thomas Tuchel's eye ahead of Euro 2028: THINGS WE LEARNED from England U21's defeat to Portugal
Sports.content:
Arsenal star Max Dowman smashes Jude Bellingham's record - but a less-familiar name should catch Thomas Tuchel's eye ahead of Euro 2028: THINGS WE LEARNED from England U21's defeat to Portugal

Max Dowman smashed Jude Bellingham's record on an icy cold night in Bristol to become the youngest player to ever play for England's Under-21s.

The 16-year-old was sent on with 30 minutes to go by Lee Carsley in a move that energised an Ashton Gate crowd that went home frustrated after a 1-0 defeat inflicted by Afonso Moreira's first half goal.

But this was to be Dowman's night, smashing the previous record set by Bellingham when he made his England Under-21 debut against Kosovo in 2020 aged 17 years, two months and six days old. Dowman does not turn 17 until December 31.

Under-21s boss Lee Carsley has been keen long before this international break to try to shield Dowman from the weight of expectation.

But on he came, replacing the lively Amario Cozier-Duberry with a smile on his face and a quiet confidence that he didn't take long to show off, bursting past two Portuguese markers before four huddled together to gang up on him.

Breaking records is nothing new to a player that already holds one for being the Premier League's youngest-ever goalscorer, thanks to his goal against Everton last season.

Max Dowman wrote his name into the record books once more, playing for England Under-21s

Dowman came on to rich applause on a cold night in Bristol to shatter Jude Bellingham's record

The Arsenal teenager was lively playing off the right as he now targets the 2027 U21 Euros

Dowman is both the youngest player to ever win the Premier League and his outing in the Champions League against Slavia Prague last season saw the then-15-year-old become the youngest-ever player to appear in that competition.

MAX DOWMAN IS THE YOUNGEST... Champions League player Premier League goal scorer Premier League starter Premier League winner Arsenal scorer Arsenal starter Arsenal u18 player Arsenal u21 player Arsenal u21 scorer Premier League 2 player UEFA Youth League scorer England u17 player England u17 scorer England u19 player England u19 scorer England u21 player

By the time next summer's European Championships, which England will attempt to win for a third successive time, rolls around, rising star Dowman could well have earned the right to be this team's main man.

'We've only got three games left before the Euros [next summer],' Carsley explained.

'So it's important that he puts himself in the shop window to be on the plane.

'It's important that he keeps playing well, getting minutes, showing a really good attitude, like he has done.

'I thought he was outstanding when he came on tonight. I thought all of the subs made a real impact.

'I thought Max was unlucky not to get an assist... he made a great pass to Mikey Moore.

'He took up some really good positions, both in the 10 and out wide, he's got a big future ahead.'

His immense talent was one reason why Arsenal sent Ethan Nwaneri, who Dowman played alongside for part of his cameo, to Marseille on loan, and then similarly to Borussia Dortmund, eager not to block the 16-year-old's pathway.

Carsley knows the diamond he has on his hands and will want to take great care in helping polish a player that this crowd, this England team and this management group know has genuine world class potential.

THE REDEMPTION ARC

Speaking of Nwaneri, this felt like a big camp for him. A big camp in the sense that he's falling down the pecking order at Dortmund and is back with a manager that has been so vital in his development.

Nwaneri was part of that 2025 group that won the Euros in front of Thomas Tuchel and he'll have seen the likes of Elliot Anderson and Alex Scott kick on to get to the seniors.

As previously mentioned, Nwaneri was moved out of the way by Arsenal to aid Dowman's development, not an easy pill for a player as talented as he is to stomach when his own development journey is at such a critical juncture given he is, to the surprise of many, still only 19.

'I think we have to remember his age as well,' Carsley added when asked about Nwaneri by Daily Mail Sport.

'He's very young is Ethan and he's another one that we've got a lot of hope for. He's got a lot of potential.'

Ethan Nwaneri was pushed to the side at Arsenal to benefit Dowman but England is different

Lee Carsley has been a crucial figure in the development of Nwaneri and this camp was timely

It was telling that even when Dowman came on, even with the groundswell of excitement at his introduction, it was Carsley's call to keep Nwaneri in his preferred No 10 position with Dowman slotting in on the right.

Nwaneri has only started four games on loan at Dortmund this season and has not managed a single start in the Champions League.

His close control, his quick burst over five yards and the fluidity of his movement was a timely reminder that yes, Dowman is the rising star everyone came out to see, but Nwaneri won't get pushed to the side again without a fight.

THE RISING STAR

Amario Cozier-Duberry is a name not all will be familiar with but come next summer, with the Euros in his sights and promotion to the Premier League on the agenda with Middlesbrough, that could all be about to change.

The 21-year-old has had to be very patient, waiting until last month to make his debut at this level after years of finding himself overlooked.

Here, in what was just his third Under-21 appearance, he showed over the course of 61 minutes why the days of being looked past should be over.

One of the big frustrations in the FA right now at Under-21 level is the lack of touchline wingers. Rio Ngumoha, still only 18, has never been capped at the level and has instead been catapulted into the first team, while many, like Ethan Nwaneri, prefer playing inside.

'The more we can get our wide players one v one the better,' Carsley said. 'I think sometimes we leave them isolated and the opposition are able to double up on them.

Amario Cozier-Duberry is not a household name at international level but his talent is immense

'It's important that our game plan can't just be to get the ball wide and hope for the best.'

Dowman, on in place of Cozier-Duberry is a 10, rather than a right winger which is where he came on, and so a player like Cozier-Duberry, who is on loan at Middlesbrough from Brighton & Hove Albion, is worth his weight in gold.

Here in Bristol he was routinely drawing two defenders and at times three; Portugal knew full well how a quick flip-flap of the ball, or one clipped pass over the top, was enough for the Englishman to take the top off the back-line.

His loan at Bolton Wanderers last season complicated an international journey that has seen him play at Under-16, Under-17, Under-18, Under-19 and Under-20 level, but that's all in the past.

England need a genuine, pacy threat out wide if they are to win a third straight Euros. Cozier-Duberry showed here exactly why he should be it.

Sports.title: Antoine Dupont is still France's Captain Fantastic as skipper spearheads famous victory for Les Bleus over South Africa and mischief-making Rassie Erasmus
Sports.content:
Antoine Dupont masterminded a famous French victory over double world champions South Africa and in the process hurt England’s Nations Championship hopes.

Fabien Galthie’s Les Bleus defied a catastrophic injury list of a mammoth 25 players to get revenge on the Springboks for their 2023 World Cup quarter-final defeat.

Captain fantastic and star man Dupont led France in totemic fashion in what was a game for the ages, the final result not helping England’s chances of topping the northern pool.

Dupont was named to start as an emergency No 10. As if things weren’t bad enough for Les Bleus already, they lost star hooker Julien Marchand in the warm-up. Dupont wore No 10, but played at scrum-half.

Maxime Lucu, meanwhile, was named No 9, but was at fly-half. Rassie Erasmus was up to his old tricks. He changed South Africa’s whole starting front row pre-game. A yellow card for Springbok lock Lood de Jager – sent off in this game last year – allowed Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang and Theo Attissogbe to put the hosts 14-0 up.

Jan-Hendrik Wessels’ close-range effort got South Africa on the board, but Louis Bielle-Biarrey made it three for the French. Erasmus responded by bringing on his front row which had been due to start.

France captain Antoine Dupont was on typically blazing form to lead France to an all-important victory against South Africa

The Springboks' head coach Rassie Erasmus took the opportunity to try and outfox Les Bleus with his late selections - but the plan failed

Lucu then saw yellow, but Kurt Lee-Arendse’s attempt at narrowing the South African deficit was ruled out for him being offside. Springbok No 8 Jasper Wiese was initially sin binned for a dangerous tackle before the incident was upgraded to a 20-minute red card.

Grandidier-Nkanang then became the fourth player to see yellow, Cobus Reinach getting South Africa on the comeback trail. Under relentless Springbok scrum pressure and after being warned for poor discipline, France were fortunate not to receive a third yellow.

But after holding their opponents up over the line, Lucu missed with a long-range penalty. Eventually, Italian referee Andrea Piardi had seen enough at the scrum and sent French prop Regis Montagne for a 10-minute break. Malcolm Marx then made it three tries each, but Manie Libbok’s missed kick meant France hung on and jumped for joy at the final whistle.

Sports.title: Kevin De Bruyne to leave Napoli 'the sooner the better', his wife announces: Man City legend, 35, desperate to quit his 'not nice existence' after rows with team-mates, bosses and fan issues
Sports.content:
Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles in Naples and desire to move back home to Belgium one day. De Bruyne, 35, joined Napoli in the summer of 2025 after leaving Manchester City following a legendary ten-year spell. But things haven't gone to plan in Italy, with De Bruyne struggling for fitness in his first season, while he also clashed with former boss Antonio Conte. The situation hasn't improved much this time around under Max Allegri as Napoli currently sit 10th in Serie A, and reports broke earlier this season that the Belgian midfielder was involved in a dressing room bust-up with team-mates. And De Bruyne's wife Michele, who he married in 2017, reflected on the turbulence in an interview with Belgian magazine NINA back in September. 'Of course, we think about the future together,' he said. 'And increasingly often, we say to each other: "We are going to live here in Limburg. The sooner we get here, the better".' Kevin De Bruyne's wife Michelle has opened up on her family's struggles living in Naples De Bruyne moved to Napoli in the summer of 2025 after a glittering 10 years at Manchester City Limburg is a province in Belgium, and although Michelle insisted that she thought Naples was a beautiful place to live with great weather and food, she spoke about the toll that life in Italy has had on her partner and their three children, Mason, Rome and Suri. 'Kevin leads a very restricted life in Napoli,' she added. 'It's not much fun for him. Besides, we can't do anything together as a family in the city. That's the other side of the coin, isn't it? 'In Manchester, it was different. Where we lived, people had seen us so often that it wasn’t special anymore. We could walk out the door there without a single photo being taken. In Naples, that is impossible.' She later added: 'At a certain point, football is no longer the priority. You have achieved everything, done everything. Why would you then turn your children’s lives upside down?' De Bruyne, who is one of the highest paid players in Italy, signed a two-year contract when he arrived at Napoli but it wasn't certain that he would make it into the second part of that deal in the summer. Reflecting on his first year ahead of the World Cup, De Bruyne insisted he was 'happy' that Conte had departed. 'Obviously it was difficult for me because Conte has a very different vision of football to mine,' De Bruyne said. 'In truth, I never had the opportunity to play in my preferred position. In any case, I always tried to give my all for the team. We played very defensively. If you try to win every game by a one-goal margin with a 4-5-1 formation, you play a certain type of football. De Bruyne signed a two-year deal at Napoli and is unlikely to extend his time in Italy 'At the start of the season, we sat back even deeper. Our centre-forward scored just 10 goals, so you know the statistics are not going to be great…' He later added: 'For me, yes (I'm happy Conte has gone). As far as I am concerned, he was not obliged to stay. There were promises made last summer on the way that we would be playing, but at the end of the day not much of it happened. 'I found that a pity. Football needs to be enjoyable, and unfortunately, I found that aspect lacking. 'There’s no point beating around the bush, we have different visions of football. I never got to play in my position under Conte.'
