While humanitarian groups and celebrities have condemned attacks on Nigerian Christians, reports of renewed violence in the country's Middle Belt and concerns about the political fallout from the U.S. midterm elections have raised concerns about the future of religious-freedom efforts.

Advocates question whether the violence will subside and hope for more attention to the crisis.

"Things have gotten worse," Stephen Osemwegie, president and founder of Save Nigeria Group USA, a nonprofit focused on the welfare of Nigerians in America and around the world, told Fox News Digital. "So as far as the scale, yes, people are still getting killed, but it's not making the news because the U.S. is a bit distracted."

He said millions of people remain displaced, churches continue to be vandalized and destroyed, and parishioners are being killed while the war in Iran and the recent midterm elections have dominated U.S. headlines.

BISHOP ROBERT BARRON: THE WAR ON CHRISTIANS IS REAL AND THE WORLD CAN NO LONGER STAY SILENT

While religious and communal strife has existed for decades, the violent conflict involving Islamist insurgencies began around 2009. Since then, the United Nations and Armed Conflict & Location Data Project (ACLED), which monitors conflict and protest, reports that violence across Nigeria has claimed upwards of 53,000+ lives across communities. Advocacy and human rights groups like Intersociety and Open Doors report that over 50,000 to 62,000 Christians have been killed since 2009.

Beyond humanitarian organizations, Christian leaders and church groups, celebrities such as rapper Nicki Minaj and actress Patricia Heaton have repeatedly addressed the crisis publicly.

In October, during an X Takeover event at Tesla's Giga Texas facility, Minaj spoke about her personal connection to Nigeria and urged fellow celebrities, influencers and Christians to raise awareness of the crisis.

In November 2025, she joined U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz at an event titled "Combatting Religious Violence and the Killing of Christians in Nigeria," where she delivered remarks and thanked President Donald Trump for his efforts prioritizing the issue, combatting extremism and trying to put a stop to violence to those who want to exercise their natural right to freedom of religion or belief.

"I stand here as a proud New Yorker with a deep sense of gratitude that we live in a country where we can freely and safely worship God regardless of one's creed, background or politics. No group should ever be persecuted for practicing their religion…," Minaj said. "In Nigeria, Christians are being targeted, driven from their homes and killed. Churches have been burned, families have been torn apart, and entire communities live in fear constantly simply because of how they pray."

NIGERIAN PASTOR HIGHLIGHTED BY TRUMP SAYS HE’S NEXT AFTER MILITIA KILLS HIS RELATIVES

Likewise, Heaton has shared social media posts and news commentary about reported massacres, beheadings and mass burials. She has also criticized what she sees as insufficient media coverage and international attention.

In May, she wrote "Pray for our brothers and sisters" while re-posting a video by Jeremy Wayne Tate noting that more than 70% of all Christians killed for their faith last year were Nigerian.

US, NIGERIA STRIKE ISIS FIGHTERS AGAIN FROM THE AIR AFTER KILLING SENIOR LEADER

Fox News Digital reached out to both Minaj and Heaton for additional comment.

Violence stemming from clashes and attacks by radical Islamist groups, including Boko Haram and Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP), as well as Fulani ethnic militias, has intensified since the 2010s. Attacks have increasingly extended into Nigeria's Middle Belt, targeting farming and Christian communities, while the crisis exists within a broader national conflict that has affected communities across religious lines, including Muslims and others.

Organizations such as Open Doors International that monitor the crisis report that thousands of Christians have been displaced and forced into camps within the country. Meanwhile, Sahara Reporters cited an October report by Aid to the Church in Need that said more than 3.5 million people had been displaced in Nigeria.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

A recent report by the news and investigative media project Truth Nigeria questioned whether Nigerian Christian leaders are reconsidering their Washington strategy following the midterm elections. While Osemwegie credited the Trump administration for highlighting the situation and designating Nigeria as a Country of Particular Concern (CPC) — particularly through cooperation between the two countries on drone surveillance and intelligence sharing — he remains concerned about potential changes in congressional pressure, religious-freedom advocacy and calls for accountability.

Osemwegie hopes that American assistance remains because of the country's "vast experience dealing with global terror."

World.title: FAA ground stop leaves College Football teams stranded on eve of crucial Saturday showdowns
World.content:
The FAA ground stop that was issued on Friday afternoon is obviously having an effect on travel across the country, but it's also having a major impact on college football teams scheduled to play on Saturday.

The second nationwide ground stop since 9/11 could disrupt travel over the next few days as passengers wait for the FAA to allow flights to resume ahead of a busy travel weekend.

But concern is growing across college athletics for teams that have yet to depart for Saturday’s games.

MISSISSIPPI STATE’S KAMARIO TAYLOR FINALIZING A REPORTED $7.5 MILLION DEAL, IN WILD COLLEGE FOOTBALL MOVE

According to multiple sources, some of those schools who are currently looking for alternative travel include Texas, Tennessee, Ole Miss, Washington, Minnesota, Baylor, Tulane, Auburn, Arizona State, Oregon State and others.

USC has already taken off for their trip to Bloomington for a showdown with Indiana, and are currently in the air.

For instance, Texas was scheduled to depart Austin and had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge ahead of Saturday's showdown against LSU, but the FAA had issued the ground stop before they had taken off for Louisiana.

In the case of a school like Tennessee, the Vols were scheduled to depart McGee Tyson Airport in Knoxville at 4 p.m. ET, but the FAA notice was issued, and the team was not able to get into the air. How they end up getting to College Station is still to be determined at this moment, though the situation remains fluid.

Other schools across the country were lucky under the circumstances, and had already departed for their road game destination.

WEEK 8 AP TOP 25 POLL SEES BIG TEN GAIN EQUAL FOOTING ON SEC AND UNBEATEN UTAH EARN MAJOR RESPECT

Some schools also had the luxury to take buses to their game, like Alabama traveling to Nashville for its game against Vanderbilt.

This could turn out to be the case for a team like Auburn, who is scheduled to play Mississippi State on Saturday in Starkville.

But, for No. 2 Utah, the Utes were grounded in Salt Lake City before they were scheduled to take off for their matchup with Arizona on Saturday night.

Schools typically travel on Friday afternoons for Saturday games, usually holding a walkthrough at their facility before heading straight to the airport for departure.

Also, most schools will have security checkpoints actually set up at their facilities, so they can just get off the bus and board the airplane that is taking them to their destination.

This is a developing story, and we will continue to provide updates here at OutKick and Fox News.

World.title: UFC boss Dana White brushes off Democratic probe threats, recalls 'crazy 48 hours' around Trump job offer

UFC CEO Dana White dismissed concerns about a potential congressional investigation by Democrats, saying he is not worried about being targeted over his close ties to President Donald Trump.

In a preview of "My View with Lara Trump," set to air in full on Saturday at 9 p.m. ET, White said he expects Democrats to go after him.

"Well, I mean, we kind of expected that," White said when asked by Fox News host Lara Trump if he was worried about being targeted by Democrats.

BERNIE SANDERS WARNS DEMOCRATS NOT TO SPEND ALL THEIR TIME INVESTIGATING TRUMP

"If you didn't do anything illegal or anything wrong, I don't know why you'd have to be worried. I've never done anything in the political world that would be illegal, where anybody should come after me or anything that we have to hide. I expect it, but no, I'm not worried about it."

The exchange comes as Democrats prepare their oversight agenda following the Nov. 3 midterms. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, recently warned Trump administration officials and allies to "lawyer up" ahead of potential investigations.

White has been an outspoken supporter of President Trump and joined him in the White House briefing room Monday, where he addressed reporters. During the interview, White described the experience as "incredible."

JACKSON THOMPSON: DANA WHITE SAYS HE'LL MEET WITH TRUMP AMID CLAIM OF WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY JOB OFFER

"No, it was incredible. What an amazing experience. Literally, when I was pulling in the gates of the White House, his assistant called and said, ‘Hey, we're going to take you right down to the press room. He wants you in the house,’" White said.

"This is crazy. It was a very unique and crazy 48 hours for me."

President Trump posted Nov. 7 on Truth Social that he had offered White the White House press secretary position following Katie Zacharia's departure, prompting some questions.

"I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States," the commander in chief wrote in the post. "Dana, please take the job!"

TRUMP'S NEW PRESS SECRETARY OUT OF THE JOB JUST DAYS AFTER ROCKY DEBUT

TRUMP CLOSING IN ON NEW PRESS SECRETARY AS ADMINISTRATION OFFICIALS PUSH FOR PICK WHO COULD BREAK THE MOLD

Both President Trump and White addressed the post during Monday's briefing, and the president explained he was only joking.

"We were having a very bad press day, and I said, 'I don't know why I thought of his name.' He's been my friend for a long time. I said, 'You know, I think I'm going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,'" President Trump told reporters.

"I said it to a group of the press, and that was it. I was sort of kidding, and then they wrote the story as though I wasn't kidding."

"I have zero political aspirations," White said. "I was at a fight for Zuffa Boxing in London when he called me and told me that he had done this, and the last 24 hours of my life have been insane."

White’s ties to President Trump have drawn attention in recent years, with White speaking at the past three Republican National Conventions. World.title: Everyone accounted for after tanker collides with a New Orleans riverboat
World.content:
A large tanker ship struck a riverboat with more than 100 passengers in New Orleans on Friday, capsizing the cruise vessel and prompting a major rescue effort in the Mississippi River.

The American Heritage ship, managed by American Cruise Lines, was T-boned by the tanker while docked near the French Quarter, a spokesperson said in a statement.

Thirty-two passengers were hospitalized in the collision, though none of those injuries were critical, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno told reporters.

All of the passengers had been accounted for, she said.

Moreno called that fact “a miracle on the Mississippi.”

The cause of the crash was unclear and remained under investigation, Moreno said.

The U.S. Coast Guard and National Transportation Safety Board will conduct that investigation. The transportation officials were delayed in making their way to the Crescent City because of the ground stop at airports across the nation, officials said.

World.title: Trump administration delays Medicaid work requirements by six months
World.content:
The federal government on Friday announced a six-month delay in enforcing a Medicaid work requirement — a central provision in President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill” that experts said would lead millions of Americans to lose health coverage.

The requirement still technically starts on Jan. 1, but under new guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, states that choose not to enforce it won’t be held accountable until at least July 1.

The move is a striking turn for an administration that has spent months defending the policy against criticism from state officials and healthcare advocates who warned that the rollout was moving too quickly and that people who should be eligible for Medicaid would lose coverage because of the additional red tape and paperwork.

CMS called the six-month window a “hold harmless” period, and the delay is optional. States that choose to take advantage of this period will still start checking on Jan. 1 whether Medicaid enrollees are working, volunteering or in school or whether they qualify for an exemption. But until July, no one in those states will lose coverage for failing to meet the requirements.

“States have made real progress, and they’ve been clear with us about what it takes to get this right for beneficiaries — at scale and for the long term,” said Dan Brillman, who oversees Medicaid at CMS.

The White House declined to comment.

00:00 00:00 How Democrats intend to deliver on their big campaign promises 03:12

Some states have already moved forward with implementing the work requirements. In Nebraska, which launched the work requirements May 1, over 1,000 people have lost coverage or been denied benefits because of the new rules, according to state figures through August.

The Medicaid work requirement was a cornerstone of Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” a massive tax and spending package that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy through tax breaks while slashing the social safety net for vulnerable Americans. Millions of Americans are expected to lose health coverage and food assistance as a result of the law, the signature domestic legislation of Trump’s second term.

The law requires many able-bodied adults under the age of 65 to prove they work, volunteer or attend school at least 80 hours a month to keep Medicaid, which provides health coverage for low-income and disabled Americans. The Trump administration argues the requirement and other provisions in the law encourage work, reduce waste and protect government benefit programs for those who need them.

The Congressional Budget Office estimated the work requirements alone would leave 5.3 million more people uninsured by 2034 and would save the federal government $317 billion, part of nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts in the law.

Pressure on the administration to delay the requirement had been building for months. Five Democratic governors last month asked Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to postpone the implementation, saying that state agencies weren’t ready. And a federal judge last month blocked the Trump administration from enforcing a portion of the requirement related to medically frail people, saying it could lead some to wrongly lose coverage.

The delay comes a little more than a week after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress on a promise to reverse the GOP’s cuts to healthcare and food assistance.

“Millions of people’s health care is at risk because of the Republican reconciliation law’s work requirement, as states scramble to implement on a rushed timeline & respond to shifting federal requirements,” Sarah Lueck, vice president for health policy at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, said in a post on X. “Today’s news lets states delay the harm.”

World.title: U.S. measles deaths rise to 10 after new reports in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin
World.content:
Total measles deaths in the United States this year rose to 10 on Friday, a grim milestone in an outbreak that has seen a record number of infections and prompted state and local health departments to ramp up vaccination efforts.

Pennsylvania and Wisconsin each reported a new measles-associated death on Friday. The Wisconsin Health Department said a child had died, but declined to release more information, citing the family’s privacy. The Pennsylvania Health Department said its latest death was an unvaccinated resident of Montour County who had tested positive for measles.

The virus, the most contagious known to humans, can lead to deadly complications, like pneumonia or swelling of the brain, in unvaccinated people.

So far this year, Pennsylvania has reported seven measles-associated deaths, Wisconsin has reported two and New York has reported one. Prior to those deaths, none of the states had seen a measles death in more than 30 years.

As of Thursday, around 5,400 measles cases have been recorded in the U.S. — more than double last year’s count and the highest since 1991. Public health experts attribute the outbreak to a sharp decline in measles vaccination rates coupled with a global resurgence of the virus.

Measles was declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000, meaning it was no longer continuously spreading, though there can be occasional outbreaks. The country now seems poised to lose that designation: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a group within the World Health Organization, met this week to determine whether the U.S. can still be considered measles-free. Their decision is expected to be announced on Tuesday.

At the center of PAHO’s deliberations is whether there has been ongoing transmission in the U.S. for a full year. Canada lost its elimination status last year after the agency determined that the virus had been spreading there for at least 12 months.

Measles is already spreading widely enough in the U.S. to threaten infants who aren’t eligible for their first shot. At least four deaths this year were in babies too young to be vaccinated. In response to their outbreaks, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin are recommending an early dose for infants ages 6 to 11 months who live in areas with high case counts.

The first dose is usually given around a child’s first birthday and the second at 4 to 6 years. Two doses are 97% effective.

Nationwide, 75% of counties and jurisdictions with measles vaccine data fall below the 95% vaccination rate needed to prevent outbreaks, according to an NBC News investigation.

The share of kindergartners who had been vaccinated for measles fell from 95% during the 2019-20 school year to 92% during the 2025-26 school year.

World.title: Rep. Lauren Boebert, conservative firebrand from Colorado, loses her race for re-election
World.content:
Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., a conservative firebrand who was caught up in several headline-grabbing controversies during her six years in Congress, has been defeated by Democratic challenger Eileen Laubacher, NBC News projects.

Laubacher is a retired Navy rear admiral and Afghanistan war veteran who served on the National Security Council in the Biden administration.

“Integrity matters. Character matters. Truth matters, and public service should always be about what you can do for other people, not what you do for yourself,” Laubacher told supporters on election night, according to The Colorado Sun. “Those things were worth fighting for when we started.”

Boebert, who won re-election in Colorado’s 3rd District by just 546 votes in 2022, shifted to the much redder 4th Congressional District in 2024 and won re-election more easily.

But that shift proved no match for the anti-Trump blue tsunami that washed over the country in these midterm elections, sweeping her and many other GOP incumbents out of office.

“There was a lot of money dumped on my head,” Boebert said after the election, while also blaming the Senate for failing to pass many House-approved Republican bills.

Eileen Laubacher thanks her supporters on election night. Hyoung Chang / Denver Post via Getty

Before her political career, Boebert was a gun-rights activist and owned Shooters Grill in Rifle, Colorado. She upset Rep. Scott Tipton, R-Colo., in the GOP primary in 2020 and became a vocal defender of Donald Trump in Washington.

But their relationship soured more recently. In November 2025, Boebert was one of four Republicans who joined Democrats in signing a discharge petition to force a vote to release the Justice Department’s Jeffrey Epstein files, against Trump’s will.

When Trump vowed to unseat Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., for leading the Epstein files push, Boebert sided with Massie and campaigned with him this May. Trump lashed out, calling her “dumb” and “weak-minded,” and threatened to rescind his endorsement of her, though he never did.

Boebert was known on Capitol Hill more for her controversies and clashes with fellow lawmakers than for legislative savvy.

In 2021, she apologized after video emerged of her suggesting that fellow Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., was mistaken for a terrorist in an elevator both were riding in the Capitol. Omar said Boebert’s description of the two riding an elevator never happened.

At the State of the Union address in 2022, Boebert and then-Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, R-Ga., stood up and heckled President Joe Biden throughout his speech, including trying to start a “build the wall” chant. The two conservative women later had a very public falling-out, with Greene calling her colleague “a little b----” on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert and her date were escorted out of a performance of the “Beetlejuice” musical in Denver. They were alleged to have been vaping, taking photos and engaging in other disruptive behavior.

World.title: As AI looms over Hollywood, Oscar hopefuls make the case for human craft
World.content:
Welcome back to ON THE LOT.

This week, we’re looking at Universal’s “Odyssey” Oscar push, Skydance’s big week and Sofia Franklyn’s “Daddy Issues.”

CRAFTY CAMPAIGNING

Christopher Nolan on stage during the special screening of "The Odyssey" in Los Angeles, on Tuesday. Matt Winkelmeyer / Getty for Universal Pictures

As awards season heats up, senior Hollywood reporter Rebecca Keegan delivers a dispatch from a massive special event for “The Odyssey” on the Universal lot this week.

When Willie Burton needed to capture the sounds of creaking oars and lapping waves for the many seafaring scenes in “The Odyssey,” the veteran sound mixer planted microphones around a 115-foot wooden Viking ship, grabbed his gear and raincoat, and climbed into the hold.

And before shooting aboard the ship, the Swedish captain issued a warning to the actors and production workers sailing with his crew.

“He said that everything on this ship would kill you,” Burton said, addressing a packed theater on Tuesday at the premiere of the documentary “Behind the Scenes of The Odyssey.” “The crew said, ’No one survives the hold.’”

There are plenty of less dramatic ways to supply sound to a movie. But Burton was one of 10 craftspersons from “The Odyssey,” along with star Matt Damon and producer Emma Thomas, on hand to explain how they made an ancient Greek epic for 2026 audiences under the defiantly analog direction of Christopher Nolan.

At a moment when much of the movie industry is adopting AI tools, the awards campaign for “The Odyssey” is leaning into the film’s handcrafted nature.

But it’s not just Nolan’s old-school habits that are animating this year’s Oscars race. Directors Phil Lord and Chris Miller have also talked up their use of practical sets over green screens on “Project Hail Mary.” Actress and director Olivia Wilde has explained why she paid out of her own pocket to shoot “The Invite” on 35 mm film instead of digitally. Travis Knight, CEO of Laika, has shared how the stop-motion animation techniques in “Wildwood” are antithetical to AI, and director Denis Villeneuve has described the “artisanal” way he shot “Dune: Part III,” relying on natural light and custom-made IMAX lenses.

Awards season is always a time for touting craft and technique, but this year’s focus on handmade films has an air of wistfulness, as it comes amid the studio consolidation and cost-cutting that has made adoption of AI tools feel virtually inevitable to many in the industry.

The 75-minute “Odyssey” documentary, which arrives alongside the home entertainment release of the film on Nov. 17, highlights just how hard the $250 million movie was to make, showcasing remote locations in Italy, Greece, Morocco and Iceland.

An exhibit that accompanied the documentary premiere also highlighted the painstaking quality of the work, with some of the 5,300 handmade costumes from costume designer Ellen Mirojnick, antique swords, bows and axes used by the actors and stunt performers, and the bronze gong and ancient lyre that musicians play on composer Ludwig Göransson’s score.

As Damon says in the documentary, “I don’t know how long we’re gonna get to make movies this way.”

SKYDANCE IN THE SPOTLIGHT

ICYMI: There’s been a lot going on at Skydance. Culture and trends editor Saba Hamedy gives you a recap.

It was a whirlwind week for Skydance, marked by a major leadership shake-up and its first post-merger earnings report.

First came the ousting of DC Studios heads James Gunn and Peter Safran, who will be replaced by former Marvel Studios executive Jeremy Latcham.

Then came the earnings. Though the company has already slashed jobs, it still has to streamline costs to help pay off its more than $80 billion debt. During the call, chief David Ellison doubled down on AI and revealed the company would launch a Paramount+ and HBO Max bundle in early 2027. But investors and Wall Street analysts didn’t appear enthusiastic: Shares of the company dropped about 2% to $8.50 on Tuesday.

By Wednesday, however, corporate headlines took a backseat as Hollywood moguls and stars — including Ellison, Jeffrey Katzenberg, actress Gal Gadot, actor Vin Diesel, producer Jerry Bruckheimer and HBO chief Casey Bloys — gathered at the Beverly Wilshire Hotel to celebrate Skydance co-CEO Ynon Kreiz.

The former Mattel chief received the 2026 Humanitarian Award from the Simon Wiesenthal Center, an L.A.-based human rights organization dedicated to combating antisemitism, which recognized him for his “leadership, generosity, and commitment to helping us educate against hate and inspire people to stand up for others.”

It was the same award bestowed upon former Warner Bros. Discovery CEO David Zaslav last year, when merger speculation was top of mind for most in the ballroom.

Speaking at this year’s event, Katzenberg expressed confidence in Kreiz and Ellison as the company — which brings together the studios behind “Mission: Impossible,” “Harry Potter” and DC Studios alongside major television and streaming networks such as CBS, CNN, Paramount+ and HBO Max — enters its next chapter.

“This is a huge responsibility and one which can actually determine the very future and the vibrancy of Hollywood,” the former Dreamworks Animation CEO said. “In my opinion, David Ellison chose well when he selected Ynon and it reflects his belief in leaders who have both the expertise and the character to lead at such an important time.”

CALL HER CANDID

Sofia Franklyn and Alex Cooper. FilmMagic; GC Images via Getty

This week, culture and trends editor Saba Hamedy also binge-read Sofia Franklyn’s memoir so you didn’t have to. Here’s what to know about the tell-all.

Daddy gang, you may get a little mad at Alex Cooper after reading “Daddy Issues.” And perhaps that was part of Franklyn’s goal.

The memoir, released on Tuesday, is a tell-all from Franklyn’s side about the end of her business relationship and friendship with Cooper, who went on to helm their famous “Call Her Daddy” podcast solo.

The duo shot to viral fame in 2018, when the podcast was still under Barstool Sports. It became known for candid conversations about commonly taboo topics for women to discuss publicly, including raunchy sex stories. But the two professionally split up in 2020, news that initially shocked their listeners and led to speculation about what went down between the former besties and roomies.

Cooper’s star continued to rise — she landed lucrative Spotify and SiriusXM deals, launched her own brand, Unwell, with husband Matt Kaplan and became a household name among young Gen Z and millennial women.

Meanwhile, Franklyn launched her own podcast titled “Sofia with an F.” Behind the scenes, she was struggling with sobriety and the dissolution of her relationship with Cooper, she writes. Among the claims she makes in the book:

The book opens with a scene in which Franklyn’s book agent calls her to say she had received an angry call from Kaplan, who told her that Cooper was threatening to sue. A representative for Unwell denied the claim in a statement to The New York Times.

Cooper negotiated a $20,000 raise for herself behind Franklyn’s back while the podcast was at Barstool. She didn’t learn about this until later, when Muji — Cooper’s childhood friend who worked on the podcast before she fired him — told Franklyn, “She didn’t tell you because she didn’t want you to know she tried to get you fired.” Muji and Lauren, another one of Cooper’s childhood friends, had warned her that Cooper was quick to discard friends.

When she and Cooper were negotiating their new contracts with Barstool, they decided their goal was to stay together. They even came up with a spinoff podcast in case the negotiations fell through, titling it “The Fathers.”

These negotiations centered on the intellectual property for “Call Her Daddy,” which Barstool Sports owned and could technically continue without Franklyn or Cooper attached. But, Franklyn writes, Barstool’s Dave Portnoy called Franklyn one day to tell her that Cooper had hired her own lawyer and claimed that Franklyn had been “the one that’s been dragging this on,” and Cooper was ready to sign a new contract. “She came to me with a plan, and I needed an episode. There’s no clear favorite,” he told her, according to Franklyn’s memoir. “You could always have your own show, and we promote the s--- out of it like we did with ‘Call Her Daddy.’ I think it would be huge.”

Thus far, Cooper has not issued a public response — though she has been a little busy lately in her mom era (she and Kaplan announced the birth of their baby last month).

Portnoy, however, went on “The Toast” podcast after the book was released. He denied Franklyn’s implication that he hooked up with Cooper and told hosts Claudia and Jackie Oshry: “I have no relationship with Sofia. None. I hate her guts.”

THE DIALOGUE

“This is one of the hardest decisions I’ve ever had to make. Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I’ll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they’ve shown us over the years. But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse, and I’ve reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors.” — Roger Taylor, the founding drummer of Duran Duran, announcing his retirement in a post on the band’s Instagram page on Thursday.

“I know this sounds weird because it was so tumultuous and it was a crazy time in my life, but I look back at it as a bit of a blessing. I was in a contract negotiation with them.” — Host Chris Harrison in an interview with The Hollywood Reporter when asked about his split with ABC’s “The Bachelor” franchise.

“I’m really truly in the business of not giving Dominic advice. He’s got it. He doesn’t need any advice from me … He’s going to be amazing, and you know, I hope that I will, I think I will, get to meet him someday — and I’m very excited about that.” — Actor Daniel Radcliffe when asked by the Associated Press if he has any advice for Dominic McLaughlin, who takes on the Harry Potter role in HBO’s upcoming series.

World.title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop, stranding thousands
World.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued a rare nationwide ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The FAA and White House said the issue appeared to be caused by a "telecommunication outage."

"The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a social media post. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them."

An update to the private communications network that connects America's air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage, multiple sources told CBS News. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters in a briefing outside the White House that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."

"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."

He said flights will be able to land safely.

"We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that's going to be in the air, that's currently on the plane, the loved ones, as I said, we're going to get you on the ground and we're doing it in a safe manner," Mullin said.

Passengers wait at San Francisco International Airport during a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights on Nov. 13, 2026. Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images

Federal agencies are all working together on the situation, Mullin added.

"I don't want to say that this is a crisis, but it is because we're ... we had to do a nationwide ground stoppage," he said.

According to the flight tracking site FlightRadar24, there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began. Mullin said all airborne flights were being dealt with on a "case-by-case" basis.

The ground stop was posted to the FAA's National Airspace System Status website. Delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston, Atlanta, Miami, Pittsburgh, New York City, Los Angeles and Baltimore.

"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."

Within a short time Friday, there were more than 10,000 delays and over 2,000 cancellations listed, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.

"By order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis," the Air Traffic Control System Command Center said in its alert.

Shortly before the FAA ordered the nationwide ground stop, both major Chicago airports, O'Hare International and Midway International, were issued a ground stop because of an equipment outage.

In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.

This is a developing story. It will be updated.

World.title: Passengers rescued after tanker hit river cruise in New Orleans
World.content:
A major rescue operation took place Friday after a tanker struck a river cruise ship on the Mississippi River near the Port of New Orleans, leaving the American Heritage passenger boat on its side and largely submerged in the water.

Everyone aboard both vessels has been accounted for, officials said, and there were no fatalities reported.

The much larger tanker, identified as the Atlantic Asphalt, crashed into the paddlewheel cruise boat while it was docked at about 12:30 p.m. local time, the Port of New Orleans said. The American Heritage had docked about two hours earlier for passengers to disembark.

In a news briefing late Friday afternoon, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said 32 passengers from the cruise ship were taken to area hospitals for treatment, but none with critical injuries. No one aboard the tanker was hurt, Moreno said.

New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said two of her officers were also hospitalized during the rescue operation, but were in good condition.

There were about 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, aboard the American Heritage at the time of the collision, according to Port NOLA.

Moreno said the tanker "lost control" and crashed into the cruise ship. As passengers were disembarking from the cruise ship, it "began to sink, and then eventually toppled over and flipped," sending people into the water, the mayor said.

The American Heritage river cruise paddleboat is seen on its side after being struck by a tanker ship in the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. AP Photo/Gerald Herbert

Some people were seen in the water in life jackets or standing near the railing as the other side of the ship listed farther into the water. Nearby boats reported rescuing more than a dozen people from the water.

Emergency responders, including Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department and the U.S. Coast Guard, conducted rescue and response operations, Port NOLA said. Moreno said that along with local and federal agencies, private vessels that happened to be on the river at the time responded "as volunteers to try and get people out of the water."

Moreno described the successful rescue operation as a "miracle on the Mississippi."

One witness, Jamie Holford, told CBS News he saw the American Heritage hit the dock after the collision. He described seeing people hurrying off the boat. Then, as it rolled over, some were climbing over the railings of the boat, he said.

"It looked like something off the Titanic," he said.

Asked what the collision sounded like, Holford said, "It sounded like a war movie. Just imagine tons of steel crunching. That's what it sounded like."

U.S. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said Coast Guard investigators were on scene working to determine what caused the tanker to lose control.

"The investigation is still ongoing, there seems to be some kind of a loss of steering," Burnham told reporters. "The exact reason why, we don't know that."

The National Transportation Safety Board also said in a statement it was sending a "Go Team" to the scene Saturday to begin its own investigation into the cause.

Burnham also noted that she was working to reopen the river, which the Coast Guard had closed when the collision occurred.

"We're going to start evaluating how to reopen it as soon as possible," Burnham said.

In a Truth Social post, President Trump praised the response of the Coast Guard and other law enforcement agencies for "doing such an incredible job of rescue, and other work, having to do with the crash of the two ships in Louisiana."

The American Heritage was built in 2015 and is operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five stories and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semisolid substance that is often used for road construction and roofing, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.

World.title: SpaceX launches first-of-its-kind Starship test flight
World.content:
SpaceX launched its huge Starship rocket on the program's 15th test flight Friday, a 22-hour mission featuring planned launch pad catches of both the booster and the Starship upper stage.

The booster sent the Starship on its way to orbit as planned, but a problem of some sort prevented a return to the launch pad capture. Instead, the rocket made a splashdown off the Texas Gulf Coast and promptly burst into flames.

SpaceX managed to catch a Super Heavy booster during three previous test flights, using giant mechanical arms on the launch gantry to snag the rockets as they descended tail first on the power of three of their 33 Raptor engines. But the flight plan also includes a splashdown option if an issue crops up preventing a safe capture.

It was a disappointment for SpaceX workers who head hoped the Super Heavy-Starship rocket's 15th test flight would be the first to demonstrate full reusability in an orbit-class rocket. The company sill plans to attempt its first ever launch pad catch of a Starship upper stage Saturday at the conclusion of the mission.

Loaded with 8 million pounds of supercold liquid oxygen and methane fuel, the rocket's 236-foot-tall first stage, powered by 33 methane-burning Raptor engines, roared to life and majestically propelled the booster away from SpaceX's "Starbase" launch site on the Texas Gulf Coast at 5:47 p.m. EST.

SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launches from Starbase in Boca Chica, Texas, on Nov. 13, 2026. Ricardo Arduengo/AFP via Getty Images

Arcing away to the southeast, the Super Heavy booster propelled the rocket out of the thick lower atmosphere before falling away about two minutes and 20 seconds after liftoff.

While the 171-foot-tall Starship continued the climb to space using six Raptors of its own, the booster flipped around and fired up a set of Raptors to reverse course and head back to the launch site.

But a little more than six minutes after liftoff, flight controllers ordered a diversion to a Gulf Coast splashdown because of a technial problem. Long-range cameras captured the big booster slowly descending to the Gulf, shrouded in steam and then a fireball as residual propellants ignited.

The Starship, meanwhile, followed a sub-orbital trajectory, ensuring a safe ocean splashdown in case of problems while giving SpaceX flight controllers time to assess its health before committing to a final push to orbit.

But no issues were found and after an 18-minute coast, a single Raptor re-ignited for a short 10-second burn to push the craft into its planned orbit. Eight-and-a-half minutes after that, the first of 26 upgraded version 3 Starlink internet satellites was expected to be pushed out into space to fly on its own.

For the rest of the flight, controllers planned to closely monitor the Starship, periodically assessing its health to make sure it could be safely de-orbited in case of problems that might prevent a safe return-to-launch site capture at the same pad where it launched Friday atop the Super Heavy booster. It will be SpaceX's first attempt to get a Starship back to its pad for possible refurbishment and re-launch.

"During this prolonged coast phase, flight control teams have several options to end the mission early and return Starship to pre-cleared areas of the Pacific Ocean if needed," SpaceX said on its web page.

"These locations include early- and late-mission splashdown options around Hawaii and a mid-mission splashdown opportunity several hundred kilometers off the coast of Chile. These pre-cleared areas ... provide a safe place to land Starship if any conditions arise that may preclude the ability to perform a safe reentry."

An hour after a final "return check" Saturday, a single Raptor is expected to fire at 3:21 p.m. to lower the far side of the Starship's orbit deep into the atmosphere for a 56-minute belly-first re-entry and return to the Texas Gulf Coast.

"During reentry, Starship can alter its flight path by moving its four control flaps," the company said. "This will permit Starship to maintain a safe and known trajectory while guiding itself with high precision control toward Starbase."

As it descends, the Starship will carry out "a series of small turns in its trajectory to intentionally fly over sparsely populated areas of northern Mexico and southern Texas."

"As Starship approaches Starbase from the west, the vehicle will weave its way around the major cities in the Rio Grande Valley, passing to the north of South Padre Island and out over the Gulf ... as it makes its final turn south towards Starbase."

Nearing the launch pad, the 171-foot-tall Starship will first three Raptors to flip upright. Once the maneuver is complete, one Raptor will be shut down as the rocket descends between the gantry's mechanical arms. Finally, with just one engine firing to slow the rocket to a near stop, the mechanical arms will move in to snag the spacecraft.

But all of that depends on a problem-free descent. If any problems develop that might lead to an uncontrolled landing, flight controllers can ensure a vehicle breakup before it has any chance to reach a populated area.

"During reentry, flight controllers will have several options to end the reentry early and safely by intentionally tumbling Starship to ensure that it breaks up in the atmosphere before reaching land," SpaceX said.

"There is also a late-reentry option to send Starship into the Gulf ... if any of its systems or the tower itself encounter an issue after reentry that would preclude a safe catch at Starbase."

SpaceX calls development of a fully reusable rocket "the holy grail of rocketry," opening the door to airplane-like cadence where a vehicle flies again rapidly.

NASA is counting on a variant of the Starship to carry Artemis astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028. But the rocket's development has taken longer than initially expected and the space agency is now hedging its bets, saying it's open to using Blue Origin's Blue Moon Mark 2 lander depending on which spacecraft is ready.

World.title: GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
World.content:
GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election

toggle caption i Lynne Sladky/AP

Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.

Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.

On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.

The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.

Sponsor Message

In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.

Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.

It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation.

The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.

Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.

"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.

The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.

Sponsor Message

A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.

While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.

Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

World.title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
World.content:
FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports

toggle caption i Bruce Bennett/Getty Images

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which is currently under investigation, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a "temporary telecommunications outage."

"Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the post reads.

The outage hasn't been linked to a threat or attack, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin told reporters at the White House. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."

Sponsor Message

As of 6 p.m. EST, more than 10,000 flights had been delayed Friday and 2,500 had been canceled in the U.S., according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The turmoil comes on the heels of nearly 7,000 flight delays on Thursday.

toggle caption i Tom Brenner/AP

The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The telecommunication issue doesn't extend to the entire U.S., Mullin said. Without naming the regions in question, he stated, "there's two areas inside the United States that are still able to communicate just fine."

Mullin also said that other countries' aviation systems don't seem to be affected by the FAA outage.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

Sponsor Message

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

Passengers stranded

The nationwide ground stop has caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancelations during the holiday season.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.

"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said.

Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she's thinking about how soon she can make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.

"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.

At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Giliann Karon was on board a plane when the nationwide ground stop was ordered. Karon said she had already experienced a flight delay the day before due to bad weather in New York City, where she is heading.

"It's just kind of like, 'Oh, of course this is happening,'" she said.

This is a developing story.

Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

World.title: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
World.content:
What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are

toggle caption i Osamah Abdulrahman/AP

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.

On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded," an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."

Sponsor Message

That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.

Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.

Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.

With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.

Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in the country's capital of Abu Dhabi this week that the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."

Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.

Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists

Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.

Sponsor Message

The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.

The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.

More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate

The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.

This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.

The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.

On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.

Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.

"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.

There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.

One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.

Sponsor Message

Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate," with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.

War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries

Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being canceled.

As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.

The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.

Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges

Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.

"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.

These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.

Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd."

There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."

It's another indication of the gridlock.

Sponsor Message

NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

World.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
World.content:
The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue

toggle caption i Mario Tama/Getty Images

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

Sponsor Message

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

toggle caption i Win McNamee/Getty Images

But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

Sponsor Message

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."

Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.

In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Looming criminal proceedings and subpoenas to election officials

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.

"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Sponsor Message

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."

What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.

The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Sponsor Message

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."

Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."

Inflated and inaccurate lists

Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.

The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.

Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.

Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."

Sponsor Message

Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.

For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.

And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.
