World.title: Stelco recalling 175 laid-off workers at Hamilton steel plant
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hamilton steelmaker Stelco is recalling its 175 workers that had been laid off earlier this fall.

Stelco made the announcement in a news release on Friday, saying that the workers would be back in the factory by Dec. 1. The company also indicated that it would retroactively pay the workers for the time they were laid off.

The American parent company, Cleveland-Cliffs, announced in September that it planned to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idled certain steel production at Stelco.

Ron Wells, president of the United Steelworkers Local 1005, told CBC News Network that Friday's announcement was a "pretty good victory."

WATCH | Joly speaks with Power & Politics: Stelco recalls 175 workers as Ottawa works to find solution for Stellantis plant | Duration closed caption 13:03 Stelco announced it would bring its Hamilton workers back on Dec. 1. It's a win for the government as it tries to prevent Stellantis from selling an auto plant in Brampton, Ont. Power & Politics speaks with Industry Minister Mélanie Joly.

"They're forced to live up to their commitments and we're happy with that," Wells told host Andrew Nichols.

The federal government said that any move to lay off workers would violate "binding commitments" Cleveland-Cliffs made when it bought Stelco in 2024.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly wrote to the Ohio-based company in mid-October, demanding that it reverse the layoffs or face possible legal action.

Cleveland-Cliffs originally cited U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as its reasons for the planned layoffs. Stelco's Friday statement also cited those issues, but said the company had been granted reassurances from its customers.

"Our customers have committed to support our Hamilton finishing operations despite the lack of response from the federal government to address the shortfalls in their tariff-response program and the continued flood of offshore imports of galvanized products that have eroded our domestic market," the statement said.

WATCH | Joly on the future of Stelco: Ottawa plans to force sale of Stelco if Cleveland-Cliffs doesn't respond by end of day: Joly | Duration closed caption 1:17 Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on Friday that she plans to ask a court to order U.S. steel company Cleveland-Cliffs to sell Ontario-based Stelco if she doesn't hear from them by the end of day. She said the federal government has this power because Cleveland-Cliffs is in breach of the Investment Canada Act. Joly made the comments before Stelco announced it would recall 175 laid-off workers on Dec. 1.

The government says Cleveland-Cliffs agreed to keep the number of unionized employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 in its original purchase agreement.

Just prior to Stelco's announcement, Joly said she would be seeking a court order to force Cleveland-Cliffs to sell the Hamilton plant if she didn't hear from the company by the end of the day.

Following the announcement, Joly told CBC's Power & Politics that the workers being called back is a "huge win." The minister said the government wouldn't be pursuing legal action once the company gives the government official notice that the workers are coming back.

"I want to make sure that I see the CEO of Cleveland-Cliffs's signature on a paper," Joly said.

"Once that's the case, then we will be able to move on and make sure that Stelco is well anchored."

Wells gave credit to the workers, union and government for forcing the company's hand.

"Our laid-off members, they deserve credit because they pressured the union, the union pressured the government and the government enforced the Canada Investment Act. So good for Canada," the union leader said.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told Power & Politics late last month that he originally bought the Hamilton plant to stop it undercutting his U.S. business.

"I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company," Goncalves told host David Cochrane.

Joly said Goncalves's comments were a "shocking admission" and asked the competition bureau to investigate whether Cleveland-Cliffs had run afoul of the Competition Act.

World.title: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski testifies he was beaten, tortured during alleged kidnapping
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Warning: This story contains distressing details about torture and graphic images

Self-described "Crypto King" Aiden Pleterski described being beaten with a gun and tortured with knives and a lighter in the back of a truck as he began his testimony at the trial of his alleged kidnappers Friday in Toronto.

"[I was] very scared, scared I'm going to die, scared for my life, in survival mode essentially," Pleterski told the Ontario Superior Court about how he felt at the time.

The Crown played a 13-second video for the jury, which showed Pleterski on his knees begging for his life while a man pointed a gun at him and counted down from three.

Before reaching one, the man appears to fire the gun beside Pleterski's head.

"It didn't hit me, but I know it was very loud and there was a constant ringing in my left ear," Pleterski testified. "When he shot the firearm I didn't know if I was shot or not."

Akil Heywood, Alfredo Paladino and Rakeem Henry are all charged with kidnapping and extorting Pleterski over the course of three days in early December 2022.

WATCH | Video from Pleterski's alleged kidnapping: 'Crypto King' Aiden Pleterski begs for his life during kidnapping | Duration closed caption 0:14

Paladino and Henry are also charged with firearms offences, the aggravated assault of Pleterski, assaulting him with a weapon, and assault causing bodily harm over that same period. All three men have pleaded not guilty.

Pleterski, 27, was convicted of fraud last month in connection with more than $30 million he took from investors to trade on their behalf, but he's yet to be sentenced.

He told the court that Heywood invested between $300,000 and $400,000 and allegedly started threatening him in texts and phone calls about getting that money back in the beginning to the middle of 2022.

Pleterski also testified that Heywood was appointed as one of the five creditor inspectors tasked with overseeing his bankruptcy proceeding.

'Driving force'

In its opening statement, the Crown alleged Heywood was the "driving force" behind the plan to kidnap Pleterski and that evidence would show another man — who is not part of the trial — was the lead kidnapper and that Paladino and Henry carried it out alongside him.

Pleterski identified Heywood, Paladino and Henry in the courtroom Friday as Crown prosecutor Julia De Vuono walked him through the events leading to the alleged kidnapping and what Pleterski said happened to him during it.

From left to right, Alfredo Paladino, Akil Heywood and Rakeem Henry are accused of kidnapping and extorting Pleterski in December 2022. (Evan Mitsui/CBC, Instagram/atlanticmastoronto)

Pleterski described how he met a man he was introduced to as "Slime" a couple of weeks before the alleged kidnapping who said he wanted help converting cryptocurrency into cash. The pair began communicating and organized a meeting at the Ritz Carlton hotel in downtown Toronto in late 2022, according to Pleterski.

He testified that "Slime" attended the meeting with two other men, including one he later pointed out as Henry in the courtroom.

A couple of days later, on Dec. 5, Pleterski said he received a message from "Slime" asking to meet up about the cryptocurrency. Pleterski testified "Slime" picked him up in downtown Toronto in a Dodge Ram but this time, after he got in the backseat, "Slime" got in beside him and pulled out a gun.

He said Henry was on the other side of him in the backseat and also had a pistol on his lap. Pleterski identified Paladino as the driver.

Sandeep Gupta, Pleterski's former landlord, testified on Tuesday and Thursday at the trial of three men accused of kidnapping the self-described 'Crypto King.' (Pam Davies/CBC)

Pleterski said he was zip-tied and reusable garbage bags were put over his head at various points. He testified the truck got on the Gardiner Expressway and that, while in transit, "Slime" made a call.

"I knew instantly it was AK, or Akil Heywood," said Pleterski, about hearing the voice on the phone, which he testified was on speaker.

Pleterski testified that Heywood said "Where the F is my money, pussy?" and told him: "You're either going to pay with your money or you're going to pay with your life."

From there Pleterski explained how he told the kidnappers that his former landlord Sandeep Gupta was "hiding a bunch of assets, [I] just need to call him." Although in court, Pleterski said that was not true.

On Tuesday, the jury heard audio of a 911 call Gupta made during a phone call with Pleterski. Pleterski testified "Slime" was instructing him on what to say during that call, including telling him he needed $2-3 million from Gupta.

The Crown asked Pleterski why he didn't tell Gupta he was kidnapped.

"If I told him on the phone that I was kidnapped, I was scared that they would kill me," he replied.

Pleterski wasn't sure whether the phone call with Gupta happened before or after he was taken to a field, where the video of him on his knees was allegedly taken.

In that video, after the gun appears to be fired, Pleterski says "Sandeep has it all."

Gupta testified at the trial Tuesday and Thursday and denied any involvement in Pleterski's Ponzi scheme and denied hiding any money or assets for him.

Pleterski's testimony continued Friday afternoon.

World.title: 'I sincerely apologize': Blue Jays outfielder Santander apologizes days after anti-Muslim social media posts
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Toronto Blue Jays outfielder Anthony Santander apologized Friday for sharing anti-Muslim social media posts, saying the content caused hurt and fell short of his own convictions.

In a statement on Instagram, Santander said reflection and conversations with people he trusts made him recognize he should have been more thoughtful about what he shared and the responsibility that comes with having a public voice.

He expressed respect for the Muslim community and pledged to avoid sharing content that promotes hate.

Santander shared the posts on Nov. 4 and deleted them the next morning. They included a video of a Christian preacher disparaging Muslims and another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the United States after Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the Senate in Michigan.

His apology came a day after Blue Jays president and chief executive officer Mark Shapiro apologized to the Muslim community and fans following a meeting with community leaders, and after general manager Ross Atkins asked Santander to publicly address the controversy.

The 32-year-old Venezuelan signed a five-year, $92.5-million US contract with Toronto in January 2025 but missed the entire 2026 big-league season because of injuries. It remains unclear whether the team will discipline him over the posts.

World.title: COVID-19 school disruptions still impacting students today, learning loss report finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian students are still recovering from the pandemic's massive upset to their schooling, with evidence of declining achievement — particularly in math — across jurisdictions, according to a new report.

The report, released Thursday by the Royal Society of Canada, the Canadian Commission for UNESCO and the University of Ottawa, also notes a discrepancy between standardized test scores and the grades kids receive in class

It takes an in-depth look at pandemic learning loss and recovery by examining students' academic results in language arts and mathematics before, during and after COVID-19. Nearly three dozen researchers parsed data from Canadian ministries of education, save Manitoba and Nunavut, which didn't participate.

They analyzed the results of standardized tests, as well as teacher-assigned grades across different grades and — depending on the jurisdiction — considered factors like gender and location (for instance, rural and remote communities versus urban ones).

The pandemic is "going to influence learning for the next few decades and that's not exaggeration," said Tracy Vaillancourt, chair of the report and a professor of education at the University of Ottawa.

"These effects are going to be felt for generations to come."

Findings differed across regions, student populations and grades — not surprising given the varying local contexts across jurisdictions, including how each assesses learning and the patchwork of pandemic approaches taken by each province or territory. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

The report is divided by studies of individual provinces and territories, with the findings differing across regions, student populations and grades, said Vaillancourt, who's also the Canada Research Chair in youth mental health and violence prevention.

That's not surprising given the varying local contexts of each jurisdiction, including how each assesses learning, coupled with the patchwork of pandemic responses taken: from how long each closed schools and opted for remote learning to physical distancing in classrooms to recovery efforts implemented afterwards.

Yet across each of the report's individual provincial and territorial studies, there are some broader commonalities, she said:

Declines in standardized test results, notably in math . In particular, an emerging gender gap with declining math achievement for girls in several regions and girls' math scores not recovering as quickly as boys have.

. In particular, an emerging gender gap with declining math achievement for girls in several regions and girls' math scores not recovering as quickly as boys have. A greater impact on younger students , who saw the very building blocks of their foundational knowledge affected — like learning what numbers mean or how to read — versus older students with the basics already established.

, who saw the very building blocks of their foundational knowledge affected — like learning what numbers mean or how to read — versus older students with the basics already established. A discrepancy between achievement measured by standardized tests, where scores have fallen, versus teacher-administered grades, which rose.

Grade inflation is real, says Vaillancourt, but "this isn't a knock on teachers at all. They were in a really difficult situation" given the high stress of that time.

Teacher grades also tend to incorporate learning progress, she said. High-stakes tests capture a snapshot of student knowledge during one window of time.

During the pandemic, many school systems dropped exams (which never returned in some cases) and asked teachers to weigh assignments differently. Some teachers were directed to reduce content being covered amid the glut of obstacles facing educators and learners alike, ranging from inconsistent or unavailable internet to quarantines to toggling between in-person and online learning.

Researchers also found the pandemic had mixed impacts on reading and writing scores, and that students in some rural, remote and northern communities saw greater declines in overall achievement — and are taking longer to recover — than urban peers.

Taking action

The report lands more than three years after COVID-19 was downgraded from global emergency status. Its authors make several recommendations to governments, starting with support for standardized testing in order to establish reliable, comparable benchmarks of student achievement over time.

In a time of emergency, "we've got to be compassionate about how kids are faring … but we should also, if possible, monitor what's going on," Vaillancourt said.

"Putting our head in the sand doesn't do anything; it doesn't identify who's most vulnerable [and] how to remedy that vulnerability."

Another recommendation urges the prioritization of evidence-based methods to tackle learning loss — paying particular attention to the most disadvantaged students — and the continual evaluation of whether these initiatives are working.

Tracy Vaillancourt, chair of Canada's pandemic learning loss report, is a professor of education at the University of Ottawa and Canada Research Chair in children's mental health and violence prevention. (Caitlin Taylor/CBC)

COVID worsened existing concerns

The report's findings and recommendations weren't a surprise, since teachers have voiced similar concerns for years, says Clint Johnston, president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation, which represents more than 390,000 teachers and education workers.

"What I see is an exacerbation of a context that honestly already exists in an under-resourced system. We've got children who are falling a bit behind, they're not getting the support they need," he said from Toronto.

"It's not surprising that when there was an interruption, there'd be an impact."

Addressing gaps in student learning requires investment, says Clint Johnston, president of the Canadian Teachers' Federation and a former school teacher. (Jon Hernandez/CBC)

Addressing gaps requires investment, Johnston said, "and right now it essentially seems like we're being asked to make up those gaps — to do more with the same amount — which isn't really feasible."

Montreal parent Katherine Korakakis, whose two kids required tutoring during and after the pandemic, praised the report for validating what parents have long worried about.

"We knew that the pandemic disrupted our children's education, but the questions always were, how significant were those disruptions?"

Katherine Korakakis, president of the English Parents’ Committee Association of Quebec, says the report validates what many parents have seen and been worried about throughout the pandemic. (Matt D'Amours/CBC)

Korakakis, who's president of Quebec's English Parents' Committee Association, backs the report's call to identify students with learning gaps, implement initiatives supporting them and provide continued monitoring.

"Parents need a clear, set plan with meaningful actions and measurable progress," she said.

A final recommendation urges emergency preparedness planners to recognize how detrimental prolonged school closures have been, including affecting kids' broader well-being. Schools are typically where youngsters find social connection, a safe space and myriad supports, including food programs and mental health services.

During emergencies, provided it is safe to do so, "schools should be the last to close and the first to re-open," Vaillancourt said.

She believes initiatives to address pandemic learning loss are required across K-12 into post-secondary and will be for years to come.

We can't think "that because the pandemic feels like it was so long ago, that there's nothing to be done, that the ship has sailed," she said.

"Even though this was in the past, we still have these learners in our system — they're still in my system at the university level — and they still need help."

World.title: 3 dead after boat crash in flooded river near Squamish, B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Three people are dead and a number of others had to be rescued after a boat crashed into a unknown object on the Squamish River Thursday amid stormy conditions.

The RCMP confirmed the third fatality on Friday after finding the body of a person who had been listed as missing. The identities of the deceased have not been confirmed.

Insp. Robert Dykstra with the Sea-to-Sky RCMP said there were approximately eight people on the boat when the accident happened.

"I don't have any details specifically about exactly the type of boat ... but I understand that it ran into something and that's what caused it to stop and people to be thrown into the water," he said.

"A number of people did get off the boat and they were rescued. They're on the on the other side [of the Squamish River] where we don't have direct access to by road right now, but they're safe."

Squamish Valley Road, which gives access to the remote area by vehicle, is closed at the Pilchuck Bailey Bridge due to flooding.

The Squamish Valley Road was washed out around two or three kilometres north of the Cheekye area. (Submitted by Glen McEachran)

Dykstra said investigators are trying to understand who owns the boat and why it was on the river in Thursday's harsh conditions.

"It could be any number of reasons. It's tragic. It's dangerous water. The flooding was quite substantial. The rainfall over the last 48 hours has been significant," he said.

Squamish RCMP responded to the accident at 1:52 p.m. PT Thursday. Cpl. Ashley MacKay said conditions that day were extremely difficult and unsafe for emergency responders.

"The weather and river conditions have played a significant role in the response efforts," she said. "Weather patterns, water levels, and river conditions can change rapidly, and those factors are being continuously assessed as search and recovery efforts continue."

The Squamish Valley Road is seen closed due to flooding on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (Troy Charles/CBC)

Police are asking the public to stay off the water due to dangerous flow rates and debris throughout the river systems.

​RCMP Air Services, the Lower Mainland District Integrated Emergency Response Team, the Lower Mainland District Underwater Recovery Team, and West Coast Marine Services were involved in the search.

"We send the condolences out to those who are affected. We're working hard to figure out exactly what happened in this investigation," said RCMP Cpl. Brett Urano.

World.title: All aboard river cruise boat survive crash with tanker in New Orleans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into a docked river cruise boat with 180 people aboard on Friday, the mayor said.

All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the cruise boat took on water and began to topple over.

Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hit the cruise boat while it was docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.

Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and several other rescuers rushed to help. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno called it "a miracle on the Mississippi."

The mayor said 32 people were taken to the hospital, but none of them had critical injuries.

The American Heritage, a paddlewheel boat, started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off it.

Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were rescued from the river and taken onto nearby ships.

'It was just chaos'

Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and saw the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water.

"It was just chaos," he said. "You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water."

PHOTOS | Photos from the scene:

The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five storeys and can hold up to 150 passengers.

The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi.

The cruise line said it was working with the U.S. Coast Guard and would share more information when it could.

The tanker involved in the crash specializes in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, a semi-solid substance often used for road construction and roofing, according to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic.

World.title: Avril Lavigne welcomes baby girl
World.content:

Canadian pop-punk princess Avril Lavigne has welcomed her first child — a baby girl — with an unnamed partner.

World.title: Colombia’s foreign minister apologizes to Democrats for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments
World.content:
Colombia’s Foreign Minister Omar Bula apologized for “inappropriate and disrespectful” comments he made in 2020, when he claimed that US Democrats “thrive in illegality.”

In a letter to the Democratic Party, Bula offered his “sincere apologies for comments I made in past social posts concerning leaders of the Democratic Party.”

The foreign minister referred to comments he made between November 2020 and September 2024 in which he claimed that “the globalists and US Democrats love everything illegal” and claimed their party “had turned into crap.”

In the letter, Bula stressed that his “perspective has evolved since then, and those messages do not reflect the views I hold today. Nor do they, in any way, represent the position of the Government of Colombia under President Abelardo de la Espriella.”

I value the contributions that Democratic leaders have made to the friendship between our countries and welcome the opportunity to continue building on that work together. Foreign Minister Omar Bula

After a stunning electoral defeat of the Republican Party, which lost control over both houses of the congress, Bula called for “mutual respect and bipartisanship” regardless of “political differences and electoral cycles.”

Starting in January, when the new Congress takes office, the Foreign Ministry will depend on the support of the Democratic majority for any type of financial aid or formal bilateral agreements.

World.title: De la Espriella failed to make Colombia secure in 90 days
World.content:
Colombia’s far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella failed to live up to his promise to “recuperate” state-control of conflict regions through a “shockwave” of hardline security measures within 90 days in office.

His first three months in office ended this week, and by almost every metric violence is rising.

Non-state armed groups and organized criminal groups alike have staged a series of attacks on security forces and their infrastructure, likely in retaliation for aggressive security actions that have included bombings carried out by Colombian aerial forces (which have killed at least 8 minors).

It would seem the shockwave is being carried out by not-state, rather than state forces.

According to new data published by the country’s Ombudsman’s Office and police, extortion, homicides, acts of “terrorism”, kidnappings, and attacks on security forces have all risen since De la Espriella assumed the presidency. Thirty-eight members of the police or military have been killed, and 213 wounded in attacks by criminal groups.

Child-recruitment by non-state armed groups has also risen dramatically: 131% higher than former President Gustavo Petro’s first 90 days in office.

Although De la Espriella has made concrete changes from the policy of his predecessor — destruction of coca is up, and the right-wing president has dismantled previously ongoing negotiations and peace processes with some criminal groups — much of his administration’s security policy has been more about optics than substance.

The president has released videos of himself walking among the bodies killed by aerial bombings, and has taken to showing up in affected cities wearing a pistol on his hip, and carrying a walkie-talkie.

During an operation in Cucuta, in the province of Norte de Santander, on November 10, De la Espriella spoke with military officials armed, wearing a military uniform and a red military-style beret.

The same day, The National Liberation Army, ELN, the largest remaining rebel group in the country, carried out a drone attack on a military base in the north of the same department that killed at least one soldier and wounded 4 others.

His Ministry of Defense released a video of him interrogating and mocking a member of FARC-dissident group the 33rd Front, telling him “welcome to Patria Milagro,” the miracle country —a slogan from his campaign during elections.

In September, paramilitary group the ACSN shut down large parts of the northern coast, including the city of Santa Marta. In a show of power, the ACSN even defied a response-deployment by Colombian military forces to the region to continue the forceful shutdown as the military largely stood by powerless.

De la Espriella has since militarized both Santa Marta and Cucuta, a measure which seems to have had little effect on the day-to-day operations of non-state armed groups in the regions.

De la Espriella has also repeatedly requested help from the US, and invited them to participate in his security crackdowns. In September, the President met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to sign a series of agreements he calls the “Barranquilla Accords.” Colombia agreed to give US companies preferential treatment regarding mining contracts, particularly involving rare earth minerals, in return for US security assistance and drone technology, among other things.

De la Espriella has attempted to align Colombian and US interests in security in the region, and talked repeatedly of extraditing “high priority targets,” to the US rather than charge them under Colombian law.

At a press conference with Rubio, De la Espriella announced what he called a “21st-Century Plan Patriot.”

Named after an aggressive security operation by former right-wing President Alvaro Uribe, the president said the agreement with the US will “modernize aircraft, radars, drones, helicopters, anti-drone systems, air defense, mobility, intelligence, cyber defense, special forces, and maintenance and operations.”

Armed groups currently operate in 24 of Colombia’s 32 provinces — roughly 75% of the country. That was true before De la Espriella took office, and the president’s promise to change that within three months has so far yielded little to change that.

World.title: Three months after 7.5M earthquake struck Colombia, “reconstruction hasn’t begun”
World.content:
Human rights officials warned on Tuesday that the reconstruction of west Colombia, which was partially destroyed by an August 10 earthquake, fails to show progress.

In a statement, the Ombudsman’s Office warned that “difficulties persist in providing assistance to and supporting the recovery of affected communities, particularly with regard to housing, access to essential services, the protection of rights, and funding for response measures.”

The top human rights official of Pereira, Leonardo Fabio Reales, told Caracol Radio that “the reconstruction of the city has not begun. There isn’t even a rough outline of what is planned to be done after the earthquake.”

Pereira is among the hardest hit by the 7.4M earthquake that destroyed more than 123,000 homes, and hundreds of hospitals and schools.

More than 450 people continue to live in tents in temporary camps that were set up in Pereira and cities like Buenaventura, according to the Ombudsman, which raised the alarm over “the lack of clear protocols for closing shelters and providing housing alternatives for departing residents, alongside infrastructure and security deficiencies in several facilities.”

Promised rent assistance, which would allow those who lost their homes to temporarily find residence, has also been insufficient.

“More than a month ago I received a million pesos ($304) stipend, although this was supposed to be three, I haven’t received any news,” Pereira resident Christian Castañeda told France 24.

“They’ve announced a so-called ‘Miracle Fund,’ but so far we’ve only seen billboards—no major progress,” said Castañeda, whose mother is one of more than 3,000 people who have yet to receive financial aid.

This Miracle Fund was set up a few weeks ago with an initial COP625 billion ($190 million) budget, which is only a drop in the COP59.29 trillion (18 billion) bucket that the government must get together for the reconstruction process.

“I’m not sure whether the Miracle Fund is working with the diligence and sense of urgency that are required, nor am I sure that they are doing so in the most transparent way,” said House Representative Catherine Juvinao, a member of the congressional commission that monitors the recovery process.

According to Senator Alejandro Toro, local governments from parts of the country that weren’t affected by the earthquake have also tried to receive emergency funds.

Sixteen departments were listed as affected—16, when everyone knows only 5 were actually impacted. It turns out that among these 16, certain departments reported every single public building and school as damaged. For instance: in Caqueta, according to the governor, there are more affected municipalities than families. No one knows the true number of victims in Caqueta; the press didn’t cover a single damaged house there. In Bolivar, along the Atlantic Coast, 11 families were reported affected—and do you know how many total people were listed under those 11 families? 467 people from 11 families! That averages to 43 people per family! Come on, that is completely false! That is a lie; it’s not as if every household belongs to [vallenato singer] Diomedes. They also reported about 189 damaged schools, which would mean 12 or 13 damaged schools per family… impossible. This same issue occurred across other departments—16 departments, including Sucre!

Senator Alejandro Ocampo

Ocampo said he would continue his lawsuits against the foundation of First Lady Ana Lucia Pineda, Colombia Luz y Sonrisas, which has failed to comply with court orders ordering transparency on what it has done with money collected in response to the earthquake.

World.title: De la Espriella claims ELN plans to attack Colombia’s corporate media
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella ordered State forces to protect corporate media, claiming alerts over “possible terrorist attacks by the ELN” guerrilla group.

De la Espriella said he issued “specific instructions to ensure that the full capacity of the State is directed toward protecting” private television networks RCN and Caracol, “their journalists, employees, and families” on social media platform X.

The president said he also ordered to increase the protection of Semana, a far-right magazine owned by the main sponsor of his campaign, the Gilinksi family.

Freedom of the press is sacred and must be respected! No narco-terrorist group will silence the media through threats, intimidation, or acts of violence. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Bogota Mayor’s Office, the orders were issued hours after the prosecution’s Technical Investigations Unit issued a “security alert” to the media outlets and the local government.

In a response, Caracol evacuated its main office in the capital and allowed police to search the premise for bombs without result.

Press freedom foundation FLIP said that “we reject and express our profound concerns over the alerts of possible attacks against media in Bogota.”

“The fact that no explosives have been found does not mean that the risk has ended. These alerts require monitoring and effective protection,” the FLIP said on X.

The alert was issued amid increased violence between guerrilla groups and State forces, who have been ordered to carry out an offensive against insurgencies and organized crime groups by the president.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.

The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Woman Reunited with Her Children Taken by Pinochet’s Dictatorship
World.content:
and sent to the USA

Teresita Padilla and her sons. Photo: BBC / Reuters

By BBC News Mundo (El Mostrador)

HAVANA TIMES – In 1985, Teresita Padilla became pregnant and gave birth to her eldest son. She thought the hospital was a safe place where she could seek refuge and receive help. But there, her trust was betrayed in ways that ultimately separated her from her children, not once, but twice.

Tim Roinick and Travis Murdoch live in the United States, where they arrived after being adopted by US American families in the 1980s.

What they did not know was that their biological mother, Teresita de Jesus Padilla, had never wanted to give them up for adoption. But the military regime governing Chile, their country of origin, decided otherwise.

And it was only this week, nearly 40 years after that journey, that Teresita was finally able to embrace two of her sons again.

“God has given me back my children, whom I thought I had lost forever,” she told Reuters after reuniting with them in Santiago.

Both Travis and Tim, as well as Travis’s twin brother, were taken from Teresita by members of the forces supporting Augusto Pinochet’s regime while she was hospitalized.

This practice was part of the state terrorism carried out by the dictatorship for nearly two decades, which included the disappearance and deaths of some 3,000 people associated with left-wing political parties and other dissident groups.

The children grew up in the United States and knew they had been adopted, but they were unaware of the circumstances that had brought them to their new families.

“I feel like I’ve known Teresita my whole life. There’s a connection,” Tim told the Associated Press after the reunion.

According to several official documents obtained by news agencies, nearly 20,000 cases of forced adoption were recorded during the 17 years of Chile’s military regime.

Some organizations, however, put that figure at around 50,000 cases.

“We don’t know exactly how many children were taken out of Chile,” Constanza del Río, director of the NGO Nos Buscamos (We look for each other) told the Associated Press.

Del Río explained that vulnerable women from the country’s poorest regions were the primary victims of networks that also included social workers, doctors, and judges who falsified documents to send children abroad.

In the 1970s, Chile ranked third in the number of illegal adoptions, after South Korea and China.

A Medical Examination

According to the Murdoch brothers’ account, their search for the truth began in 2020, when Tim needed to learn about his medical history and discovered that he had an entire family in Chile.

During his inquiries, he learned that his relatives, particularly his cousins, had been searching for him for decades through a foundation, which soon contacted him. “That opened a Pandora’s box,” he explained.

The first thing he discovered was that he had three brothers: twins — including Travis’s brother, Carl — who also lived in the United States, and another brother who had remained in Chile.

“I always wanted to have a brother. Now I have three,” he told Reuters.

Tim contacted them, and in the middle of this year, they decided to travel to Santiago to meet Teresita. Carl was unable to make the trip to the Chilean capital because of lingering injuries from an accident he suffered in 2013.

Teresita was waiting for them. She is now 66 years old and has spent much of her life living in precarious economic circumstances.

In 1985, she became pregnant and gave birth to her eldest son. She thought the hospital was a safe place where she could seek refuge and receive help. But there, her trust was betrayed in ways that ultimately separated her from her children, not once, but twice.

“Those women took my children away under threats, and that is why I have suffered my entire life,” she told Reuters.

According to Travis and Tim, their intention now is to maintain and strengthen the bond with the biological mother they have just met, on the other side of the continent.

Read more from Chile here at Havana Times.

World.title: Cuban Journalist Abducted and Threatened at Gunpoint
World.content:
to force him to quit CubaNet

Vladimir Turró was held in police custody for approximately ten hours and threatened with imprisonment if he continued working as a journalist. / CubaNet

Vladimir Turro Paez says State Security agents took him to a wooded area and tried to force him to record a video.

By 14ymedio

HAVANA TIMES – Independent journalist Vladimir Turro Paez reported on Friday that three State Security agents forcibly took him to a secluded area of Havana, where they threatened him with a gun while attempting to force him to record a video announcing his resignation from CubaNet.

The reporter was held in police custody for approximately ten hours before being released, after receiving further threats of imprisonment if he continued practicing journalism.

The incident occurred on Thursday November 12, when Turró was visiting his mother in the Havana municipality of La Lisa. According to his account, three officers arrived at the house and ordered him to accompany them. They forced him into an unmarked vehicle and, during the journey, made him keep his head down between his legs.

The vehicle eventually stopped in a wooded area, far from the city’s usual activity. There, one of the agents pulled out a pistol while another prepared a phone to record the statement they intended to extract from the journalist.

“They pointed a gun at me and demanded that I resign from CubaNet,” Turro reported. According to his testimony, the armed man repeatedly manipulated the magazine and pulled the trigger. The reporter said he did not know whether the weapon was loaded and that he feared for his life.

The agents insisted that he publicly announce his departure from the independent news outlet, but Turró remained silent. Two days earlier, the journalist had received an informal summons to appear at Villa Marista, the headquarters of State Security in Havana, but he decided not to attend.

Following the incident, he was taken to the Sixth Police Station, where an investigator who said he was from Villa Marista handed him an official warning notice. The official accused him of “usurpation of legal capacity” and maintained that independent (non-government) journalism was not permitted in Cuba.

Turro rejected that argument and reiterated his determination to continue working. He was finally released at around nine that evening. “I’m going to keep practicing journalism,” he stated in his testimony published by CubaNet.

The incident comes amid a new wave of arrests and threats against independent reporters. On November 5, Yoani Sanchez, director of 14ymedio, was detained for nine hours after being intercepted as she left her home in Nuevo Vedado. During her detention, political police agents threatened to prosecute her for propaganda against the constitutional order.

Two days earlier, Camila Acosta, a contributor to CubaNet, was arrested while taking her cat to the veterinarian. She spent several hours at a police station and received a fine of 3,000 pesos, along with renewed threats of imprisonment. On November 2, Adelth Bonne Gamboa, another journalist associated with the same outlet, had also been arrested.

On November 9, Reporters Without Borders denounced those three arrests in just four days as a new offensive against press freedom. Its Latin America director, Artur Romeu, demanded an end to the harassment and emphasized that reporting on matters of public interest is not a crime.

The situation is particularly serious for Henry Constantín, director of La Hora de Cuba, who has been imprisoned in Camagüey since September and placed in pretrial detention on a charge of disobedience. His case has been denounced by international organizations calling for his release.

Intimidation against reporters also includes surveillance of their homes, restrictions on movement, and threats. On November 6, several journalists woke up to find police patrols stationed outside their homes to prevent them from attending a cultural event organized by the US Embassy in Havana.

In Turro’s case, the complaint introduces a particularly alarming element: the use of a firearm in an attempt to obtain a public resignation. His testimony describes an operation intended not only to prevent journalistic coverage but also to force the reporter to abandon his profession permanently.

First published in Spanish by 14ymedio and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: Data Centers Store Hazardous Chemicals in Mexico
World.content:
A view of the roof of the data center operated by the Mexican company KIO Networks, in the state of Querétaro, in central Mexico, showing the facility’s ventilation system, which is necessary to keep the interior temperature low due to the enormous amount of heat generated by the servers operating inside. Credit: KIO

Por Emilio Godoy (IPS)

HAVANA TIMES – At first glance, a data center in Mexico draws little attention, as it is usually housed in an industrial park, out of public view. But, in addition to emitting greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2) and nitrogen oxides, its cooling and fire suppression systems contain substances with strong environmental and health impacts: the so-called “forever chemicals”.

IPS found that at least five data centres operating in Mexico use hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), a group of synthetic gases with a global warming potential up to 7,000 times higher than that of CO2, the human-induced gas responsible for global warming. These gases also have an atmospheric lifetime of 15 years, according to data from ATMOsphere, an independent global accelerator for the air conditioning market.

Mexico hosts at least 144 data centres run by 44 providers in 69 cities, but most of the companies do not disclose whether their cooling and fire suppression systems use forever chemicals

Research published by U.S. government institutions has concluded that these gases accumulate in air, water and soil, and can be absorbed by animals and plants through ingestion or contact. They are also highly mobile, to the point of being present in the Arctic and the Himalayas, according to a 2023 study.

Forever chemicals, also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), are a large family of over 15,000 synthetic chemicals. They are needed to cool the hundreds of servers housed in data centres, which is key to prevent overheating and interruptions to their operations. However, the extent of their use in Mexico is unknown.

Mexico hosts at least 144 data centres run by 44 providers in 69 cities, but most of the companies do not disclose whether their cooling and fire suppression systems use forever chemicals.

Although Mexico is a party to the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, an international agreement that entered into force in 2004 and aims to eliminate and restrict the production and use of dangerous chemicals, these substances are not regulated under national law, there is no inventory of contaminated sites and there is no systematic monitoring.

Teresa Roldán, member of the environmental advocacy group Vocer@s de la Madre Tierra in Querétaro, Mexico’s data centre hub in central Mexico, denounces the lack of oversight by the authorities and of transparency by the companies.

“Since they (the data centres) arrived, there has been no clear information, and as a result (the government) has let them operate without any supervision. We know nothing about the chemical substances. (…) They leave us in uncertainty about the substances and the discharges of liquid waste. There is no way they are not contaminating”, she said to IPS.

Roldán and her group have showered state and federal authorities with requests for information on issues such as water use, greenhouse gas emissions and waste management, but the authorities say they do not have the information or refuse to provide it.

Air conditioning system at the data centre of the U.S.-based company HostDime in the western city of Guadalajara. Credit: HostDime

Widespread use

Most of the data centres operating in the country do not have Environmental Impact Assessments describing the type of cooling and fire suppression systems they use. Only a few companies have made the information available on their websites.

For example, the MEX3 data centre of the Mexican corporation KIO Networks, located in Mexico City, explains the operation of a very early smoke detection apparatus (VESDA) that automatically detects smoke even before it is visible and proceeds to extinguish it. It works with the gaseous hydrofluorocarbon FM-200, also known as HFC-227ea or heptafluoropropane.

The KIO MEX5 data centre, in the municipality of Tultitlán, in the state of Mexico, which borders Mexico City, also says it uses a clean agent suppression system. Most clean agents are hydrofluorocarbons, although the company does not specify which one it uses. The same is true of the KIO MTY1 centre, located in the municipality of San Pedro Garza García, next to Monterrey in the state of Nuevo León, northern Mexico.

Clean agent fire suppression systems are normally used instead of water-based systems because of their non-conductive, residue-free properties, while the latter can damage servers.

Novec, an evaporative fluid, has become the popular choice for high-capacity data centres. The substance boils on contact with electronic components and thus absorbs a large amount of latent heat of vaporisation.

The Mx1 Querétaro facility, owned by U.S.-based Equinix Inc., uses Novec 1230 gas in its fire suppression system, which contains PFAS. The U.S.-based 3M, its manufacturer, has announced the discontinuation of Novec to comply with international regulations to eliminate the use of forever chemicals.

The data centre of the binational NGX Networks in Nogales, in the northern state of Sonora, also uses a refrigerant gas containing forever chemicals.

Various scientific studies have found PFAS at the poles and in the oceans. Multiple studies in the United States and Europe link them to cancers of the kidney, pancreas, testicles, uterus and endometrium, as well as to multiple myeloma. They are also considered endocrine disruptors. Their useful life exceeds 20 years. In the PFAS life cycle, the usage stage is the critical one because of its high emissions to the environment.

Hydrofluorocarbons emerged under the Montreal Protocol, which came into force in 1989, to replace gases containing chlorine and bromine that deplete the ozone layer and to meet growing demand for industrial, commercial and residential refrigeration. But these gases are very powerful climate pollutants, which is why they are the target of global reduction, as happened with the halogens covered by the Montreal Protocol.

The risk of chemical contamination clashes with the Mexican government’s promotion of data centres as part of its drive for industrialisation under the National Strategy for Industrialisation and Shared Prosperity, known as Plan México, a mix of energy, technology, pharmaceutical and even food projects.

It also adds to the centres’ high energy and water consumption in places already suffering water stress, such as Mexico City and Querétaro.

The data centre operated by the Mexican company KIO Networks in the central state of Querétaro is located in a populated area, near homes and schools, where air, soil and water pollution can spread. Credit: KIO

Forever chemicals in cooling systems

Recent research by Leonard Siegel, the California-based non-governmental organisation Center for Public Environmental Oversight executive director, shows that the data centre industry uses PFAS as an alternative to reduce the use of water, the liquid most commonly used in cooling systems.

Like Roldán in Querétaro, Siegel questions the lack of information on the forever chemicals consumed in data centres in the United States.

“The companies are not sharing the information. And we are now more concerned about the planned ones than the ones under construction”, he said to IPS, citing their size, the scale of their operations and, consequently, the type and quantity of equipment required.

In both Mexico and the United States, data centre companies do not disclose the volume of refrigerant they replace each year, the chemical releases during the normal operation of the centres, or the losses during the installation and maintenance of equipment.

Nor is it clear whether forever chemicals contaminate the wastewater discharged by data centres.

PFAS are used in data centres mainly as refrigerant gases and in immersion cooling fluids. The most common cooling method consists of using PFAS gases in a compressor system, like a refrigerator, to cool air or water for the computers.

The problem grows when the degradation of PFAS leads to the formation of trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), which has appeared in rain, beer, tea and fruit crops, according to a 2024 study by five experts from scientific institutions in Norway, Sweden and Switzerland. TFA alters levels of thyroxine, a thyroid gland hormone that is vital for regulating human metabolism, according to a 2025 study by 11 specialists from Austria.

Racks of servers in the data centre of U.S.-based company Equinix in the state of Querétaro, in central Mexico. Credit: Equinix

Traditional data centres use heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems that include a condenser, whose main function is to convert vapour into liquid or release heat to the external environment. Most air conditioners contain forever chemicals. In the HVAC case, these liquids can be recycled or become part of the liquid waste the facility discharges.

A more advanced setup is the computer room air conditioner (CRAC), which regulates temperature, humidity and airflow using a compressor, an evaporator and a condenser, and is designed for small and medium-sized data centres.

Larger facilities operate computer room air handlers (CRAH), using chilled water from a central chiller plant. These require greater investment in infrastructure but are more efficient, which results in long-term savings, as explained by Exposiciones Industriales de México, organiser of the largest air conditioning trade fair in the country.

Historically, data centre chillers and CRAC and CRAH systems have used the refrigerant gas R-134a, which contains PFAS.

Data centres of companies such as Equinix, KIO and Scala use CRAC or CRAH systems, according to their public reports. The facility of the U.S.-based HostDime, planned to operate in Guadalajara, will have an HVAC system.

The density of a data centre relates to the amount of computing capacity installed in a given area. Data centres currently being built to support the development and operation of artificial intelligence systems can concentrate tens of kilowatts in a single structure.

This gives an idea of the volume of heat to be generated and of the forever chemicals or water needed to cool the servers.

For example, Ascenty-01, Microsoft’s data centre, plans a first phase of four data rooms, out of a total of 10, with a total of 2,992 electronic equipment racks, according to the environmental impact assessment obtained by the Latin American Observatory of Data Centers. Each data room, with a capacity of 2 MW, will have 13 CRAH units, 11 in operation and two on standby.

KIO and Ascenty did not respond to the reporter’s request for comment. The Mexican Association of Data Centres initially replied to the reporter but declined to answer the query on the subject. Nor the Ministry of the Environment and Natural Resources answered the question about the lack of PFAS regulation in the country.

According to Noemí Quiroz, senior consultant for non-governmental organisation Centro de Estudios e Investigación en Asuntos Públicos (CEIAP), installing data centres without a regulatory framework to identify their positive and negative consequences has been a bad idea.

“There is no regulatory framework for environmental issues or for placement, and there is no standardisation of procedures. The states do not have regulation either. International evidence was not considered. The situation now calls for regulation”, she told IPS.

In an upcoming study, CEIAP assessed all the country’s towns to identify the most suitable ones for building data centres, based on the availability of resources such as water, land, labour and security.

It also analysed the digital policy of the country’s 32 states against 79 standards, seven of them on data centres.

Racks of servers operated by the Mexican company KIO Networks in the central state of Querétaro, which require intensive cooling systems to dissipate the heat generated by the computer equipment. Credit: KIO

Suspensions in the face of risk

In a document submitted to federal authorities, activist Roldán requested a suspension of the operations of all data centres in Querétaro, as well as a moratorium on the approval of new projects, until water, environmental and risk information on substances such as forever chemicals is made public. “What problem are they going to leave us with? We must prevent them before they keep granting more land concessions and electricity”, she warned.

For Siegel, the prospect of facilities with greater computing capacity opens a window to curb further chemical pollution, as he believes that “we are in a situation where we have an opportunity to stop the use of PFAS in cooling before its use begins, but powerful companies are waiting for authorisation for their commercialisation” in the United States.

Specialist Quiroz suggests a national policy that identifies and fills existing regulatory gaps and addresses territorial and energy planning, as well as encouraging the disclosure of information.

“A regulation determined by size (of the facility), with specific criteria and municipal and federal jurisdictions, that establishes comparable indicators for energy, water and resource-use efficiency, through which regulators can learn the characteristics of data centres” she proposed.

While data centres process poisons, answers must emerge from the depths of their powerful systems, as Roldán and Siegel demand: which substances, and in what quantities, they use to cool their computing systems; how much they release into the environment; what they do to prevent these releases; what they do to replace hazardous substances and polluting gases; and whether they will be liable for the environmental damage.

*This investigation was supported by the grant ‘Un Polo a Tierra’ escuela de periodismo para la industrialización verde en México’, sponsored by Periodistas por el Planeta.
