World.title: Sheinbaum denies ‘friction’ in bilateral ties after US reportedly shelters a wanted Mexican official: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🔎 Sheinbaum asks Security Cabinet for information on Zuany: Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts.

Responding to a Thursday New York Times report that former Chihuahua special prosecutor Guillermo Zuany Portillo has fled to the U.S. and is under U.S. government protection, Sheinbaum said “the story about this character is long” and that she didn’t want to discuss it. However, she said his alleged collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” and that she will ask the Security Cabinet for all the information it has on him, including his whereabouts. 🇲🇽 🇺🇸 No friction expected with U.S.: Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t.

Asked whether the Zuany situation could strain bilateral ties, Sheinbaum said it wouldn’t. 📊 Gap between INEGI and SESNSP homicide data under review: Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers.

Sheinbaum said a working group is looking into why INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) is well above the SESNSP’s (24,348), a difference of 5,140. She noted that the monthly figures presented at her press conference come from state Attorney General’s Offices, while INEGI uses death certificates and other records. INEGI data shows a 12.1% drop in homicides in 2025, compared to 21.2% per the SESNSP’s numbers. 🏍️ Drug lord’s motorbikes fetch 71 million pesos: INDEP director Mónica Fernández said the auction of Ryan Wedding’s luxury motorcycles raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million), about 11 million pesos above expectations. Fifty-seven of the 62 motorcycles were sold, and the remaining five will go up for auction in late November. Proceeds will go to the Office of the Presidency to fund social justice projects, including for the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and for Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo communities.

Why today’s mañanera matters

The New York Times’ reporting on Guillermo Zuany Portillo, a former special prosecutor in Chihuahua, was once again a topic of discussion at President Sheinbaum’s morning press conference.

The Times reported on Tuesday that Zuany had facilitated the operation of the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency in Chihuahua and, in exchange, his U.S. visa — reportedly revoked “because of his suspected ties to the very cartels the C.I.A. wanted to root out” — was reinstated. At her Wednesday morning press conference, Sheinbaum described the report as “very interesting,” and said that it was “worth learning about” who Zuany is “and how he collaborated with one of the U.S. agencies.”

On Thursday, the Times reported that Zuany — who is wanted by Mexican authorities — had fled to the United States.

The former prosecutor’s alleged cooperation with the CIA is part of a larger story that has remained in the headlines in Mexico for much of 2026. In April, CIA officers allegedly participated in a drug lab raid alongside Chihuahua state forces without the authorization or knowledge of the federal government. Two CIA agents and two Chihuahua police officials were killed in a car accident after the raid.

The CIA’s alleged participation in the operation has strained relations between the federal government and the Chihuahua government, which is led by Governor Maru Campos of the National Action Party, Mexico’s main opposition party. It also led Sheinbaum to accuse the U.S. government of interference in Mexico. The former attorney general of Chihuahua, César Jáuregui, was taken into federal custody last month on a charge of treason related to the CIA’s alleged involvement in the drug lab raid.

Beyond the case involving Zuany and the CIA, another notable topic at today’s mañanera was homicide statistics.

A range of experts have expressed skepticism about the accuracy of the Sheinbaum administration’s homicide statistics, with claims that state-based Attorney General’s offices — which provide homicide data to the federal government — are fudging the numbers. There has been renewed focus on the accuracy of the data this week after the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI) reported over 5,000 more homicides in 2025 than the federal government’s Executive Secretariat of the National Public Security System (SESNSP), the largest gap in more than a decade.

Sheinbaum: US collaboration with former Chihuahua prosecutor won’t cause friction in bilateral ties

A reporter asked the president about a report published by The New York Times on Thursday that states that Zuany “has fled to the United States and is now under the U.S. government’s protection, according to U.S. and Mexican officials.”

“The story about this character is long,” Sheinbaum said.

“I don’t want to talk about it here at this time,” she added.

Sheinbaum said that Zuany’s collaboration with U.S. authorities is “very significant, even for the bilateral relationship” between Mexico and the United States.

She said she would ask the federal government’s Security Cabinet to provide all the information it has about Zuany, including anything it knows about his current whereabouts.

🚨Claudia Sheinbaum considera que el caso de Guillermo Zuany, exvicefiscal de Chihuahua señalado por presunta corrupción y vínculos con el crimen organizado, es relevante para la relación entre México y Estados Unidos. La presidenta pidió al Gabinete de Seguridad informar sobre el caso de Zuany, quien se encuentra en territorio estadounidense. 🗞️Israel Aldave | @Radio_Formula — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) November 13, 2026

“Hopefully the federal Attorney General’s Office or the Security Cabinet can provide information,” Sheinbaum said.

Asked whether “the situation” with Zuany could create “friction” between Mexico and the United States, the president responded:

“No, because it’s been spoken about with the U.S. government.”

Sheinbaum said in April that the U.S. government had agreed to comply with the Mexican Constitution and Mexican laws in bilateral security cooperation. She also expressed confidence that U.S. participation in a security operation on Mexican soil wouldn’t be repeated.

Sheinbaum says government is reviewing discrepancy between INEGI and SESNSP homicide numbers

A reporter asked the president about the discrepancy between INEGI’s 2025 homicide statistics and those of the SESNSP.

Sheinbaum said that the gap between INEGI’s 2025 homicide total (29,488) and that of the SESNSP (24,348) is “something we’re reviewing with INEGI.”

She stressed that the homicide statistics presented at her press conference on a monthly basis come from the country’s Attorney General’s Offices. Sheinbaum noted that INEGI looks at death certificates and records (among other information) when classifying deaths as homicides. She also noted that INEGI publishes preliminary and final data on homicides. Sheinbaum said that the upward revision in INEGI’s 2025 homicide count between its preliminary and final figures was larger than in previous years.

“We have a working group to look at why this situation occurred,” she said.

“And we’re also looking at the difference in each state between what the Attorney General’s Offices reported and what the civil registry later reported. This revision is done with INEGI,” Sheinbaum said.

The Security Ministry said in August that the difference between INEGI’s homicide numbers and those of the SESNSP is “expected” as “each institution performs different functions, uses different [data] integration procedures, has different collection, validation, and publication periods, and generates information for specific purposes.”

However, “both sources show the same trend with respect to the evolution of intentional homicide,” the ministry said.

INEGI’s final data shows that homicides declined 12.1% in 2025 compared to the previous year, whereas the SESNSP reported a significantly larger reduction of 21.2%.

Auction of drug trafficker’s motorbikes raises 71 million pesos

Mónica Fernández, director of the Institute to Return Stolen Goods to the People (INDEP), reported early in the press conference that the auction this week of a collection of luxury motorcycles formerly owned by Canadian drug lord Ryan Wedding raised 70.91 million pesos (US $3.8 million). That amount was around 11 million pesos above expectations.

“We sold 57 of 62 motorcycles,” Fernández said, noting that the motorbikes were seized by authorities and subsequently handed over to INDEP in July.

Wedding’s motorcycles were seized last December after authorities raided four properties in Mexico City and México state linked to the former Olympic athlete known as The King of Cocaine. Wedding turned himself into Mexican authorities in January after more than a decade on the run.

Fernández noted that there was a large turnout at the auction of the drug trafficker’s motorbikes, which was held in Mexico City.

She said that the five motorcycles that weren’t sold will be put on the block at another INDEP auction to be held in late November.

The resources obtained from this week’s sale of Wedding’s motorbikes and other seized assets will be allocated to the Office of the Presidency, and will be used to finance social justice projects, including actions benefiting the widows of the 2006 Pasta de Conchos mine disaster and communities of the Indigenous Raramuri and Amuzgo peoples.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: El Tri is back in action Saturday in its first official match of the Rafa Márquez era
World.content:
After a winless start to the Rafa Márquez era, Mexico’s national soccer team has an opportunity to right the ship on Saturday evening in Kingston, Jamaica.

El Tri will take the field at Independence Park against underdog Jamaica in the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, making it Márquez’s first official match as Mexico manager.

Márquez, who succeeded Javier Aguirre after serving as his top assistant during the 2026 World Cup, has yet to win a match as Mexico’s top man. El Tri is 0-2-2 since he took over, including an embarrassing 3-0 loss to Team USA.

For this two-game stretch (the second leg will be played in Monterrey on Tuesday), Márquez summoned a more experienced squad than he did for the four friendlies during the September-October window.

Back with the team is forward Julián Quiñones, who was Mexico’s leading scorer during the World Cup. Also returning are winger Jesús Corona (a 33-year-old with experience in Europe) and fullback Rodrigo Huescas, who missed the World Cup after suffering a knee injury 13 months ago.

However, the team will be without top striker Raúl Jiménez, who underwent surgery to repair his medial collateral ligament last month.

Teen midfielder Gilberto Mora will be expected to direct the El Tri attack, while captain Johan Vásquez and Erik Lira form the backbone of the defense. All eyes will be on goalie Raúl Rangel whose two howlers against Team USA won’t soon be forgotten.

As humiliating as it was to lose to the U.S. in the manner they did, Mexico’s players realize that, as heavy favorites to advance to the semifinals, a loss to Jamaica would be even more devastating.

The defending Nations League champions are ranked 59 spots above Jamaica in the FIFA World Rankings (Mexico is No. 10, Jamaica No. 69), losing just three of 29 matches against The Reggae Boyz, while winning 21 and drawing five. And El Tri has outscored Jamaica 72-15 overall.

However, Mexico is only 3-3-1 in its last seven official matches against Jamaica, including a 1-0 loss in the 2017 Copa Oro semifinals.

Jamaica’s other two victories over Mexico were by identical 1-0 scores: in an Oct. 11, 2008, World Cup qualifier and in a Nov. 17, 1996, World Cup qualifier.

Still, The Reggae Boyz failed to qualify for this summer’s World Cup even though Concacaf had six slots in the tournament. Jamaica finished second to an upstart Curaçao side in the regional final group stage, then lost to DR Congo in an interconfederation playoff.

With reports from SBNation, ESPN and Soy Fútbol

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Pilgrimage preparations, ancient remains and delivery protests
World.content:
From preparations for one of Mexico’s largest annual religious gatherings to archaeological discoveries and transportation projects, Mexico City has plenty happening this November.

Authorities are gearing up to welcome millions of pilgrims to the Basilica of Guadalupe, while construction of a major passenger rail connection revealed an unexpected discovery. Meanwhile, a proposed licensing overhaul for motorcycle delivery workers hit a roadblock following protests.

Let’s get into it.

Authorities outline priorities for ‘Operation Basílica 2026’

Mexico City authorities have begun organizing a major security and public services operation ahead of Día de la Virgen de Guadalupe, the annual December celebrations honoring the Virgin of Guadalupe. Approximately 13 million pilgrims are expected to visit the Basilica of Guadalupe this year, which is on par with last year’s figures.

The Gustavo A. Madero borough, home to the religious complex, held its first interagency planning meeting earlier this month to coordinate the “2026 Operativo Basílica.” More than 30 federal and local government institutions are expected to participate in the effort.

The operation will cover public security, traffic management, emergency medical assistance, civil protection, sanitation and more. Participating agencies include the National Guard, Mexico City’s Citizen Security Ministry, the Navy, the National Defense Ministry, the Red Cross, the fire department and the city’s Metro and Metrobús systems.

Planning and coordination

Gustavo A. Madero Mayor Janecarlo Lozano said early coordination is necessary to manage crowds and ensure authorities can respond quickly to emergencies.

“Our responsibility begins with the planning stage and continues until the pilgrims begin their journey home,” Lozano said, according to Excelsior. “We want them to find guidance when they need it, assistance when they require it, and dignified treatment at all times.”

The holiday and pilgrimage honor an event in 1531, when an apparition of the Virgin of Guadalupe is said to have appeared to an Indigenous peasant named Juan Diego on a mountain above the holy site.

Last year’s operation provides a starting point for this year’s preparations. In 2025, the borough deployed 10,600 city workers, 250 law enforcement officers and 110 law enforcement vehicles. Authorities also installed 450 portable toilets, 26 hydration stations and two bike parking structures capable of housing 12,000 bicycles.

“We have years of experience and the opportunity to improve,” Lozano said, according to Milenio. “Let’s make each meeting a source of clear agreements and use all our institutional capacity to provide a timely response to the people. Because governing is about caring, we work together to live up to the trust of millions of people.”

INAH discovers possible pre-Hispanic ossuary during Mexico-Querétaro train works

Meanwhile, archaeologists have uncovered what may be an ancient ossuary containing human remains and artifacts at Mexico City’s Buenavista railway terminal, according to a news release from Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH). The discovery was made Sept. 17 during construction work on the Mexico City-Querétaro train line.

Researchers have so far identified nine human skeletons, five mandibles and several other bones, including ribs, femurs and pelvic fragments.

According to Secretary of Culture Claudia Curiel de Icaza, the discovery reveals new dimensions to the region’s pre-Hispanic funerary practices and how they honored their dead.

1 of 3

“A possible ossuary speaks not only of death: it raises questions about how the ancient communities of this territory treated and remembered their dead during a time of profound change,” Icaza said in a statement.

The burial deposit may date to the Late Postclassic period (1200-1519) or the early years of Spanish contact (1519-1535). Associated artifacts include domestic pottery, miniature spindle whorls, figurines and stone tools. Several obsidian blades may have originated in Hidalgo’s Sierra de las Navajas region.

“Taken together — bone fragments and ceramics — they could correspond to the final years of the pre-Hispanic period and the colonial era (1535-1821),” said José Manuel Cervantes Pérez, head of the Physical Anthropology Laboratory.

The recovered materials have been transferred to laboratories in Hidalgo for cleaning, restoration and further study.

“The associated materials offer clues to this encounter between different historical moments; it will be up to the INAH to study them rigorously and explain what they reveal,” Icaza said. “In this way, a history that lay hidden beneath the city can be incorporated into the knowledge of everyone.”

Mexico City-Querétaro train line construction is now 32% complete

Speaking of the Mexico City-Querétaro train line, construction has reached 32% completion, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Oct. 31 during a visit to a portion of the project in Polotitlán, State of Mexico.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Expansion (@expansionmx)

Additionally, Sheinbaum said 90% of the land rights needed for the project have been secured and that construction is progressing according to schedule.

At a cost of roughly 700 billion pesos, the approximately 230-kilometer railway will connect Mexico City with Querétaro, passing through the State of Mexico and Hidalgo. The journey is expected to take approximately two hours, with trains averaging 130 kilometers per hour.

The route will feature six stations: Buenavista in Mexico City, Huehuetoca and Teoloyucan in the State of Mexico, Tula de Allende in Hidalgo, and two stops in Querétaro.

Sheinbaum described the project as part of a broader effort to revive passenger rail services across the country, which in turn would offer an alternative to increasingly congested highways.

According to officials, 47 trains have been contracted and are currently being manufactured.

Mexico City suspends special license and commercial plate plan for delivery drivers

And now a win for the thousands of men and women who keep this city humming via Rappi, Uber Eats and countless other delivery services …

Mexico City authorities have suspended a pilot program that would have required motorcycle delivery workers operating through digital platforms to obtain special licenses and commercial plates, following protests over the proposed regulations.

The city’s Mobility Ministry (Semovi) reached the agreement Nov. 9 after Secretary Héctor Ulises García Nieto met with representatives of several groups to discuss their concerns. Both sides also agreed to establish additional working groups to review any revised proposals and develop an alternative regulatory framework.

The announcement followed several hours of demonstrations in western Mexico City, where app-based delivery workers blocked major roads in the Santa Fe area, causing traffic delays.

‘Unnecessary administrative hurdles’

Protesters argued that the proposed requirements would impose unnecessary administrative hurdles and additional expenses on workers who already hold motorcycle licenses. Some also complained about frequent police enforcement operations targeting delivery riders during their shifts, as well as unsafe working conditions.

“I mean, we already had a license, first the regular one, then they made us get another one for a motorcycle, and now a special one. It’s tough,” a delivery driver who did not give their name told La Gazzetta DF. “Besides, the police are around all the time on this side; there are operations, they keep driving their trucks around us, and now the National Guard is involved, they show up and everything. It’s like we’re criminals, and we’re not.”

Semovi said the initiative was intended to organize motorcycle-based delivery services and improve protections for workers in a sector that has historically faced precarious working conditions.

The program’s suspension leaves the proposed licensing and registration requirements under review, with further discussions expected between authorities and motorcycle delivery groups.

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: ‘No one was believing me’: An in-depth look at school bullying in Mexico
World.content:
As is often the case with Mexico’s private schools, children stay in the same institution their entire lives, forming insular cliques. As a result, for those who join a school later on, it can be difficult to integrate into a group of friends.

At best, the situation proves lonely and isolating. At worst, they become the victims of severe bullying.

“The teachers are former students,” says Andrea, now 32, “and so are the parents,” meaning social circles can be extremely closely knit.

According to Andrea, the dynamic at her middle school was not unlike the 2004 film “Mean Girls.” Social groups were sharply defined, with the so-called popular kids on one side and the geeks on the other, almost as if they were imitating American schools.

“It was a constant process of pigeonholing one another,” she says.

Authorities turning a deaf ear

Andrea felt the pressure of being the newcomer right away.

It began with rumors about things she had supposedly said. Soon enough, her friends stopped talking to her. The violence, however, escalated.

Her peers started attacking her with comments about her body. At one point, Andrea says, “They would shout at me and threaten me directly, telling me that no one would ever love me because I was flat-chested.”

When she tried to report the abuse, school authorities decided that all the students were equally to blame — “as if we were all sinners” — and there was never any real support.

The bullies were never reprimanded, nor did they face any consequences for harassing her.

The situation became so unbearable that Andrea decided to “fail nine out of 12 subjects because I just didn’t want to be there anymore.”

Long-lasting, devastating consequences

Based on his years in private clinical practice, psychotherapist Pedro Isla recognizes Andrea’s response as typical behavior for someone experiencing school bullying.

Working with the non-governmental organization CONCIEO, Isla notes that warning signs can vary. They may range from “difficulties with eating, sleeping or concentrating” to “a lack of motivation to try new things, or a decline in academic performance.”

Harassment between students remains a widespread issue in Mexico. According to the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI), roughly 28% of adolescents aged 12 to 17 report having experienced bullying or discrimination at school.

Similarly, advocacy NGO Bullying Sin Fronteras estimates that up to 28 million children and teens across all educational levels are affected nationwide.

According to Isla, adolescents are particularly vulnerable because “they are more distanced from their families due to the stage of life they are in; often, their peers serve as mirrors.”

In a bullying situation, Isla says, “what the mirror reflects is a deficient self-concept,” fostering the belief that “there is something wrong with me as a person.”

In her case, the bullying was so intense that Andrea simply decided to dissociate: “At one point, I felt like it was everyone against me, and no one was believing me.”

Isla notes that school bullying “has profound consequences for an individual’s self-concept.” That is, “the idea young people have of themselves, which persists into adulthood.” The long-term consequences, he says, can be “devastating.”

What’s more, nowadays, bullying is not limited to the schoolyard, classrooms, cafeteria and hallways.

Dr. Diana Guerrero has spent more than three decades working in schools, and notes that technology now means “bullying in Mexico follows victims outside of school through cyberbullying.”

Bullying in Mexico — The numbers

Overall, reports of school bullying in Mexico increased by 205% in 2024, compared to 2019, according to the Consejo Ciudadano para la Seguridad y Justicia, with most cases handled through an official helpline.

In 2024 alone, more than 1,000 children and adolescents were treated in hospitals across the country for injuries resulting from physical violence that occurred strictly within schools.

Of these hospitalized victims, almost 70% were between the ages of 12 and 17, a demographic that has been identified as the most vulnerable to this type of violence.

“Young people are bombarded via social media, viral challenges and a range of largely unchecked messages that glorify violence,” Dr. Guerrero says, “leading them to believe that being violent and hurting others makes them popular.”

A negligible decline

At the same time, OECD PISA reports suggest that frequent bullying has declined only marginally. In 2015, 20.2% of Mexican students reported being bullied at least a few times a month — 1.5 percentage points above the OECD average of 18.7%.

By the most recent PISA report, Mexico’s rate stood at 19.5%, sitting just 0.1 percentage points below the OECD average of 19.6% and comparable to countries such as Vietnam, Hungary and Canada.

Of course, staff and faculty should be trusted to provide an educational environment free from violence — one that respects students’ basic human rights, as outlined in the General Law on the Rights of Girls, Boys and Adolescents.

However, the figures point to a reality that is quite the opposite.

While OECD figures suggest bullying in Mexico has seen a decrease in recent years, dipping 0.7 percentage points since 2015, the change is relatively negligible given just how many adolescents experience such violence as part of their daily lives.

A restorative approach to bullying in Mexico

In Mexico, there is no fixed or exclusive budget for child, adolescent and teen mental health services.

Rather, the general budget allocated to mental health accounts for between 1.3% and 2% of total public health spending. This translates to less than 4 billion pesos — a percentage well below the 5% recommended by the World Health Organization.

In her experience, Dr. Guerrero says the main challenge for bullying in Mexico is a lack of “genuine follow-up” with reported cases.

“Training, follow-up and disciplinary measures — as well as formal complaints filed with public prosecutor’s offices that specialize in cases involving adolescents — are necessary,” she says.

Regarding schools, Dr. Guerrero believes that “training the teaching community” is essential, as is “establishing very clear protocols, so that teachers know what to do and how to act.”

Similarly, Isla believes it is important to address not only the victim but also the perpetrator. “Beyond having a policy of punishment,” Isla says, “we need to establish protocols for reparation for those who engage in harassment.”

When it comes to prevention, Isla believes that “consciously embracing the role that families play as mirrors for children” is imperative. “We must reflect to them the qualities they already possess or have the potential to develop,” so that they may experience genuine validation.

“In this way, children can begin to recognize these qualities within themselves,” Isla says, adding, “this is not something they have to go through alone.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: Baja Court Chief Says No US Visa Notice
World.content:
Mexico: Baja California

Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Report. Mexican local reporting says the US revoked the tourist visa of Baja California’s chief judge. —His reply. Alejandro Fragozo López says he has received no official notice and will wait for the competent authority. —Washington. We found no public US confirmation, and US law keeps visa records confidential. —His role. Fragozo presides over the Tribunal Superior de Justicia, which heads the Baja California state judiciary. —As of. Friday 13 November 2026, 6:45 p.m. ET.

Mexican local reporting says the United States has revoked the tourist visa of Alejandro Isaac Fragozo López, who presides over Baja California’s state courts. He says nobody has told him officially, and Washington has not publicly confirmed anything.

Why It Matters

Baja California is the Mexican state that borders California. A visa loss for the head of those courts would show how US entry rules can reach senior officials across the border.

The case is unconfirmed, and it is not an allegation of any offence. A visa revocation is an administrative step, and no official source we found gives a reason in this case.

Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In Plain English Tribunal Superior de Justicia. This is the top body of Baja California’s state court system. Its president magistrate leads the state judiciary. Visa revocation. The US cancels a visa that was already issued. US law lets the Secretary of State or a consular officer revoke a visa at any time. State Department. This is the US foreign ministry, which runs visas through its consulates. Its visa records are confidential under US law.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on US Mexico Border Email address Follow

What Has Been Reported

On Thursday 12 November 2026, Mexican local reporting said the US had cancelled Fragozo’s tourist visa. The same day he issued a personal statement, without court logos, saying he had received no official notification from US authorities.

In it he said he respects the journalists’ work and does not doubt their investigation. He added that it is important to wait for any decision directly from the competent authority.

The statement does not say the visa remains valid. It says only that no official notice has reached him.

On Friday 13 November the same reporting said unnamed US State Department officials told it he was notified by email, at the address he gave when he applied. It also said the revocation took place in July 2026, and that the officials gave no details of the grounds.

We could not find that account confirmed by a named US official or a document. The Mexican reports we found cite the same original report.

What US Law Says

US law lets the Secretary of State or a consular officer revoke a visa at any time, at their discretion. That provision, section 221(i) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, sends notice of a revocation to the Attorney General and bars most court review of it.

Section 222(f) of the same act treats State Department visa records as confidential. Its exceptions let the Secretary of State release certified records to a court and share lookout-database information with foreign governments on a reciprocal basis.

Public records do not show whether an email was sent. So a claim of email notice cannot be checked.

What Is Not Known

Neither the reason for any revocation nor its exact date has been confirmed by a US official on the record. It is also unclear whether a notice was sent, and to which address.

A revocation is an administrative step, not a finding of any offence. None of the reports we reviewed gives a reason for the revocation.

What To Watch Next

No dated checkpoint has been confirmed by an official source. A statement from the US State Department or from the Baja California judiciary would settle the question of notification.

For wider context on Mexico news, see our hub. It collects our latest coverage of the country.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the case shows that the US can cancel a visa after issue and that the process is confidential by law. For travellers from Mexico, the statute allows revocation at any time and leaves little room for a court appeal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Has the US confirmed the revocation?

We found no public confirmation from the State Department. Local reporting cites unnamed US officials, which we could not verify.

What does Fragozo say?

He says he has received no official notification and wants to wait for the competent authority. His statement does not say the visa is still valid.

Can the US revoke a visa at any time?

Yes, section 221(i) lets the Secretary of State or a consular officer do so at their discretion. Court review is largely barred.

Are US visa records public?

No, section 222(f) treats them as confidential. Exceptions let the Secretary of State release certified records to a court and share lookout-database information with foreign governments on a reciprocal basis.

What Copa and the FAA Said

Copa warned passengers on Friday that a temporary halt of air operations in the United States could cause delays and cancellations. The airline has not said which routes or how many flights are affected.

The FAA said on X on Friday 13 November that there had been “a temporary telecommunications outage” and that all flights had been halted “out of an abundance of caution”. It added that every flight had been accounted for and that international flights would be handled case by case.

The outage hit air route traffic control centres, the regional facilities that guide aircraft between airports. By about 6 p.m. New York time the FAA said departures would be allowed as those facilities recovered, and its airport status feed listed no ground stops at 6:42 p.m., though we found no formal notice declaring the nationwide stop over.

Why It Matters for US Travellers

Most of Copa’s US flights connect through Tocumen airport, Panama City’s main airport, so a US-wide departure halt can disrupt connections on both sides. We have no confirmed count of Copa flights delayed or cancelled.

Copa Holdings, the airline’s parent company, trades on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker CPA, so US investors also follow such disruptions. The FAA has not said how long normal operations will take to return.

Panamá Viejo, the ruins of Panama City’s first settlement. File photo. Photo: Editorpana, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

What Prediction Markets Say On Polymarket, a prediction market where users trade real money on outcomes, a contract on the FAA declaring the nationwide stop lifted by 10 p.m. ET on Friday 13 November was priced at 51.5% at 6:43 p.m. ET. The contract for midnight stood at 88.0% and for noon Saturday at 91.5%, on trading volume of US$496,963 across the contracts. These prices are bets, not forecasts from the FAA, and the market pays out only if the FAA or the US Department of Transportation officially announces the nationwide stop is no longer in effect. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

The FAA has not published a root cause, and the end time of the nationwide halt was not confirmed when we wrote this. Copa has not said which routes or how many flights are affected.

What to Watch Next

The FAA’s National Airspace System status page at nasstatus.faa.gov shows live airport delays and ground stops, and the FAA said its technicians were investigating the outage. Copa’s flight-status page and app are the airline’s own channel for changes; the next FAA or Copa update has no announced time.

For background on the airline’s parent, see our Copa Holdings company profile. More is in our Panama coverage.

Copa warned that a temporary halt of air operations in the United States could cause delays and cancellations. The FAA said a telecommunications outage prompted the halt.

What should Copa passengers do?

Copa’s flight-status page and the FAA’s airport status page at nasstatus.faa.gov show live changes. Copa has not published a list of affected flights.

World.title: US Supreme Court Takes Up Asylum Curbs
World.content:
Mexico: US Immigration Law

Key Facts RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Order. On Friday, 13 November 2026, the US Supreme Court agreed to hear case No. 26-239. —Scope. The Court took two questions: is the ban lawful, and may courts order class-wide relief. —In force. The asylum restrictions stay in force while the case proceeds. —Timing. No argument date is set, according to the Court’s docket. —Border. People who cross from Mexico illegally cannot apply for asylum while the proclamation stands.

The US Supreme Court will decide whether a president can suspend asylum claims at the Mexican border by proclamation. Its order on Friday leaves the restrictions in force while the justices take the case.

Why It Matters

Since 20 January 2025, people who cross the border from Mexico illegally have been barred from applying for asylum under a presidential proclamation. On Friday, 13 November 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to test whether that bar is lawful.

US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the federal border agency, said on 16 October 2026 that Border Patrol recorded fewer than 99,000 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal 2026, which ended on 30 September. It calls that a 95% decline from the more than 1.8 million a year recorded under the previous administration.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 70.8 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Supreme Court (Mexico) Email address Follow

What the Court Agreed to Decide

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, No. 26-239, named for Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security Secretary. The Court’s docket shows it granted the government’s petition on 13 November 2026, limited to the first two of three questions.

Question 1 asks whether Proclamation 10888, titled “Guaranteeing the States Protection Against Invasion”, and its implementing guidance are lawful. Question 2 asks whether a federal law, 8 U.S.C.

1252(f)(1), bars the class-wide relief the district court ordered.

In Plain English Asylum. US protection for people who fear persecution at home, which lets them stay and work. Proclamation. A presidential order; this one, dated 20 January 2025, blocks asylum claims by people who cross the southern border illegally. Class-wide relief. One court order that protects everyone in a defined group, not only the people who sued. Solicitor General. The Justice Department lawyer who argues the federal government’s cases at the Supreme Court. RAICES (the Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services). One of three immigrant legal service providers that brought the lawsuit.

How the Case Got Here

Three immigrant legal service providers and 13 individuals sued over the proclamation in federal court in Washington. On 2 July 2025 the district court ruled for them in substantial part, held the asylum bar unlawful and certified a class of people subject to the proclamation.

On 1 August 2025 a panel of the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit paused the asylum part of that ruling while the appeal ran. On 24 April 2026 a different panel upheld the district court in a divided opinion, with Judge Walker dissenting in part.

The appeals court denied a rehearing by its full bench on 23 July 2026. The ruling is on hold, and the asylum restrictions have stayed in force during the litigation.

Two Sides of the Argument

The government, in a petition signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, argues that asylum is “a purely discretionary benefit” and that officials need not accept applications that would be denied. It also says the class-wide order violates federal law and that the class is too broad.

The government adds that border encounters fell 93% after the proclamation, to the lowest levels since the 1960s. It says the asylum limits are central to that result.

Lee Gelernt, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union, is counsel for the plaintiffs on their brief opposing review. In their filing opposing review, the plaintiffs said the appeals court applied a reading of the law that the executive branch itself held for decades.

A Separate Case on the Same Border

This is not the earlier case Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, No. 25-5, about “metering”, the practice of limiting how many people officers inspect each day at border crossings. The Court decided that case on 25 June 2026, after arguments on 24 March 2026.

It held that a person standing in Mexico has not “arrive[d] in the United States” under the asylum statute until he crosses the border. That ruling concerned people waiting at the line, while the new case concerns people who cross without permission.

What the Ban Means at the Mexican Border

Anyone who crosses from Mexico illegally still cannot apply for asylum today. The Court’s order does not change who is covered today.

The Court’s order does not address Mexico’s side of the border. We found no official count of migrants now waiting in Mexican border cities because of the proclamation.

What to Watch Next

Under the Court’s Rule 25, the government’s main brief is due 45 days after the grant, which falls on Monday, 28 December 2026 unless the Court extends it. The plaintiffs then have 30 days after that filing to respond.

The Court has not published an argument date for this case. Arguments are heard after the parties file their written briefs.

What Is Not Known

The docket gives no argument date. No Supreme Court ruling on the merits exists, and the justices’ views are unknown.

What It Means for You

If you follow US border policy, this case asks whether an entry-suspension power can end asylum claims at the southern border. The restrictions apply while the case is pending.

Our earlier report on asylum claims filed in Mexico covers the other side of the line, and our story on a Chilean father held in Utah after an asylum bid shows the process on the US side. More coverage is in our Mexico news section.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Supreme Court decide on 13 November 2026?

It agreed to hear the government’s appeal in No. 26-239 and limited review to two of the three questions raised. It has not ruled on the merits.

Is the asylum ban in force now?

Yes. The appeals court ruling is on hold, so the restrictions have stayed in place during the litigation.

When will the Court hear arguments?

No date is set on the Court’s docket. Arguments are heard after the parties file their briefs.

Who brought the case?

Three immigrant legal service providers and 13 individuals sued on behalf of a class of people covered by the proclamation. Lee Gelernt of the American Civil Liberties Union is their counsel on the brief.

Sources: US Supreme Court docket, No. 26-239; Government petition for certiorari (24 August 2026); Plaintiffs’ brief in opposition (23 September 2026); White House, Proclamation of 20 January 2025; Supreme Court opinion, Mullin v. Al Otro Lado (25 June 2026); Supreme Court Rules (2026); US Customs and Border Protection release (16 October 2026).

World.title: Brazil Bank Says Some Big Farmers Skip Loans
World.content:
Brazil: Banking

Key Facts RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesMarkets, currencies and the economy › RT Ask Rio Times Latin American markets, currencies and companies. × Markets today The currency Rates & inflation Economy outlook Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Claim. Banco do Brasil’s chief executive says some large farm borrowers chose not to pay or renegotiate. —Profit. Adjusted third-quarter profit fell 66.5% to R$1.27 billion (about US$0.22 billion). —Overdue loans. Loans overdue 90 days or more reached 6.08% of the bank’s book, up from 4.51%. —Pushback. Aprosoja Brasil, an association of soy and corn growers, criticised the remarks. —As of. Friday 13 November 2026. Exchange rate: R$5.67 per US$1.

Brazil’s biggest farm lender says some of its largest borrowers are holding back payments on purpose, a charge the farm lobby rejects.

What the Bank Said

Banco do Brasil (BB), the state-controlled bank with the farm loan book described below, reported its third-quarter results on Wednesday 11 November 2026. Its chief executive, Tarciana Medeiros, told investors on Thursday 12 November that part of its medium and large farm borrowers had refused to pay or to renegotiate.

She called it “moral hazard,” meaning a bet that a later government rescue will make non-payment cheap. She said the bank had not expected the problem to last, and that the arrears are concentrated in the Centre-West, Brazil’s main grain region.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Brazil 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What the Numbers Show

BB’s results summary of 11 November reports adjusted net profit of R$1.27 billion (about US$0.22 billion), down 66.5% from R$3.79 billion (about US$0.67 billion) a year earlier. The cost of credit, the money set aside for loans that may not be repaid, reached R$21.2 billion (about US$3.7 billion) in the quarter.

Loans overdue by 90 days or more stood at 6.08% of the bank’s portfolio at the end of September 2026, against 4.51% a year earlier, the summary says. BB’s agribusiness book was R$403.6 billion (about US$71.2 billion), down 4.3% from June and up 1.2% from a year earlier.

Loans overdue 90 days or more: 6.08% of BB’s book in September 2026, against 4.51% a year earlier. Banco do Brasil results summary, 11 November 2026.

Why It Matters

BB is a state lender to Brazilian agriculture, so its overdue loans are a direct reading of stress on farms that export soy, corn and beef to world markets. Its farm book of R$403.6 billion (about US$71.2 billion), reported on 11 November, is the base on which that stress is measured.

The question for readers is whether the arrears reflect crop losses and high interest rates or a deliberate wait for relief. The bank’s own figures show higher overdue loans but do not say which borrowers chose not to pay.

What Farm Groups Say

Aprosoja Brasil, an association of soy and corn growers, criticised the remarks and said that debt problems in the sector need solutions rather than accusations. Brazil’s Congress has meanwhile sent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a farm debt relief bill that the Senate approved on Wednesday 11 November 2026.

Our earlier report on that debt relief bill explains its terms, and our report on BB’s results covers the share price reaction. The bill is a separate matter from the bank’s claim about moral hazard.

In Plain English

—Adjusted profit. Profit with one-off items removed, as the bank reports it. —Moral hazard. Not paying a debt in the hope that a later rescue will cancel the cost. —Overdue 90 days or more. Loans on which a payment is at least three months late. —Centre-West. Brazil’s main grain-growing region, west of São Paulo.

What To Watch Next

Brazil’s constitution gives the president 15 working days after receiving a bill to sign or veto it, and the date on which the debt relief bill reached Lula has not been published. The bank has not said when it will publish its next set of results.

What Is Not Known

BB’s summary does not break down which borrowers are overdue or why, and the bank has not named any borrower. The size of any relief package and its cost to the public purse are also unconfirmed.

What It Means for You

For a US reader, the story is a credit signal from the lender at the centre of Brazil’s farm economy, a major supplier of soy and beef. It does not by itself show how crops or export volumes will move.

Farmers who repay on time are affected if the bank tightens lending in response, and taxpayers are affected if relief is granted. Neither outcome has been decided.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Banco do Brasil say about farm borrowers?

Chief executive Tarciana Medeiros said some medium and large farm borrowers refused to pay or renegotiate. She called it moral hazard.

How much of the bank’s loan book is overdue?

Loans overdue by 90 days or more were 6.08% of BB’s book in September 2026, against 4.51% a year earlier. That is the bank’s figure for the whole portfolio, not only farm loans.

Did farm groups respond?

Yes. Aprosoja Brasil, an association of soy and corn growers, criticised the remarks and called for solutions to farm debt.

Is a farm debt relief law coming?

The Senate approved a farm debt relief bill on 11 November 2026 and it now goes to President Lula. He has not announced whether he will sign it.

Sources: Banco do Brasil, results summary for the third quarter of 2026 (11 November 2026, ri.bb.com.br); Federal Senate, news service, vote of 11 November 2026 (senado.leg.br); Brazilian Constitution, article 66.

World.title: Bogotá Power Group Seeks 450 Million Shares
World.content:
Office towers in northern Bogotá, the city that controls GEB. File photo. photo. Aerial view of northern Bogotá, Colombia, with the office towers of the Santa Bárbara business area, March 2018. Photo: Alejandro Turola, CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

Companies: Colombia

Grupo Energía Bogotá (GEB), an electricity and natural gas company controlled by the city of Bogotá, will ask shareholders on Monday 30 November 2026 to approve issuing up to 450 million new shares. The company announced the call on Friday 13 November 2026 as part of its plan to list in the United States.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. —Proposal. Shareholders vote on 30 November on issuing up to 450 million new ordinary (common) shares. —Size. The cap equals about 4.9% of the roughly 9.18 billion shares now in issue. —Control. The city of Bogotá holds 65.68% of the company, on GEB’s latest shareholder list. —Open terms. Price, final number of shares and timing would be set later by the company’s board. —Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index, with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

What GEB Is Asking Shareholders to Approve

GEB said its board called an extraordinary shareholder meeting for 30 November 2026 so the company would have the option of raising capital through an issue of ordinary shares and a possible public offering at home and abroad. The company links the step to its international listing project and its growth strategy.

The agenda covers an issue of up to 450 million ordinary shares, placed without the preemptive rights that normally let existing owners buy first, according to the notice summarised by Bogotá’s business press. It would also hand the board the decision on timing, final amount and placement terms.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Grupo Energía Bogotá (Colombia) Email address Follow

Who Controls the Company

GEB’s own latest list of top shareholders shows Bogotá Distrito Capital, the city government, with 6.03 billion shares, or 65.68%.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

By our arithmetic, the shares in issue come to about 9.18 billion, so 450 million new shares would be about 4.9% on top. If the city did not buy any and the full amount were sold, its stake would fall to roughly 62.6%.

Why It Matters for US Investors

On 28 September 2026, GEB said, holders of 99.97% of the shares represented at an extraordinary meeting backed starting registration with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, the American market regulator. The same vote approved a US listing through American depositary receipts (ADRs), which are certificates that trade in dollars and stand for shares in Colombia; see our

plan for a US listing.

A new share issue would be the way fresh money could reach the company ahead of such a listing. The city keeping a majority, or not, will shape how US investors weigh the stock.

Plaza de Bolívar in central Bogotá, seat of the city government. File photo. photo. Plaza de Bolívar in Bogotá with the Palacio de Justicia, the cathedral and Monserrate hill, Colombia, 2011. Photo: Baiji, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

What Is Not Known

GEB has not published a price, the final number of shares or a date for any sale. It also has not said how much would go to which project, and we have no confirmed US$ value for the issue.

What to Watch Next

The extraordinary meeting is set for Monday 30 November 2026, and GEB said it would publish the meeting documents on its website within the notice period. Any placement date is not confirmed.

For earlier context, see our report on GEB’s

third-quarter results and our Colombia coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many new shares could GEB issue?

Up to 450 million ordinary shares, if shareholders approve on 30 November 2026. That is a ceiling, and the board would set the final number.

Would existing shareholders get first call?

The proposal is to place the shares without the preemptive rights in GEB’s bylaws. That means current owners would not automatically be offered new shares in proportion to their stake.

Who controls GEB?

The city of Bogotá holds 65.68% through Bogotá Distrito Capital, according to GEB’s latest shareholder list. No sale price has been set.

World.title: Brazil Retailers End Dispute Dating to 2009
World.content:
Companies: Brazil

Casas Bahia, Brazil’s large home-goods retailer now under court-supervised restructuring, and GPA, owner of the Pão de Açúcar supermarkets, settled their dispute over a 2009 partnership on Friday 13 November 2026. Casas Bahia keeps tax credits GPA gave up and takes on tax debts, while GPA’s own filing adds R$174 million (about US$31 million) in reversed provisions.

Casas Bahia takes on tax debts of about R$424 million (about US$75 million). —Still owed. What the Two Companies Agreed

Both companies published a “Fato Relevante” (a material-fact notice) on Friday 13 November 2026 with the CVM, Brazil’s securities regulator. Grupo Casas Bahia (BHIA3 on the São Paulo stock exchange, in judicial recovery, Brazil’s court-supervised protection from creditors) and Companhia Brasileira de Distribuição, known as GPA (PCAR3), said the deal closes pending issues from their 4 December 2009 association agreement.

The two companies also committed to cooperate and not to sue each other on the subjects it covers.

The São Paulo skyline. File photo. photo: the São Paulo skyline behind Ibirapuera Park. Photo: Sérgio Valle Duarte, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Who Gets What

Casas Bahia said GPA’s right to a share of PIS/COFINS credits, federal tax credits that arose when state sales tax was removed from the tax base, is extinguished. The company put them at about R$700 million (US$124 million) and said it may now use them without passing money to GPA, while GPA’s notice gives the figure as R$708 million (US$125 million).

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

In return, Casas Bahia said it takes responsibility for contingencies tied to the 2009 agreement, including tax debts of about R$424 million (US$75 million) in nominal value. GPA said its duty to reimburse Casas Bahia for those tax contingencies, estimated at R$424 million, is extinguished.

A R$231.8 million (US$41 million) credit that Casas Bahia holds against GPA, recognised in arbitration, remains owed, Casas Bahia said. It will be paid under GPA’s out-of-court recovery plan, and enforcement of that award is suspended until the securities the plan provides for are subscribed.

GPA said it keeps paying the tax instalment plans linked to the 2009 agreement and will reimburse Casas Bahia for certain past guarantee and legal-process costs. Neither company disclosed those amounts.

What It Means for You

For investors in either stock, the notices show a trade rather than a cash payment: Casas Bahia gains usable tax credits but takes on debts of about US$75 million. GPA said it will reverse a R$174 million (US$31 million) provision in the fourth quarter of 2026, after it wrote off the full R$708 million of credits in the third quarter.

Casas Bahia said the settlement brings “more legal certainty and financial predictability” and lowers future litigation costs. GPA said it “resolves one more structural liability”; our earlier reports cover the

Casas Bahia court case and GPA’s debt plan.

What Is Not Known

The notices, as we read them, give no net value of the deal for either company. They also give no effective date or further approvals needed.

What to Watch Next

GPA’s fourth-quarter 2026 results will show the R$174 million reversal, and the date is not confirmed. The date for subscribing the securities under GPA’s recovery plan is also not confirmed.

Our reports on both companies are linked above. More is in our

Brazil coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Casas Bahia and GPA agree?

They ended disputes from their December 2009 association agreement. GPA gave up its claim to about R$700 million (US$124 million) of tax credits, and Casas Bahia took on contingencies including tax debts of about R$424 million (US$75 million).

Does GPA still owe Casas Bahia money?

Yes. A R$231.8 million (US$41 million) credit recognised in arbitration remains owed and will be paid under GPA’s out-of-court recovery plan.
