World.title: Brazil Police Probe Flood Pump Contracts
World.content:
Security: Brazil

Key Facts RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —Raid. Brazil’s Federal Police searched 13 addresses on Friday 13 November 2026 over flood pump contracts. —Money. More than R$10 million (about US$1.8 million) was blocked and three vehicles were seized. —Overpricing. Police estimate Canoas paid at least R$7 million (about US$1.2 million) too much. —Status. The targets are under investigation. No one has been formally charged. —As of. Friday 13 November 2026, 6:50 p.m. ET. Exchange rate used: R$5.67 per US$1.

Brazilian police are examining whether two cities near Porto Alegre paid several times the real price to rent water pumps during the deadly 2024 floods, using federal disaster money.

Brazil’s Federal Police, the national force that investigates federal crimes, carried out 13 search warrants on Friday 13 November 2026 in a case code-named Operação Deságue (“Operation Drainage”). The probe covers emergency contracts to rent and run motor pumps in Canoas and Cachoeirinha, two cities in the Porto Alegre, the capital of Rio Grande do Sul state metro area, after the May 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul state.

The contracts were paid with federal money meant for disaster response, so the case tests how Brazil supervises emergency spending. No US company or US funds are named, and readers in the United States are affected mainly as observers of how a large emerging economy polices disaster aid.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Why It Matters

Emergency contracts are signed fast, with little time for price checks, which is where overpricing can hide. The floods hit hard: an official bulletin of the Rio Grande do Sul civil defence agency on 27 June 2024 counted 179 confirmed deaths, 34 missing people and 2,398,255 people affected across 478 municipalities.

Police say the pumps were rented from a company without the operating capacity to run them. They say that company was favoured and passed the work to specialised firms for less than the cities paid.

In Plain English —Federal Police. Brazil’s national police force for federal crimes, comparable to the FBI. —Motobombas. Motor pumps used to move floodwater out of streets and neighbourhoods. —Overpricing. Charging far more than the real cost of a service. —Target. A person police are investigating, who has not been charged or found guilty.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Brazil 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

What Police Say They Found

Police say the warrants were served in eight municipalities, seven of them in Rio Grande do Sul state: Pelotas, Porto Alegre, São Leopoldo, Cachoeirinha, Gravataí, Capão da Canoa and Canoas. They were also served in Itapema, a coastal city in the neighbouring state of Santa Catarina.

In Canoas, the investigation points to charges between nine and ten times the real cost for certain services. Police put the overpricing in the Canoas contracts at no less than R$7 million (about US$1.2 million).

In Cachoeirinha, the service under investigation involved two pumps used from 13 May to 13 June 2024, a period of one month. Police also say some price quotes were drawn up or signed after the work had started, or even after it had ended.

Money Trail and Possible Charges

Investigators say they found cash withdrawals and transfers to individuals and companies with no apparent link to running the pumps. A court order froze more than R$10 million (about US$1.8 million) in financial assets and three vehicles were seized.

The suspects could be formally indicted for bid or contract fraud, active and passive corruption, criminal association and money laundering. Active corruption means offering a bribe, while passive corruption means accepting one.

What To Watch Next

No court dates, deadlines or formal charging decisions have been made public yet. The next visible step would be a decision by prosecutors on whether to bring charges, and no date for that has been confirmed.

Analysis of the seized material and the frozen accounts will shape that decision. No official body has yet published a timetable.

What Is Not Known

Police have not published the names of all the targets, the identity of the pump-rental company, or the exact contract values. It is also unclear how the “nine to ten times” comparison was calculated for each contract.

The cities’ own accounts of how the contracts were awarded are not part of the police statement. Targets are presumed innocent unless a court rules otherwise.

What It Means for You

For US readers, the story is a case study in disaster-aid oversight rather than a threat to any US investment. It matters most to anyone who follows how Brazil handles public money after climate events.

The people most affected are residents of flooded neighbourhoods and taxpayers in the two cities, whose emergency budgets are in question. More cases may follow if investigators widen the probe, and the 2024 floods may keep drawing scrutiny.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Operação Deságue?

It is a Brazilian Federal Police investigation into suspected fraud in emergency flood contracts. It was launched on Friday 13 November 2026.

How much money is involved?

Police estimate overpricing of at least R$7 million (about US$1.2 million) in Canoas. More than R$10 million (about US$1.8 million) in assets was blocked.

Has anyone been convicted?

No. The targets are under investigation and could face charges, but none has been formally charged.

Which cities are involved?

The contracts were with Canoas and Cachoeirinha, near Porto Alegre in Rio Grande do Sul state. Warrants were also served in other cities, including Itapema in Santa Catarina.

World.title: Brazil Court Gives Lula 3 Days on Spending
World.content:
Politics: Brazil

Key Facts RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesWhat this means, and what's next › RT Ask Rio Times This story and the bigger picture. × Economy impact Key players Stability What's next Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times → —As of. Friday, 13 November 2026, 6 p.m. ET. —Order. Minister Dias Toffoli of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE) gave Lula’s ticket three days to answer. —Dates. Signed Thursday, 12 November; made public Friday, 13 November 2026. —Questions. Court accountants queried subcontracting, flight tickets, official vehicles, boosted online ads and supplier capacity. —Status. This is a request for explanations, not a finding of wrongdoing or a ruling on the accounts.

A minister of Brazil’s electoral court has given President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s ticket three days to explain spending questions raised by court accountants. Reviewing campaign accounts is routine, and a finding at this stage is a request for answers, not a verdict.

What the Order Says

Dias Toffoli, a minister of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court (TSE), the body that runs and judges elections, ordered Lula’s ticket to explain its 2026 campaign accounts within three days. The ticket pairs Lula with Vice President Geraldo Alckmin.

The order was signed on Thursday 12 November and made public on Friday 13 November 2026. It follows a request from the court’s technical accounts unit, known as Asepa.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 74.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The order warns that missing the deadline could bar new documents at this stage, a rule Brazilian courts call preclusão. The public record does not say whether the three days run in calendar or working days.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Brazil 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

The Questions Court Accountants Raised

The technical unit listed several points on which it wants documents or explanations. The list below follows the order’s own categories, and none of the points is a finding of wrongdoing.

Points Raised in the Order —Subcontracting. Signs that suppliers paid with public campaign money from the Special Campaign Financing Fund passed work to others, and proof they could do the work themselves. —Flight tickets. Apparent mismatches in dates, times or itineraries, and proof the tickets were tied to the campaign. —Official vehicles. Possible use of state cars and drivers for campaign trips, and any reimbursements owed to public funds. —Boosted ads. Paid promotion of campaign posts; the order asks for documents tied to a separate case in which another TSE minister, André Mendonça, found paid boosting irregular on 25 September 2026.

Parties receive public money for campaigns from the FEFC, the Special Campaign Financing Fund. That makes questions about suppliers and official vehicles a matter of public money, which is why the accountants press for receipts.

Why a Routine Review Is Not a Verdict

Every candidate in Brazil must file campaign accounts, and the court’s accountants check them before judges decide. Asking for clarification is a normal step in that process, and a technical finding is not a verdict.

Under TSE Resolution 23.607 of 2019, judges can approve accounts, approve them with reservations, disapprove them or declare them not filed. Disapproval can require a campaign to return irregular money to the Treasury.

The same court approved the Lula and Alckmin accounts unanimously on Tuesday 6 December 2022, after a minister had also given the campaign three days to explain some spending. That earlier case shows a request for explanations can end in approval.

In Plain English —TSE. Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, which runs elections and judges campaign disputes. —Asepa. The court’s technical unit that examines campaign and party accounts. —Preclusão. The loss of the right to file something after a deadline has passed. —Treasury. The federal government’s public funds, to which misused campaign money must be repaid.

What Happens Next

After the deadline, the technical unit is expected to review whatever the campaign files. A judgment by the court’s ministers would follow only after that review.

No dated checkpoint beyond the three-day deadline has been confirmed by the court. A technical opinion and a scheduled judgment are the next dates to look for, and neither has been announced.

We found no public statement from the Lula and Alckmin campaign on the points raised. Its written reply to the court is where its view will appear.

What Is Not Known

Whether Toffoli is the rapporteur (the judge who steers the case) and the exact start of the three-day count are not confirmed. The court’s own case file was not reachable at the time of writing, so the full text of the order is unchecked.

The campaign has not yet said which points it disputes. Nothing in the public record shows how much money, if any, would need to be repaid.

What It Means for You

For US readers the direct effect is limited, because this is an accounts review and not a market-moving ruling. It matters mainly to those following Brazilian politics and the rules on campaign money.

A separate abuse-of-power case against the same ticket is covered in our report on the electoral court probe of the Lula and Alckmin ticket. More coverage sits in our Brazil news hub and in our report on the fight over Brazil’s House speaker.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Dias Toffoli order?

He gave President Lula’s ticket three days to explain questions about its 2026 campaign accounts. The order was signed on Thursday 12 November and made public on Friday 13 November.

Is this a finding of wrongdoing?

No. The points come from the court’s technical accounts unit and are requests for documents and explanations, not a judgment.

What can the court decide on the accounts?

Under TSE Resolution 23.607, judges can approve the accounts, approve them with reservations, disapprove them or declare them not filed. No judgment date has been announced.

Which items did the accountants question?

They queried subcontracting, flight tickets, possible use of official vehicles, boosted online ads and supplier capacity. The order does not say whether any of these points amounts to a breach of the rules.

Sources

Superior Electoral Court (TSE) order of 12 November 2026, made public 13 November; TSE Resolution 23.607 on campaign accounts.

World.title: Costa Rica Flights Caught in Only the Third Nationwide US Ground Stop Ever
World.content:
If you’re flying between the United States and Costa Rica this afternoon or tonight, expect delays and possible cancellations. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) stopped every departing flight across the United States on Friday, citing “extraordinary circumstances” and “reasons of safety.”

The order took effect shortly before 4 p.m. Eastern time, just before 3 p.m. in Costa Rica. It stays in place until further notice. Any flight scheduled to leave a U.S. airport for San José or Liberia is grounded for now. That includes flights from the Florida hubs that carry much of Costa Rica’s U.S. traffic, such as Miami, Fort Lauderdale and Orlando, as well as other major gateways.

Planes already in the air are being allowed to continue to their destinations. Flights from Costa Rica to the United States are less clear. The FAA said inbound international flights will be handled case by case. Even if your flight is cleared, it may still be late. Many U.S. airlines fly a plane into Costa Rica and send the same aircraft back, so a jet stuck on the ground in Miami or Houston means a late or canceled departure here.

The FAA hasn’t officially said what caused the stop. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue is affecting all of the country’s Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which handle planes flying between airports. Outages on radio frequencies used by controllers had been reported in parts of the country before the order was issued.

There’s no confirmed time for flights to restart. Some flight-tracking services listed 5 p.m. Eastern time, or 4 p.m. in Costa Rica, as the first point the order would be reviewed, but it could be extended. Delays will likely last well past the end of the stop, because planes and crews will be out of position. In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop of about 90 minutes, triggered by the failure of a computer system that sends safety notices to pilots, led to more than 11,000 delays and cancellations.

Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare. The January 2023 one was the most recent. Before that, the only other was ordered after the September 11, 2001, attacks. Check your flight with your airline before you head to the airport. Airline apps and text alerts usually update before airport departure boards do.

Look for a travel waiver on your airline’s website. During large disruptions, airlines often let you change your flight without a fee, which can be easier than waiting for a rebooking. If your flight is canceled and you decide not to travel, U.S. rules entitle you to a cash refund, even when the cause is out of the airline’s control. Airlines aren’t required to pay for hotels or meals when the disruption isn’t their fault, so keep your receipts if you have travel insurance that covers delays.

If you’re connecting through a U.S. hub, you may miss your connection even after flights restart. Rebook through the airline that issued your ticket rather than each carrier separately. Updates on local flights are posted on the official social media channels of Juan Santamaría International Airport and Guanacaste Airport.

This is a developing story and will be updated as the FAA and airlines release more information.

World.title: Banks and Businesses in Costa Rica Must Accept Digital ID Starting January
World.content:
Starting January 1, 2027, banks, government agencies, businesses and other institutions in Costa Rica will be required to accept the Costa Rican Digital Identity (IDC), the smartphone version of the national ID card, for any transaction or procedure that requires identification. The Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) said the digital credential carries the same legal validity as the traditional plastic ID card. From that date, institutions will no longer be able to turn it away simply because it is presented on a phone.

The digital ID has been available since September 9, 2025, but until now institutions could decide whether to accept it. According to the TSE, 107,243 people had requested one as of November 1, 2026. The change could make everyday procedures simpler, from banking to administrative paperwork and any service that requires proof of identity. It does not replace the physical card, which will continue to be issued and accepted throughout the country.

Unlike the physical ID, which is free for most applicants, the digital version costs 2,600 colones (about $5.80) and is valid for four years. Senior citizens are exempt from the fee. The service is available only to Costa Rican citizens. Applicants need a valid physical ID card, a smartphone with an active phone line running iOS or Android, and no identity document waiting to be collected at the TSE.

People applying for their first Costa Rican ID must get the physical card before they can request the digital version. Applications are handled online through the TSE website at tse.go.cr/idc. Applicants enter their ID number, complete an identity verification step, provide a valid email address and pay with a Visa or Mastercard credit or debit card.

Once the application is approved, the credential is activated through the official IDC-Ciudadano app, available on Apple’s App Store and Google Play. It is protected by a personal PIN and facial recognition, which the TSE checks against the biometric data collected during the holder’s most recent physical ID procedure.

Citizens can still obtain or renew their physical IDs free of charge at the TSE’s headquarters in San José or at any of its 32 regional offices. A fee applies only when a person exceeds the annual limit on duplicate replacements. The January requirement applies to the institutions that must accept the credential, not to citizens. Getting a digital ID remains optional, and anyone who prefers the plastic card can keep using it.

World.title: Heavy Storms Could Drop Nearly 3 Inches of Rain on Costa Rica Today
World.content:
The rest of this Friday afternoon could bring short, heavy downpours and thunderstorms to the Central Valley, the northern zone and the Caribbean. If you still have to get somewhere today, plan your trip around them. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) expects intense storms lasting one to three hours, with 20 to 40 millimeters (0.8 to 1.6 inches) of rain in most affected areas. In the Central Valley, the Caribbean and the northern zone, totals could reach 70 millimeters (2.8 inches).

That much rain in a short window can overwhelm city drains and push creeks over their banks, especially in the Central Valley. If you live or park near a stream or on a street that floods, move your car early and don’t drive through standing water. Wind is the other risk. Isolated gusts could reach 80 kilometers per hour (50 mph), strong enough to bring down branches and power lines. When a storm hits, get indoors and keep away from trees and fallen cables.

The mountains and the eastern and northeastern parts of the Central Valley have the highest chance of storms. Rain could also spread to the northern lowlands and the northern Caribbean. On the Pacific side, expect storms in the mountains of the Central and South Pacific. The Nicoya Peninsula and the southeast of the North Pacific should see less activity.

The storms come in bursts rather than as an all-day rain. If one hits while you’re on the road or about to drive home, it is usually safer to wait it out than to push through it. The reason for the change is the trade winds. They usually keep the Pacific side dry at this time of year, and earlier this week they were bringing strong gusts across the country. Now they have weakened, which lets sea breezes and westerly winds carry moist Pacific air inland. Warm temperatures then build storm clouds over the mountains by afternoon.

This back-and-forth is typical of the transition from the rainy season to the dry season, which has already begun in Guanacaste and the Central Valley. Unsettled weather continues into Saturday, with more chances of afternoon rain. From Tuesday, the IMN expects rising pressure over the Caribbean Sea to strengthen the trade winds again.

If you’re driving between the Central Valley and the Caribbean coast, keep an eye on Route 32. Heavy rain in the mountains is what brings rock and mud down onto the highway through Braulio Carrillo National Park, which has closed repeatedly this year. If Route 32 closes, the usual alternatives are Route 10 through Turrialba and Route 126 through Vara Blanca. Both are narrower and slower, so leave extra time.

Check the IMN’s website and social media for updated warnings before you head out this afternoon or on Saturday.

World.title: Salvadoran Troops Turn Haiti National Stadium Into Base After Retaking It From Gangs
World.content:
El Salvador will turn Haiti’s national soccer stadium into a forward base for its troops after Salvadoran and Haitian forces retook the Sylvio Cator stadium in Port-au-Prince from armed gangs on Thursday, President Nayib Bukele announced. The joint operation took place in the early hours yesterday and involved the Haitian National Police, the Armed Forces of Haiti, a government-contracted security unit known as the Task Force, and Salvadoran special forces, according to Bukele and Haitian police. Bukele said it was carried out under a bilateral agreement between the two governments.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that its officers had taken full control of the stadium and its surroundings before handing security of the complex to the Salvadoran armed forces. More than 20 armored vehicles and trucks carrying Salvadoran military personnel were stationed inside the stadium after the operation, according to local media reports.

Bukele said troops found several human skulls inside the facility. Authorities have not announced any identification of the remains or said whether they will be examined. The Salvadoran president said his forces would use the stadium as a base to advance deeper into territory held by gangs, and that the allied forces now hold the advantage on the ground.

In a message addressed directly to gang members, he told them to leave the area before the next phase of operations begins and warned that those who stay to fight Salvadoran and Haitian forces will face the consequences. He did not give a start date. The stadium, home ground of Haiti’s national soccer team, had been held by gangs since early 2024. Its loss forced Haiti to play every one of its home qualifiers for the 2026 World Cup outside the country.

The recovery is the latest step in a rapidly expanding Salvadoran military presence in Haiti. El Salvador has deployed more than 2,000 troops since October 18, when gangs ambushed an armored vehicle carrying four Salvadoran Air Force aviation technicians in Croix-des-Bouquets, northeast of Port-au-Prince. The Salvadoran military said the vehicle was struck by gunfire and explosives and caught fire, and that the four men got out before going missing.

The technicians were serving with the Gang Suppression Force, a multinational mission authorized by the United Nations Security Council to support Haitian police against armed groups that control large parts of the capital and other areas. Salvadoran officials have described them as non-combat personnel whose main job was carrying out medical evacuations.

The Salvadoran government maintains that the four are alive, but their whereabouts remained unknown as of now. Bukele has previously offered to withdraw all Salvadoran forces from Haiti if the technicians are released unharmed. The Gang Suppression Force has distanced itself from the actions of the Salvadoran troops sent in after the ambush, which operate under the separate bilateral arrangement with the Haitian government. Bukele has said the contingent is focused on confronting the gangs responsible for the October attack and related violence.

The stadium operation came two days after Bukele said Salvadoran troops had destroyed the headquarters of the 400 Mawozo gang, an operation for which Haiti’s prime minister publicly praised the Salvadoran leader. Gang violence in Haiti has forced nearly 1.5 million people from their homes, and the international force sent to help contain it has so far deployed only a fraction of the 5,550 personnel the Security Council authorized.

World.title: Shakira Returns to Costa Rica in 2027 After More Than 15 Years
World.content:
Shakira’s world tour has added Costa Rica to its 2027 Latin American leg. It’s the strongest sign yet that the Colombian superstar will perform at the National Stadium in La Sabana on Sunday, January 31. It would be her first concert in the country since April 2011. The tour’s official accounts posted a graphic this week listing six countries for the new leg: Brazil, Venezuela, Guatemala, Costa Rica, Puerto Rico and Panama. The post gave no dates or venues for any of the stops.

The January 31 date comes from the Ministry of Economy, Industry and Commerce (MEIC). In October it authorized a presale plan for the show. The authorization lists an 8 p.m. start at the National Stadium and lets the production company, Two Shows Ltda., sell 53,114 tickets through eticket.cr.

Ticket prices and the on-sale date have not been announced. The ministry requires a presale authorization before any large event goes on sale, to protect buyers, but it doesn’t mean tickets are available. Wait for an official announcement and buy only through the authorized seller.

There is a reason for caution. In September 2024, the ministry approved a presale of 51,446 tickets for a Shakira concert at the same stadium on March 27, 2025. That show never happened bug the difference this time is that the tour itself has named Costa Rica as a stop.

The show is part of the Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour, named after her 2024 album, her first studio record in seven years. The tour opened in Rio de Janeiro in February 2025. Her production team says the tour has grossed more than $534 million and sold over four million tickets worldwide. Shakira recently closed a 13-show residency in Madrid that drew more than 700,000 people.

She has played Costa Rica twice before. She brought her Pies Descalzos tour to the Palacio de los Deportes in Heredia in 1995. She then performed at the National Stadium on April 3, 2011, shortly after the stadium opened. A full stadium on the last Sunday of January would also land in the middle of high season, when flights and hotels around San José are already busy.

Prices, seating sections and the sale date are expected once the producers make a formal announcement.

World.title: Finish Your Government Paperwork by Dec. 21 as Costa Rica Offices Close
World.content:
The government has ordered seven days of collective vacation for public employees: Dec. 22, 23, 24, 28, 29, 30 and 31. With Christmas, New Year’s Day and two weekends in between, offices that work Monday to Friday will be closed from Tuesday, Dec. 22, through Sunday, Jan. 3. Staff return on Monday, Jan. 4, 2027.

President Laura Fernández signed the directive with Planning Minister Carla Morales Rojas and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla. The government announced it on Thursday, Nov. 12. It takes legal effect once it’s published in the official gazette La Gaceta. The tricky part is that not every public office follows the same calendar. If you assume everything closes, or that everything stays open, you could be caught out.

The directive covers the central and decentralized public administration, meaning the ministries and the agencies under them. Five groups set their own dates instead: the Education Ministry (MEP), the Office of the Attorney General (Procuraduría General de la República), the National Registry, police forces and emergency institutions. The leaders of each will decide based on what their services need.

Other branches of government don’t have to follow the order. The Legislative Assembly has already approved its own recess, from Dec. 21 to 31. The judiciary sets its own year-end closure under its 2026 vacation plan. In June it ruled that a similar government directive was not binding on the courts.

Autonomous institutions and municipalities also decide for themselves. When the government ordered a collective vacation week in July, the Social Security System (CCSS), the Comptroller General’s Office, the public universities and the judiciary all chose to keep working. Some services keep running no matter what. Every institution must keep essential services open and have staff ready for emergencies. Health care and public security must not be interrupted.

Each institution must also publish its holiday hours and say which service channels stay open. Most had not done so as of Nov. 13. Check the schedule for the office you need before you make the trip. Immigration is where an unplanned gap hurts most. If you have a residency application, a DIMEX renewal or another filing with the General Directorate of Migration and Immigration, finish it well before Dec. 21 and expect appointments to be in high demand. In past years, Migración has partly closed its main office in La Uruca over the holidays. In 2023 it also stopped accepting new filings on its digital platform until offices reopened.

Immigration control at airports and border crossings continues through the holidays because it is a security function. Some land border posts have changed their hours over the holidays in past years. If you plan to cross by land, check the hours first. If you’re buying property, registering a company or transferring a vehicle, the National Registry’s dates matter. The Registry will set its own schedule, so ask your lawyer or notary when it will stop receiving documents. A sale signed in late December may not be recorded until January.

One deadline does not move: the 2027 marchamo, the annual vehicle circulation fee, is due by Dec. 31. It’s collected by the National Insurance Institute (INS), not a ministry. You can pay it online, in banking apps or at authorized payment points. From Jan. 1, unpaid vehicles face fines, surcharges and possible removal of their plates.

If you need a Costa Rican criminal record certificate (hoja de delincuencia), request it early. The Judicial Registry issues these certificates. During last year’s judicial closure it shut for the first week and reopened with shorter hours in the second. Tax filings with the Finance Ministry are made online, but the ministry has not announced its holiday schedule. If a filing or payment deadline falls between Dec. 22 and Jan. 3, ask your accountant whether it moves. If you have a court case or a legal deadline, the judiciary’s calendar applies, not the government’s.

The state-owned banks compete with private banks, and in the past the government has only invited companies like them to join its collective vacations. Online banking normally runs through the holidays, but check branch hours before you go. The government says the closure will reduce the large backlog of unused vacation days in the public sector. It also expects savings on electricity, water, telecommunications and fuel. The seven days come out of each employee’s own vacation balance.

The directive also allows the Ministry of the Interior and Police to give public employees in central San José the day off on Dec. 31 for the city’s year-end civic festivities. The simplest plan: if a task needs a government stamp, signature or appointment, finish it by Dec. 21. Then check the published schedule of the specific office before heading out in late December.
