World.title: Prosecution miss? Pia Cayetano hits questioning on support for sports
World.content:
During the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, Senator-judge Pia Cayetano expresses 'disdain' over the prosecution's questions for defense witness Chadrin Parian

At the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, an emotional Cayetano took a jab at the prosecution over its line of questioning of a defense witness who is a parent of a young athlete.

Cayetano, an athlete and sports advocate, appeared to take personally the questions of House prosecutor Reynaldo Robles for witness Chadrin Parian, expressing her “disdain” over the line of questioning.

“I will not hide my disdain. I cannot,” Cayetano told Robles.

Parian, whose children belong to the same basketball team as Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio, testified during the trial on Thursday, November 12, to explain the P256,000 credit card charge Carpio incurred at a Nike store in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Parian said Carpio had voluntarily offered to pay for the team’s shoes after their international competition.

Robles scrutinized Parian’s explanation, asking whether the witness considered it appropriate for a relative of a public official to spend more than P250,000 on a single purchase, given the constitutional provision directing public officials and their families to lead modest lives.

“My children were 6 and 9 years old when I served my first term as senator. If this happened then, you would impress upon me that, as a law-abiding citizen, I should not put my kids in sports because I will be criticized,” an emotional Cayetano said.

House prosecutors, in separate media interviews, repeatedly clarified that they had no objection to supporting young athletes, stressing that this was not the issue being examined in the impeachment trial.

“That is not the issue. The issue here is our public officials and their relatives should set an example and shy away from what the law calls as ‘ostentatious’ display of wealth, as well as extravagant expenses,” Robles told reporters.

The expenses of public officials, including senators themselves, who support Filipino athletes — including those who end up competing in the Palarong Pambansa, however, hit a sympathetic nerve even among majority senators. Philippine sports, after all, has not been getting a generous share of the budget pie. Was that a miss on the part of the prosecution?

To refocus the questioning, Senator-judge Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri urged the impeachment court to move beyond discussions of credit card expenditures and dwell instead on other substantive issues, including alleged remittances from China to Calle88, a company linked to Duterte.

The credit card purchases are part of lawyer Alex Cabrera’s financial forensic report, which alleged that Duterte and Carpio had accumulated P817 million in undeclared wealth from 2022 to 2025.

“Let’s move on and listen to other witnesses that can give us more substantive answers to the case at hand,” said Zubiri.

Cayetano managed to call attention to the plight of Filipino athletes and the need for greater government support, but the impeachment court’s focus is on the allegations against Duterte. – Rappler.com

World.title: Industry disruption continues: GMA’s profit falls 98% in Q3, ABS-CBN still in red
World.content:
GMA cites the 'continued shift of audiences and advertising budgets from traditional media to digital platforms' and the 'challenging business environment' for its disappointing earnings

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ broadcast industry leader GMA Network (GMA) disclosed a steep 98% fall in net income in the third quarter of 2026, while its erstwhile competitor ABS-CBN reported it was still deep in the red.

In its earnings disclosure on Friday, November 13, publicly listed GMA saw its net income spiral down from P2 billion in Q3 2025 to only P32.85 million in Q3 2026. Revenues fell 31%, or by P4.3 billion, in the same period. EBITDA was also “significantly lower,” dropping 68% from P4.5 billion to P1.4 billion.

Screenshot from GMA Network’s disclosure on November 13, 2026.

“The downturn was attributable to the absence of political advocacies and s in relation to the 2025 mid-term election as well as softening of recurring revenues year-on-year,” the company said.

Advertising revenue was the main culprit, declining 33% or from P12.8 billion in Q3 2025 to P8.6 billion in Q3 2026, but GMA also cited the “continued shift of audiences and advertising budgets from traditional media to digital platforms” for the disappointing performance.

Aside from industry disruption, it also noted the “challenging business environment marked by elevated fuel prices, persistent inflation, supply chain disruptions, rising labor and utility costs, and ongoing geopolitical uncertainties stemming from the Middle East conflict.”

“These conditions drove up production and distribution costs, squeezed profit margins, and prompted businesses to exercise greater caution in their advertising expenditures,” the network said.

GMA’s poor earnings wouldn’t be a big surprise if it hadn’t kept its industry leadership. But, in fact, GMA was still the top television station in the whole country in the first three quarters, based on Nielsen TV Audience Measurement data.

Among its top TV programs were Kapuso Mo, Jessica Soho, and its flagship 24 Oras nightly news show. Its radio stations, Super Radyo DZBB and Barangay LS 97.1, are also ahead in ratings.

GMA’s digital business continues to be a key contributor to revenues, with digital advertising revenues providing the company’s “second largest revenue contributor,” signaling the continued rise of digital platforms.

Meanwhile, still Lopez-led ABS-CBN Corporation, which lost its lucrative broadcast business in 2020 no thanks to the Duterte administration, reported a consolidated net loss of P2.95 billion in Q3 2026 compared to P2.24 billion in Q3 2026, a decline of 32%. (READ: The secret to the Lopez family’s enduring control of ABS-CBN)

Screenshot from ABS-CBN’s disclosure on November 13, 2026.

Total revenues fell by 11% from P11.75 billion in Q3 2025, an election year, to P10.5 billion in Q3 2026.

“The Company continued to face a challenging market environment into the 3rd quarter. Global economic and geopolitical developments, the pace of domestic economic growth and subdued consumer and business sentiment weighed on advertising and subscription demand in both segments,” the pre-2020 broadcast industry leader said.

ABS-CBN, which produces and sells entertainment content to foreign audiences, said growth in licensing and international syndication (plus co-production revenues) “offset the decrease in advertising and other consumer revenue streams.”

Play Video

A movie starring ABS-CBN’s popular DonBelle love team, Donnie Pangilinan and Belle Mariano, and the Philippines’ top girl group, BINI, were big contributors to the company’s revenues during the period.

“Star Cinema released Tayo Sa Wakas in May 2026, and BINI’s world tour began in June 2026 after the group’s April appearance at the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival. ABS-CBN Global staged 27 events across international markets, including ASAP XP Australia, which featured two sold-out performances in July. These further contributed to the Group’s revenue growth,” ABS-CBN said.

Play Video

ABS-CBN strongly pivoted to digital after it lost its franchise more than six years ago. It also now sells content to its former competitors, GMA and TV5, or partners with them to produce shows.

ABS-CBN recently got a capital infusion from new investors, which is helping the company survive the industry disruption. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan declares Zaldy Co’s 3 co-accused as fugitives
World.content:
The three are facing graft and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in the procurement and construction of a P289.4-million flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro

MANILA, Philippines – The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has declared three co-accused of dismissed Ako Bicol representative Zaldy Co as fugitives.

In its ruling on Tuesday, November 10, the anti-graft court named Sunwest board members Anthony Ngo and Consuelo Aldon, and Department of Public Works and Highways Mimaropa materials engineer Timogen Sacar as fugitives. The court said they had demonstrated “an unmistakable intent to evade warrants and avoid prosecution.”

The three are facing graft and malversation charges over alleged irregularities in the procurement and construction of a P289.4-million flood control project in Naujan, Oriental Mindoro. The allegedly defective project was first exposed by Oriental Mindoro Governor Humerlito “Bonz” Dolor.

According to prosecutors, the three remain at large despite the issuance of arrest warrants on November 21, 2025, nearly a year ago.

“Given the high-profile nature of the case, it is reasonable to conclude that the accused are aware of the criminal proceedings and the outstanding warrants issued against them. Thus, by staying beyond the reach of law enforcement while fully aware of pending warrants of arrest confirms accused’s deliberate intent to evade the judicial process,” the Sandiganbayan said.

Co, the beneficial owner of Sunwest, also remains at large despite facing multiple cases. He reportedly fled the country.

Sunwest was identified by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. as one of the top flood control contractors under his administration.

The Sandiganbayan also ordered the cancellation of the passports of Ngo, Aldon, and Sacar to prevent them from seeking refuge overseas.

“Removing the official travel document necessary for the fugitive to leave the country or to travel between foreign countries hinders the attempts to evade judicial process,” the court said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines, UAE go after Filipino visa scammers
World.content:
ASSURANCE. Migrant Workers Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac tells Filipino household service workers during a get-together in Dubai on November 7, 2026, that there are legal services and funds available to them.

The Philippines and UAE are collaborating to pursue visa scammers who duped hundreds of OFWs. The two countries also roll out new digital recruitment systems.

DUBAI, UAE – The Philippines’ Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) is working with the United Arab Emirates’ Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratization (MOHRE) to go after the Filipinos who allegedly victimized fellow Filipinos seeking freelance visas.

“We have coordination with the host government in running after the scammers, protecting victimized visa scams as well as cooperation with respect to addressing and finding those who prey upon OFWs,” DMW Secretary Hans Leo Cacdac told overseas Filipino workers (OFWs) in Dubai on November 7.

Cacdac was in Dubai until November 8 for the fourth Serbisyo Caravan of government agencies to provide one-stop services for OFWs, and for the Salamat Kabayan early Christmas celebration for household service workers.

Rappler earlier reported that two Filipinos — Junie Sorsano, a prominent Dubai-based content creator for over a decade, and Ryan Ronel Baco — allegedly duped some 400 overseas Filipino workers of AED 3.6 million (around P62 million) in visa facilitation.

The victims were mostly domestic helpers, caregivers, and retail sales staff, who sought freelance visas to legally pursue independent, self-sponsored employment.

Cacdac said he had raised the issue during a meeting with MOHRE head Dr. Abdulrahman Abdulmannan Al Awar.

“We have stronger cooperation now,” Cacdac said, noting this was his fourth meeting with Al Awar this year.

“If the alleged visa scammers have already fled UAE and are hiding in the Philippines, we will also talk to the DOJ, to Secretary [Fredderick] Vida about this matter and determine what charges can be filed against them,” he added.

He highlighted that victims can access MWO’s legal services and action fund.

“Rest assured, we have the legal services of our legal retainer that will help victims and in coordination with MOHRE on this issue. We may also tap the action fund on this,” the DMW secretary said.

He urged OFWs to consult the MWO to avoid scams.

Digitalized

Cacdac also signed an agreement with DataFlow Group to pilot the Digital Recruitment and Employer Accreditation Management (DREAM) System, an online platform allowing UAE employers, principals, and recruitment agencies to submit documents and pay fees digitally.

Designed to cut processing time and costs, the system complements MWO Dubai’s Online Employment Contract Verification System (OECVS), which has verified over 100,000 contracts since July 2025.

“Our 20 to 30 people at MWO will not anymore be sitting behind desks doing clerical or documentation work because these can now be done through the digitalized system, which means more of our people will be out there talking to the Filipino community, going to places where the Filipinos usually congregate visit hospitals, visit prisons to deploy legal services,” Cacdac explained.

Abu Dhabi Dialogue

Cacdac also discussed the upcoming Manila meeting of the Abu Dhabi Dialogue (ADD), which the Philippines will chair in 2027.

Established in 2008 as a voluntary consultative forum and currently chaired by Oman, ADD member states include the UAE, Philippines, Afghanistan, Bahrain, Bangladesh, India, Indonesia, Kuwait, Malaysia, Nepal, Pakistan, and Qatar.

The 9th edition (2026–2027) will focus on Artificial Intelligence and digitalization.

Cacdac also visited Pinas Cargo, a logistics firm shipping care boxes to the Philippines, meeting with founder and CEO Marlyn Castro. (READ: Dubai OFWs pay it forward with scholarships for Filipinos back home) – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Old Remulla video misused to falsely claim Dela Rosa has no ICC warrant
World.content:
A January 2026 interview clip released months before the ICC unsealed the warrant recirculated on social media and was falsely presented as a current update on Dela Rosa’s arrest

Claim: Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) Secretary Jonvic Remulla said there is no arrest warrant against Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A reel posted on November 6 by the Facebook page “Pobre Nga Uyamot” shows an interview clip of Remulla with the overlaid text, “Klaro walang warrant (Clearly no warrant).”

Additional overlaid text read: “Walang kaso si Bato sa Pinas! Pag lumaban, mamatay pulis order sa taas ma-blame! High risk! Law of the land pa rin.”

(Bato has no case in the Philippines! If he fights back, police will die and whoever gave the order will be blamed! High risk! The law of the land still applies.)

In the clip, Remulla says: “Si Bato, ano hahanapin namin? ‘Di ba, alam naming nasa Davao siya. Pero wala naman kaming warrant of arrest. Wala. So bakit namin hahanapin? Ba’t namin aarestuhin? Kung gusto niya, siya [ang] mag-citizen’s arrest.”

(Why will we search for Bato? We know he’s in Davao, but we don’t have an arrest warrant. None. So why would we search for him? Why would we arrest him? If he wants to, let him make a citizen’s arrest.)

As of writing, the video has 2.5 million views, 15,000 reactions, 2,300 comments, and 3,400 shares.

The facts: The clip is old and was misleadingly presented as a current update on Dela Rosa’s status as a subject of an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant.

The clip was from Remulla’s January 27, 2026 interview on ANC, during which he addressed former senator Antonio Trillanes IV’s suggestion to search for Dela Rosa, who at the time had not been attending Senate sessions amid rumors of an ICC warrant against him.

Remulla then made the remark shown in the Facebook reel, adding that he would personally go to Davao to fetch Dela Rosa. He also suggested that Trillanes could carry out a citizen’s arrest if such a warrant existed.

At the time Remulla said this, the ICC warrant had not been made public. The ICC’s records show it was issued as secret on November 6, 2025, and unsealed only on May 11, 2026, several months after the interview from which the clip was taken.

Dela Rosa is accused of murder for crimes against humanity involving at least 32 killings between July 2016 and April 2018 under the bloody drug war of former president Rodrigo Duterte.

What happened after January: In May, the Supreme Court denied Dela Rosa’s request for a temporary restraining order seeking to block the ICC warrant. Justice Secretary Fredderick Vida then said a valid ICC arrest warrant exists and is now enforceable, allowing the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the Philippine National Police (PNP) to effect the senator’s arrest.

Dela Rosa went into hiding shortly after the warrant was issued and is now the subject of a P50-million bounty. (READ: Bato dela Rosa’s escape: Timeline, analyses, opinions from experts)

Manhunt for Dela Rosa: On October 23, Remulla described Dela Rosa as “armed and dangerous.” He also warned that an attempt to arrest the senator by force could result in a “bloodbath.”

Dela Rosa’s camp continues to dispute how the warrant can be enforced. His lawyers argue that no local court has issued an arrest warrant and that the bounty cannot replace domestic judicial procedures that they said were necessary before the senator could be arrested.

Authorities have received at least 500 tips about Dela Rosa’s whereabouts, PNP chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said on November 9. The NBI has said it hopes to arrest the senator before the year ends. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: 23 haulers seek to clear Kanlaon lahar-clogged creek
World.content:
EARTH MOVER In this file photo, an excavator loads lahar deposits from Ibid Creek in Barangay Biak-na-Bato, La Castellana, Negros Occidental, as part of the clearing operation to remove volcanic debris from the waterway following recent eruptions of Kanlaon Volcano. —NEGROS OCCIDENTAL GOVERNMENT PHOTO

BACOLOD CITY—About 23 haulers have expressed interest in removing 67,530 cubic meters of lahar deposits clogging Ibid Creek in Barangay Biak-na-Bato, La Castellana, Negros Occidental, Provincial Environment and Management Office head Julie Bedrio said on Thursday.

The haulers attended an orientation conducted by the provincial government and were instructed to submit formal letters of intent, Bedrio said.

READ: Lahar threat from Kanlaon forces evacuations

Article continues after this 

According to the provincial government, the letters must indicate the number of trucks each hauler intends to deploy and the volume of debris they plan to remove.

The clearing operation will proceed following the provincial government’s receipt of an environmental compliance certificate (ECC) from the Department of Environment and Natural Resources–Environmental Management Bureau. The permit authorizes the removal of lahar deposits that accumulated in the creek following recent eruptions of Kanlaon Volcano.

Bedrio said an ECC was required because Ibid Creek is located within the Mount Kanlaon Natural Park, a protected area.

Ground markers

To prevent over-extraction, the provincial government will put up an ECC billboard and install ground markers to clearly delineate the boundaries of the area approved for clearing.

Bedrio said the operation will begin as soon as possible once hauling schedules are finalized, with a target of approximately 30 truckloads per day.

Hauler-buyers will be charged fixed fees for the volcanic debris under an existing ordinance enacted by the provincial board. INQ

World.title: Myanmar Regime Seeks Closer Ties With Russian-Led Economic Bloc
World.content:
A delegation from the Eurasian Economic Commission (EEC) visited Naypyitaw this week, as Myanmar’s heavily sanctioned military regime intensifies its geopolitical pivot toward Russian-led multilateral blocs.

During the delegation’s visit—its third to the Myanmar capital—EEC Minister in charge of Integration and Macroeconomics Daniyar Imanaliev held talks with junta Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe on Wednesday.

According to regime media, discussions centered on securing observer status for Myanmar within the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), Myanmar’s participation in Eurasian integration forums and exhibitions jointly held by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the EEC.

The EEC minister also held talks with the regime’s commerce and investment ministers, focusing on boosting bilateral cooperation across various sectors including manufacturing, agriculture, e-commerce, energy, transport and digital transformation. The Myanmar side discussed boosting exports of Myanmar’s agricultural and fishery products to five post-Soviet states, and invited investment from the countries in the Dawei Special Economic Zone in southern Myanmar.

Simultaneously, an EEC sub-delegation led by Dmitry Fesenko, head of the industrial development monitoring and analysis department, met with Deputy Industry Minister Dr. Aung Zeya to discuss technical cooperation regarding micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and agro-based industries.

The EAEU—comprising Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Armenia—represents a critical bloc of junta allies. Naypyitaw initiated multi-sector dialogue with the EAEU and EEC in 2022, signing memorandums of understanding for closer cooperation in 2023.

Trade between Myanmar and the EAEU member states more than tripled between 2019 and 2024, surpassing US$1.5 billion, according to EAEU data released last year. Myanmar’s primary exports to the bloc include rice, coffee, palm oil and cocoa beans, while it imports EAEU fertilizers, consumer goods, machinery, metals, cement and pharmaceuticals. The official trade figures exclude weapons and military equipment supplied to the regime by Russia and Belarus, both major arms suppliers.

Despite these figures, regional analysts argue the junta’s Eurasian pivot is driven more by diplomatic survival than viable economic strategy.

“Compared to neighbors like China and Thailand, trade and investment from these [EAEU] countries is worlds apart. Even under the previous governments of U Thein Sein and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, how much investment actually came from them?” an analyst pointed out.

“If the regime wants to do business, it has a massive ASEAN market to tap. The regime’s focus on those faraway markets suggests its motivations are far more geopolitical than economic. They desperately want to join the Russian-led geopolitical bloc.”

Regime chief Min Aung Hlaing, who has publicly condemned major powers for utilizing economic sanctions and political pressure as violations of global norms, personally attended the 4th Eurasian Economic Forum in Belarus last year. During the summit, he made an urgent appeal for Myanmar to be granted EAEU observer status—a demand his foreign minister aggressively reiterated during Imanaliev’s visit this week.

Naypyitaw’s push to integrate into Moscow’s economic architecture mirrors the generals’ broader strategy to embed an isolated regime in non-Western multilateral organizations; in May 2023, Myanmar was formally recognized as a dialogue partner of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), led by China, Russia and India.

World.title: Myanmar’s Dwindling Debt to China, Scammers Nabbed in Shan, and More
World.content:
China no longer Myanmar’s biggest creditor

China is no Myanmar’s principal creditor, even though the military regime is bound for life and beyond by the money and favors it owes its protector. On paper at least, Japan is now Myanmar’s largest foreign government lender, while Beijing’s focus has shifted from extending new loans to managing existing debts.

According to the World Bank’s International Debt Statistics, Myanmar’s public and publicly guaranteed external debt stood at US$10.34 billion last year, down from around US$13.5 billion in 2021. Country-to-country debt accounted for $5.68 billion, with Japan holding $3.86 billion. China was owed only around US$1.5 billion, according to the World Bank’s creditor-by-creditor breakdown.

Prior to the political opening in 2011, China was effectively Myanmar’s only major lender, at interest rates as high as 4.5 percent. But after reforms began, Myanmar regained access to financing from institutions and partners including the Asian Development Bank and the Japan International Cooperation Agency on far more favorable terms.

“Myanmar will not borrow money from China any more if interest rates remain high,” then-deputy finance minister Maung Maung Win pledged in June 2020.

An AidData assessment released in May shows that China committed $14.7 billion in development finance to Myanmar between 2000 and 2023 through 505 projects. Nearly 92 percent took the form of loans, mainly from the Export-Import Bank of China and China Development Bank.

But AidData estimates that Myanmar’s outstanding debt to Chinese creditors had fallen to around US$1.7 billion by the end of 2024 or just about 19 percent of its external public debt.

The loans from China simply stopped. AidData found that China Eximbank, historically the largest lender, has not issued a new loan since 2019. While it was the COVID-19 pandemic that initially slowed lending, the trend has continued throughout the post-coup period.

The reason seems to be that the operating environment in Myanmar is deteriorating. Many planned Chinese-backed projects under the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) are in conflict areas or regions entirely beyond the putschist regime’s control. Key trade routes, resource projects and infrastructure investments increasingly depend on arrangements with ethnic armed groups rather than Naypyitaw alone.

Bangladesh ties Rohingya crisis to Beijing’s Indian Ocean ambition

Dhaka has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) that rules most of Myanmar’s Rakhine State as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis—and that could force China’s hand in dealing with the new reality there.

At stake for Bangladesh is the burden of hosting over 1 million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled the military’s brutal 2017 clearance operations. And since the AA controls entire Bangladeshi border with Myanmar, including Paletwa Township in neighboring Shin State, Dhaka has opened pragmatic dual-track discussions, engaging both the AA and the military regime after Naypyitaw’s repeated failures to facilitate the repatriation.

China, meanwhile, remains focused on its multi-billion-dollar projects under the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC). The key project—a deep-sea port and special economic zone in Kyaukphyu—is designed to solve Beijing’s “Malacca Dilemma” by giving it maritime access to the Indian Ocean. Kyaukphyu also serves as the terminus for the twin oil and gas pipelines currently pumping energy to Yunnan Province. Yet the port project remains stalled, with Kyaukphyu under AA siege.

Dhaka is increasingly looking to China for leverage. During Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s visit to Beijing in June—which closely followed a trip by Myanmar regime chief Min Aung Hlaing—Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed a tripartite China–Myanmar–Bangladesh economic corridor. That would provide Beijing with an alternative overland route to the Indian Ocean while Kyaukphyu remains in limbo.

In July, China’s ambassador to Bangladesh explicitly tied this proposed corridor to resolving the refugee crisis, suggesting it could facilitate Rohingya repatriation.

International scrutiny of the western front is intensifying. UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar Kelley Currie is currently in Bangladesh to assess the armed conflict in Rakhine and the deteriorating situation in the refugee camps. Yet Beijing’s diplomatic shield of the military usurpers in Naypyitaw remains firmly in place. Addressing the UN General Assembly’s Third Committee in late October, China’s representative reiterated that the crisis must be resolved bilaterally between Myanmar and Bangladesh, free from Western interference, a process China insists it is facilitating.

The International Court of Justice will rule next week whether the Myanmar military’s crackdown against the Rohingya people constituted a genocide.

No end to arrests of Chinese scammers in Shan

Some 759 foreigners were arrested between Aug. 1 and Oct. 31 for alleged involvement in scam operations in Shan State, and 502 were Chinese, regime media report.

Another 15 Chinese scammers were arrested on Monday in rural parts of Kyethi Township, southern Shan State. The township lies in an area that is contested by two rival ethnic armed groups: the Restoration Council of Shan State (RCSS) and the Shan State Progress Party (SSPP), whose headquarters are in nearby Wan Hai.

After a Chinese-led crackdown on industrial-scale scam compounds in the Kokang region of northern Shan State in late 2023, operations scattered across at least 17 townships in southern and eastern Shan, including Tangyan, Laihka, Tachileik and Muse. Others famously relocated to Karen State’s Myawaddy Township on the Thai border.

In other words, the syndicates adapted, their units becoming smaller and more nimble across scattered locations and moving further inland from prying eyes on the international border. Now they settle in places like Kyethi, where they can exploit lawlessness and administrative vacuums or collaborate with junta-aligned militias and armed groups.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: ASEAN Should Accept Myanmar Back at Diplomat Level: Bangkok
World.content:
BANGKOK—Myanmar’s foreign minister should be allowed back into meetings of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) regional bloc, Thailand’s top diplomat said on Thursday after a visit to the war-torn country.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow said his meetings with regime leader Min Aung Hlaing and others had revealed “a desire on the part of Myanmar to engage, to return to ASEAN.” But he said there was no talk of specific steps.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level meetings of the 11-nation ASEAN since a 2021 military coup that ousted the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi and triggered an ongoing civil war.

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize ties since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president earlier this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

“For Thailand, we believe that the next step is to have the foreign minister of Myanmar participate in the ASEAN meetings at the level of foreign minister,” Sihasak told reporters.

His comments came ahead of a meeting of ASEAN leaders starting Sunday in the Philippines.

Sihasak said he had also raised the “very urgent problem” of water pollution among tributaries of the Mekong River, which straddles five Southeast Asian countries and China, saying a working group would meet later this month.

Last week, authorities in northern Thailand suspended tap water production after arsenic levels at the waterworks intake was found to be 30 times higher than the safety standard. More than a dozen villages were affected by the suspension.

A subsequent field sample from the nearby Sai River measured arsenic at 25 times the safety standard, the government said.

Thai officials previously pinned the toxic sediment on wastewater from mining activity upstream in Myanmar.

Sihasak said he also raised the issue of a spillover of violence into Thailand.

World.title: Myanmar Faces Year of Blackouts as Regime Admits 30% Power Shortfall
World.content:
Myanmar’s rotating power cuts will remain in place through 2027, with generation expected to meet only 70 percent of national demand, Deputy Energy Minister Aye Kyaw announced Wednesday.

Addressing the regime’s rubber-stamp parliament, he said next summer’s 24-hour electricity demand is forecast at 5,010 MW, while generation capacity is only 3,540 MW.

“That’s why we need to continue the load shedding measures,” he said.

Despite having the poorest electricity access in the region, Myanmar made significant progress in grid connectivity under the National League for Democracy’s 15-year National Electrification Plan in 2015. By 2020, more than half of households had electricity access, and the NLD’s World Bank-backed plan aimed to achieve nationwide electrification by 2030.

However, the plan was scrapped after the 2021 coup, and regime mismanagement has since triggered rolling power outages across the country.

The World Bank says reliable supply has dropped sharply since the military takeover, affecting nearly half of connected households — with 41.6 percent receiving only enough electricity for basic lighting and phone charging, and 9.1 percent getting no electricity at all.

It blames the deepening generation crisis on the suspension of LNG power plants, declining domestic gas production, hydropower stress, infrastructure damage, and stalled investment.

In response, the regime reintroduced nationwide rolling blackouts, leaving residents in even major cities struggling to manage households and livelihoods.

“We have to be ready to fill up the water, cook meals, and iron our clothes the moment the power comes back on,” Ko Thant Zin from Insein Township in the suburbs of Yangon told the Irrawaddy.

He said the electricity supply rotates between four hours on and four hours off.

“Under the civilian government, the roads were bright with lights. Now, I have to open my eyes wide to see the way ahead while driving at night,” he commented.

The deputy energy minister told citizens to install solar panels if they want a reliable supply. However, import curbs and surging prices have put solar options out of reach for most urban residents.

“Forget about solar panels, most people can’t even afford a portable power pack,” a resident of downtown Yangong’s Botahtaung Township told The Irrawaddy. “Prices have been skyrocketing because of import restrictions.”

He added that power cuts would cause major suffering during the El Niño heatwave forecast for November through January.

“I can’t imagine how we will get through next summer,” he said, reacting to the rationing announcement. “It will be especially tough for young children and the elderly.”

Demand driven by outages has seen the price of solar panels surge to a record high. Yangon residents said a household solar power system now costs at least 10 million kyats (around US $4,760), putting it beyond the reach of ordinary families.

Last month, Yangon City authorities mandated that all commercial projects and high-rise buildings must install solar power systems to operate elevators and emergency lighting, as part of a nationwide push for solar amid deepening power blackouts.

The World Bank says chronic power shortages remain one of the main constraints on Myanmar’s economy, limiting its recovery and keeping poverty persistently high.

The deputy energy minister also announced plans to develop two 55 MW small-modular-reactors in cooperation with Russia’s atomic agency, ROSATOM, starting in fiscal 2028-29. The project is slated for completion in fiscal 2035-36 but locations have yet to be announced.

World.title: Three Years After Operation 1027, Hopang Transformed Under Wa Rule
World.content:
Friday marks three years since Hopang in the Wa Self-Administered Zone experienced its first taste of the joint ethnic offensive known as Operation 1027, when drones deployed by the Brotherhood Alliance bombed a monastery sheltering retreating Myanmar military personnel from nearby Kunlong base.

For the Myanmar military, which had controlled Hopang for decades, the drone strike was an early warning that its grip on the town was nearing an end. For the United Wa State Army (UWSA), it presented an opportunity to gain one of the most important towns in Wa territory without firing a shot.

Less than two months after the Nov. 13 drone attack, forces of the Brotherhood Alliance—which grouped the Arakan Army, Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA)—and allied groups entered Hopang with little resistance. Rather than holding the town themselves, they quickly handed it over to their ally, the UWSA.

Operation 1027, which inflicted one of the most devastating military setbacks in the Myanmar military’s history, had begun on Oct. 27, 2023, in Chinshwehaw, a border town just 8 km from Hopang. Just 19 km away, Kunlong, a key town on a China-Myanmar trade route, also fell after sustained drone attacks by alliance forces.

As Kunlong collapsed, its commander, officers and wounded soldiers fled to Hopang.

“A battalion commander and a soldier entered the monastery building and pleaded for shelter,” recalled a witness who was in the compound. “They told the abbot they had been under drone attacks for four days, and had only managed to retreat after receiving supporting fire.”

That same night, drones struck the monastery.

For Hopang residents, who had watched the fighting around Kunlong from hilltop pagodas, the attack on the monastery signaled that war was coming closer. By the next morning, many were fleeing the town, leaving their homes and shops behind.

Some local drivers found themselves ferrying displaced families back and forth, while others stayed behind to guard their properties. Residents feared not only a potential urban battle similar to the fighting in Kunlong, but also the prospect of Myanmar military airstrikes.

One restaurant owner recalled watching looters load crates of beer from his shop onto vehicles through CCTV cameras while he was fleeing.

Among those who fled were a monk who was injured in the November 13 drone attack, as well as health workers from a public hospital in Hopang.

Hopang was home to a military battalion and a police station, but all the surrounding towns including Kunlong and Chinshwehaw were controlled by the Brotherhood Alliance. At this point, Hopang was effectively isolated.

When MNDAA troops entered Hopang in early January 2024, the remaining military and police units reportedly surrendered with little resistance. Under a prior arrangement between the MNDAA and the UWSA, control of the town was then transferred to the Wa army.

Unlike Lashio, Laukkai, Chinshwehaw or Kunlong, Hopang largely escaped major battle damage. Yet residents say the town has since undergone a different kind of transformation, one increasingly shaped by Chinese capital and Wa administration.

The ethnically diverse town, home to Shan, Wa, Bamar, Kachin, Ta’ang and other communities, was once known for its Buddhist, Christian and traditional ethnic festivals. Today, residents say casinos, bars, hotels, massage parlors and prostitution-related businesses funded by Chinese investors have proliferated.

Some residents also complain of heavy taxation and a justice system that includes public executions, practices rarely seen under previous administrations.

The yuan now dominates much of the local economy, with residents increasingly pricing goods in the Chinese currency rather than kyats. In the healthcare arena, expensive Chinese-run private hospitals have emerged alongside the only public hospital.

Over the past three years, rumors have repeatedly surfaced that the UWSA will return Hopang to the regime. Residents say they see no sign that this is imminent, however.

The town, which participated in the 2010, 2015 and 2020 elections, did not take part in the regime-organized 2025 poll and is absent from the list of constituencies scheduled to be put to a vote in additional elections scheduled for April 2027.

Recently, regime Defense Minister and peace negotiator Lieutenant General Yar Pyae visited Panghsang, the UWSA headquarters. There was no indication that Hopang’s status was discussed during his meetings with Wa leaders, however.

While the UWSA remained officially neutral during Operation 1027, it emerged among the campaign’s biggest beneficiaries. Without openly joining the offensive, it gained full control of Hopang and Panlong, while also securing partial control along with the Myanmar military over Tangyan, a strategically important town on the route to Lashio, the largest town in northern Shan.

Three years after the first drone bombs fell on Hopang, the town has changed beyond recognition for longtime residents.

During Operation 1027, the MNDAA and TNLA went on to seize almost the whole of northern Shan State including the capital Lashio and all vital trade routes with China.

However, under strong Chinese pressure, in 2025 the ethnic armies were forced to halt fighting the Myanmar military and hand back several liberated towns to the regime.

World.title: Myanmar’s Coup President Barred From Upcoming 49th ASEAN Summit
World.content:
The Philippines announced Wednesday that Myanmar regime leaders remain barred from joining the 49th ASEAN summit and high-level meetings in Manila from November 15 to 17, upholding a ban imposed after the 2021 military coup.

Myanmar will instead be represented by the Director-General of its ASEAN affairs department, according to a statement issued by Manila’s Department of Foreign Affairs.

“We welcome this official confirmation that there is no place [at the summit] for junta leader Min Aung Hlaing,” Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights foundation, told The Irrawaddy.

“ASEAN made the right decision in line with its principles. We have been demanding that no junta member be permitted to join the summit.”

She added that ASEAN would have sacrificed its credibility and responsibility to the people of Myanmar by inviting the junta leader, who faces a genocide ruling at the international court later this month.

Confirmation that the ban remains in place came after domestic and international rights groups warned the regional bloc against legitimizing a regime that is intensifying violence against civilians.

On Monday, the Special Advisory Council for Myanmar (SAC-M) and ASEAN Parliamentarians for Human Rights urged regional leaders “to immediately confirm” that Min Aung Hlaing and his junta cohorts would be excluded from the summit.

It also called on ASEAN leaders to adopt “measurable benchmarks for compliance” with the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), along with “a series of escalating punitive steps” if the junta continues to defy the peace plan.

Regime leaders were barred from regional summits for failing to implement the April 2021 consensus, including an immediate end to violence and constructive dialogue with the opposition.

The regime largely ignored the 5PC before formally rejecting it in a July 2026 vote by its rubber-stamp parliament. However, it continues to pay lip service to the plan.

During his latest talks with ASEAN special envoy Theresa Lazaro in Naypyitaw in October, Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe claimed the regime was implementing the 5PC “without compromising its national interests and sovereignty in accordance with its own roadmaps and objectives.”

The UN reports that at least 8,384 civilians have been killed by regime forces since the coup, in an escalating military campaign that has also left over 4 million displaced. Meanwhile, nearly 23,000 political prisoners remain in detention, including deposed democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

However, ASEAN members began bilateral engagement with the regime after it rebranded in civilian clothing in April following elections widely condemned as a sham. Since then, coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been invited on official visits to bloc members Laos, Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Malaysia.

Both Malaysia—once a vocal critic of the regime—and Thailand drew widespread condemnation from rights groups for hosting the junta leader.

Both nations defended the visits as pragmatic re-engagement in search of solutions to challenges they face, such as refugee repatriation for Malaysia and transborder issues for Thailand.

Critics have warned that bi-lateral engagement may sway a collective ASEAN decision to reintegrate the regime.

However, the move to uphold the summit ban marks a major setback for a junta desperate for legitimacy on the international stage.

“This is a huge blow to the junta. I am sure it has not expected this kind of decision,” Khin Ohmar commented. “It also signals that the junta’s election farce failed to confer legitimacy, since even those advocating its return to the international stage want to avoid being seen as complicit in its violence.”

World.title: Myanmar Junta Seeks Record Military Budget as Millions Struggle With Poverty
World.content:
The Myanmar regime plans to increase the military budget to a record high for the 2026-27 fiscal year, even as approximately one-third of the country’s population lives in poverty.

Since 2021, the regime has been waging war against several established ethnic armed organizations as well as newly emerged resistance forces, including the People’s Defense Force, across the country, spending a large portion of its budget on military expenses.

Last Thursday, the regime’s rubber-stamp Union Parliament (Pyidaungsu Hluttaw), where the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and its allies hold a majority of seats, debated a supplementary budget allocation bill.

The proposed allocation would bring total defense spending to 10.53 trillion kyats (US$5.01 billion), combining the initial 2026-27 fiscal year estimate of 7.95 trillion kyats with a supplementary grant of 2.58 trillion kyats.

Chit Swe, an Upper House lawmaker representing Ayeyarwady Region’s Constituency No. 11 and first deputy chair of the Joint Public Accounts Committee, urged parliament on November 5 to approve the regime’s proposed budgets, including the record-high military budget.

He said the committee had only eight days to verify the budget, with some items requiring ground observation, and that at least two weeks would be needed for verification.

If the supplementary allocations are approved, the budget deficit is projected to surge from 8.98 trillion kyats to 11.41 trillion kyats, he stated.

The military budget has surged continuously since the coup.

Under the last civilian government, led by ousted democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi, defense expenditure for the 2020-21 fiscal year stood at just 3.4 trillion kyats.

In the 2023-24 fiscal year, it increased to over 5.6 trillion kyats. Although defense expenditures for the remaining years were not officially released, the current budget figures show that spending has nearly doubled compared to 2023-24.

Meanwhile, approximately 17.9 million people are “multidimensionally poor”, while two-thirds of the population are either poor or at risk, according to a UN Development Programme (UNDP) report published on October 8.

After five years of military regime rule, Myanmar people continue to suffer from soaring prices of basic goods and living costs amid the civil war, and face personal safety and security concerns.

Although the budget is still in draft form, the proposed military expenditure has drawn widespread criticism from the public.

“The budgets that should be spent on the country’s education, health, social welfare and nation-building are instead being used to kill the people,” said Naung Yoe, a military defector who now works with the Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute.

According to the MDSI, the Directorate of Defense Industries, which manufactures ammunition and aerial bombs used in the regime’s indiscriminate attacks, has consumed the largest share of the military’s budget since the coup.

“It is deeply tragic and unfortunate,” he said.

World.title: Mideast Crisis Fuels Oil Conflict in Myanmar’s Heartland
World.content:
Myanmar’s small-scale oil prospectors are under fire from all sides as rebels and the military battle to capture a cottage industry that is becoming increasingly lucrative amid the ongoing Middle East crisis.

“As long as we work here, bad luck can kill us,” said Htun Aung, a worker on an oil well in Myanmar’s arid heartlands.

“But if the reality of death is hard to face, then making a living is even harder,” said the 52-year-old, speaking under a pseudonym for security reasons.

Myanmar imports 90 percent of its fuel oil, official figures show, making it particularly vulnerable to supply issues caused by the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

But the central region of Magwe hosts a hardscrabble industry of domestic prospectors manning grimy derricks that squelch up crude oil in humble quantities.

The area is dubbed “Anyar Dubai,” associating the Anyar or central dry zone landscape with the oil boom emirate, despite the pitiable US$50 per week earned by workers like Htun Aung who spend their days drenched in foul crude run-off.

With prices at Myanmar’s petrol pumps nearly double what they were in late February, the underground “black gold” is a coveted prize.

“We just want to live in peace,” said Htun Aung. “But now they strike from one side and the others strike from the other—they keep attacking each other.”

“We’ve had to flee three, four, five times already,” he added. “We run here, we run there. We fill up our motorbikes with fuel and run again.”

Digging in

Pro-democracy rebels claim to have controlled oil fields in Magwe’s Myaing Township since 2023.

They patrol the dusty territory in a westward crook of the Irrawaddy River in ragtag columns and outfitted with rocket-propelled grenades, flak jackets, tote bags and flip-flops.

Air and drone strikes in Myaing so far this year have already exceeded 2025’s total, according to ACLED, a monitor that estimates more than 100,000 people have died since the 2021 putsch.

Rebels shelter in foxholes, camouflaged among thousands of oil wells dug in an unregulated practice dating back centuries.

Engine winches chug day and night, plunging plumbing tubes dozens of meters down boreholes before dragging them up filled with crude oil slurry.

Prospectors pay landowners up to $3,500 to lease a spot to drill, one veteran said, with no guarantee they will hit oil.

Some wells yield dribbles while others gush, filling tarpaulin-lined pits and barrels with oil hauled off to improvised refineries for processing into petrol and diesel.

“Anyar Dubai” has been “going viral” for its plentiful supply, said rebel spokesman Pyae Phyo Kyaw, at a time when regime-held areas are rationing petrol.

He touted recent offensives fending off military advances but admitted being battered by counter-attacks.

“We see it primarily as an attempt to destroy what has been a strong supply route and source of revenue for us,” said the 35-year-old.

Myanmar’s military could not be reached for comment.

In September, the military claimed a month-long military operation captured over 130 wells in Myaing and 735 more in neighboring Pakokku Township.

Black market

Scores of pro-democracy factions and ethnic armed groups are fighting the military.

As the war grinds on, all sides battle to fill their war chests with the tax or trade of natural resources: gem mines, rare earth mineral deposits, gold or teak.

Oil projects are not generally contested.

The major ones are under staunch military guard, and on-the-books output is tiny by international standards at around 6,000 barrels a day last year, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

But the artisanal fields are coveted by rebels precisely because of their modest size, according to Thomas Kean, a Myanmar consultant for the International Crisis Group.

“Part of the reason why they’re significant is because they’re not globally significant,” he said, explaining that they are small enough to thrive under the radar yet big enough to fund guerrillas.

Spiking oil prices may not directly drive conflict, said Kean, highlighting a broader military campaign to evict rebels from heartland footholds by squeezing revenue sources.

But as the spoils of war become more profitable, the stakes get higher.

“We’re talking about millions of barrels a year coming out of these oil fields,” he added. “With global prices what they are, that’s a significant amount of money.”

World.title: Tokayev Calls for Stronger Logistics and Digitalization at Security Council Meeting
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for greater efficiency and modernization of Kazakhstan’s transport and logistics sector during an operational meeting of the Security Council on Nov. 13, criticizing the performance of national railway operator Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ) and urging improvements in its profitability and operational efficiency.

According to Akorda press service, Tokayev emphasized that timely adaptation of transport infrastructure is a key factor in the country’s strategic development.

He called for optimizing KTZ’s operations, including through digitalization, and improving the company’s financial performance. He also stressed the need to expand logistics centers, streamline border and customs procedures, and remove infrastructure bottlenecks that hinder the seamless movement of cargo.

Tokayev highlighted the importance of comprehensive digitalization across the transport industry and called for creating favorable conditions for investors and transport and logistics companies while ensuring compliance with the principle of Law and Order.

During the meeting, Tokayev also addressed the detention of senior executives of the Samruk-Kazyna sovereign wealth fund and KTZ on suspicion of corruption-related offenses. He emphasized the importance of personal accountability among national company executives and transparency in the operations of strategically important enterprises.

Following the meeting, relevant government agencies and organizations received instructions to advance the transport and transit sector and strengthen the competitiveness of international transport corridors passing through Kazakhstan.

The Security Council Secretariat was tasked with overseeing the implementation of the instructions.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Global Partnerships, AI Ambitions and International Recognition
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest explores the country’s growing role in international water cooperation, expanding ties with Europe and India, international recognition of its equestrian heritage, and more.

Shimmering Aqzhan – carrying the spirit of Kazakhstan

The Australian equestrian magazine Hoofbeats has featured Aqzhan, an Akhal-Teke mare from the Presidential Stables of Kazakhstan. She appears on the cover of the October-November publication alongside President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

“A young Akhal-Teke mare with extraordinarily rare isabelline colouring is capturing attention in Astana, the rapidly developing capital of Kazakhstan, and beyond, offering a striking connection between the country’s rich horse heritage and its vision for the future,” reads the article.

Kazakhstan proposes UN-backed international water organization at COP31

Kazakhstan has proposed establishing an international water organization under UN auspices to strengthen global cooperation on water security, Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov said Wednesday, reported by Anadolu Agency on Nov. 12.

Speaking at the COP31 UN climate conference in the Turkish city of Antalya, Bektenov said Central Asia faced growing challenges from rising temperatures, shrinking glaciers, desertification and water scarcity, requiring closer regional cooperation.

He invited international partners to support the initiative, which was proposed by Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

Swiss rail maker Stadler steps up Kazakhstan expansion

The company has put its first “Charme” sleeper carriages – produced locally in Astana – into service on behalf of the Kazakhstan Railways (KTZ), reported swissinfo on Nov. 11.

The contract provides for the delivery of 557 sleeper carriages and their maintenance over 20 years, with commissioning scheduled to continue until the end of 2030.

More than 100 carriages, manufactured locally, were already taken delivery of in October. They will operate, in particular, on the 1,300-kilometer line linking Astana to Almaty.

Kazakhstan’s AI ambitions open a new chapter in its economic ties with Europe

Growing technology exports and major investment in computing infrastructure are giving Kazakhstan a stronger foothold in the digital economy. The challenge is to turn that momentum into lasting gains for businesses and workers, according to an EU Reporter article published on Nov. 3.

In Ekibastuz, Kazakhstan is preparing to put its energy resources to a new use: powering the computing systems behind artificial intelligence. The planned Data Centre Valley represents an attempt to build another export industry, selling access to advanced computing alongside the country’s established trade in natural resources.

For European businesses and policymakers, the development raises an increasingly practical question. Could Kazakhstan become a significant partner in digital services, industrial AI and the infrastructure connecting European and Asian markets?

National Bank of Kazakhstan sells its first tokenized notes

The National Bank of Kazakhstan sold short-term notes in the form of digital tokens for the first time at a November 9 auction on the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE). The tokenized notes accounted for 10 billion tenge (about $22.3 million), or one-fifth of the issue’s total face value of 50 billion tenge (about $111.7 million), reported the Times of Central Asia on Nov. 11.

The central bank said selling conventional and tokenized notes together allowed it to apply the same pricing rules to both forms and test how the digital platform worked alongside the existing securities market. It sees the trial as a step toward tokenizing other government securities.

Kazakhstan inks new deals to supply Uranium to Indian cos

Kazakhstan, the world’s largest producer of uranium, has signed new contracts to supply natural uranium to major energy companies in India in 2026, as the country seeks to expand its international partnerships and diversify its uranium export markets, reported The Economic Times on Nov. 10.

World.title: IMF: Uzbekistan’s Next Growth Challenge is Productivity and Regional Integration
World.content:
ASTANA – Uzbekistan’s strong economic growth is creating opportunities to strengthen its position as a regional trade and logistics hub, but sustaining the momentum will require deeper structural reforms, greater private sector participation and closer economic integration across Central Asia, International Monetary Fund (IMF) officials said Nov. 13 at a roundtable at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan in Tashkent.

Roberto Cardarelli, assistant director of the IMF’s Middle East and Central Asia Department, and Koba Gvenetadze, the fund’s resident representative in Uzbekistan, discussed the country’s growth prospects, inflation risks and structural reform priorities, highlighting the need to translate strong economic performance into higher productivity and sustainable job creation.

Uzbekistan’s economy has expanded strongly over the past five to six years, supported by domestic demand and continued structural reforms. However, the strength of domestic consumption also creates potential overheating pressures, making the coordination of fiscal and monetary policies increasingly important, Gvenetadze said. He cautioned against treating a particular growth rate as the ultimate measure of economic success. Instead, the priority should be to ensure that growth is sustainable, increasingly productivity-driven and supported by private businesses rather than the state.

“It’s a very important moment for Uzbekistan to make sure that all this performance and very impressive performance in terms of growth is translated into higher productivity,” Gvenetadze said.

The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook projects Uzbekistan’s economy to grow by 7.8% in 2026, up from its previous forecast of 6.8%. Growth is expected to moderate to 6.5% in 2027, compared with the earlier projection of 6%. The revised outlook reflects the country’s strong economic performance and places Uzbekistan among the region’s fastest-growing economies. The improved forecast comes as the country seeks to accelerate annual economic growth toward 9%-10%. Achieving such ambitions without intensifying inflationary pressures will depend on the country’s ability to strengthen its economic foundations and improve productivity.

Moving beyond first-generation reforms

The next phase of Uzbekistan’s economic transformation will require moving beyond the initial wave of liberalization toward more difficult institutional and structural changes. Cardarelli described this as a broader challenge facing economies across the region. Having implemented many first-generation reforms, including market liberalization, countries now need to address more complex issues related to private sector development, state-owned enterprises, financial markets and human capital.

For Uzbekistan, reducing the state’s economic footprint remains a central priority. Gvenetadze identified stronger corporate governance, stricter budget constraints for state-owned enterprises, transparent privatization and stronger competition as key areas for reform.

The financial sector also requires further modernization. The IMF sees a need to phase out directed and preferential lending, strengthen banking supervision and improve the regulatory framework, alongside advancing the long-discussed capital markets law.

These reforms are closely connected. A more competitive banking system and deeper capital markets could improve access to financing for private businesses, reduce reliance on state-directed credit and create conditions for more efficient investment.

Governance improvements will also matter. Gvenetadze noted that Uzbekistan had already adopted a conflict-of-interest law, while legislation on whistleblower protection and asset declarations would further strengthen institutional accountability.

The IMF also highlighted the importance of expanding women’s and young people’s participation in the labor market. For an economy with a growing young population, creating jobs will depend not only on investment and infrastructure but also on developing the skills required by a more diversified economy. Cardarelli stressed that human capital would be particularly important as countries seek to move toward services and higher-value economic activities. Diversification into these sectors is difficult without a workforce equipped with the necessary skills.

Growth, inflation and fiscal discipline

Maintaining macroeconomic stability will be another test for Uzbekistan as economic activity remains strong. The IMF identified inflation as a major macroeconomic stability challenge across the region, driven by domestic demand pressures and external shocks. Cardarelli noted that bringing inflation down from double-digit levels is generally easier than achieving further reductions, requiring monetary policy to remain appropriately tight.

In Uzbekistan, strong domestic demand and higher-than-budgeted gold revenues have created additional fiscal policy considerations. Higher commodity revenues can encourage governments to increase spending, potentially reinforcing demand-driven inflation.

Gvenetadze said Uzbekistan had so far demonstrated fiscal discipline. He noted that the budget deficit was set at 3% of GDP for this year and said he expected the actual figure to come in below that level. He also referred to discussions with the authorities on analyzing the non-mineral budget deficit. Such an indicator would help assess how much public finances depend on gold revenues and provide a clearer picture of the underlying fiscal position. Gvenetadze clarified that the IMF had not recommended establishing a separate sovereign wealth or stabilization fund for Uzbekistan. The broader challenge is to prevent temporary revenue gains from translating into permanent spending commitments while maintaining sufficient fiscal space to respond to future shocks.

Uzbekistan’s regional role and the Middle Corridor

Beyond domestic reforms, Uzbekistan’s geographical position gives it an opportunity to become an increasingly important link in regional and international trade, Gvenetadze said. Stronger economic links with neighboring countries could generate positive spillovers across the region by expanding trade, investment and market opportunities.

The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, currently under construction, illustrates the potential of improved regional connectivity. The project could open new trade routes and strengthen Central Asia’s links with global markets.

However, the benefits extend beyond transit. Better transport connections can lower trade costs, attract investment and give businesses access to larger markets. Cardarelli also pointed to the changing geography of global trade as an opportunity for the region. Disruptions linked to conflicts in the north and south have pushed businesses to explore alternative routes, increasing Central Asia’s strategic importance. The Middle Corridor is part of this wider shift.

Yet infrastructure alone will not determine whether the region can capitalize on changing trade patterns. The IMF’s analysis highlights the importance of improving logistics and governance, lowering trade and regulatory barriers, streamlining customs procedures, digitalizing trade processes and harmonizing standards across countries. These measures are essential to turn transport connectivity into deeper economic integration.

World.title: Kazakhstan Considers Unified Strategy for Three Financial Platforms
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is considering a unified strategy to coordinate the development of three financial platforms, the Kazakhstan Stock Exchange (KASE), the Astana International Financial Center (AIFC) and Alatau City, while preserving their distinct specializations, according to the National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov, who announced it, speaking at the 14th Congress of Financiers of Kazakhstan on Nov. 13.

Under the proposed framework, cooperation would include mutual recognition of participants across platforms, regular exchange of supervisory information between regulators, harmonized regulatory approaches and a clear division of responsibilities, Atameken Business reported.

National Bank Governor Timur Suleimenov also emphasized the importance of keeping the three financial markets interconnected as they develop independently. He said Alatau City was emerging as another source of financial innovation, with its own regulatory and tax frameworks, alongside the capital market developing within the AIFC.

“In our view, it is extremely important to ensure synergy between these markets through mutual recognition, mutual compatibility and mutual circulation, so that they can develop while remaining interconnected,” Suleimenov said.

He stressed that the proposed strategy would not involve micromanagement or dictate specific actions to each platform. Instead, it would set common strategic priorities and define each market’s specializations.

“It is extremely important to ensure that each market does not become confined within its own jurisdiction or geographical location. Capital and money are liquid by nature; they are fluid and therefore cannot be locked in,” he said.

AIFC and Alatau City: complementary roles

The potential relationship between the AIFC and Alatau City was also discussed at the congress, amid questions about whether the new city could compete with the financial center for foreign investment.

AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov said the two jurisdictions had different objectives, including at the legislative level, according to the National Business Agency.

The AIFC focuses on attracting investment, developing the capital market and innovative financial products, and providing an independent regulatory framework. Alatau City, meanwhile, is intended to accelerate urban development through special regimes covering investment, construction, science and innovation.

“This involves special regimes for attracting investment, as well as for the construction industry, science and innovation. The foundation of Alatau City’s legal system is territoriality. Financial products, however, are extraterritorial. For example, how could you create a token linked to a specific property that would be traded only in Alatau City? Naturally, this would not be the case,” Bekturov said.

He said the AIFC did not expect competition with Alatau City but rather an exchange of experience. The regulatory and institutional practices developed by the financial center could support the new city’s future development and create opportunities for cooperation between the two jurisdictions.

“The argument that the AIFC was established solely for foreign investment is incorrect. Our task is also to facilitate the development of the capital market in Kazakhstan,” Bekturov said.

World.title: Cultural Weekend: Music, Art and More
World.content:
ASTANA – As winter approaches, warm up your weekend with art, music and theater. From multimedia exhibitions and classical concerts to ballet performances, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events to enjoy with friends and family.

Astana

“Fallen Angels” and “Bolero X” ballets, Nov.13 – 14

Three choreographic works come together in a programme that explores different emotions and styles of movement. Inspired by the music of Edith Piaf, the first work tells stories of love, heartbreak and loss. The programme also features Jiří Kylián’s energetic Fallen Angels and Bolero X, a contemporary interpretation of Maurice Ravel’s famous composition, bringing together around 50 dancers in a powerful display of movement and rhythm.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Classical concert, Nov. 14

The concert celebrates the sound of the flute through works by Kazakh and international composers. Audiences can hear the instrument in a variety of styles, from classical compositions to more contemporary works.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Concert featuring Ludovico Einaudi’s greatest hits, Nov. 15

Fans of film music can enjoy a concert dedicated to the work of composer Hans Zimmer. Performed by a symphony orchestra and choir, the programme features familiar soundtracks from films such as Interstellar, Inception, Pirates of the Caribbean, The Lion King and The Dark Knight. The performance brings some of cinema’s most memorable musical moments to the concert stage.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“The Mysterious Worlds of Hieronymus Bosch” exhibition, Nov.14 – Jan.31

Visitors can explore the unusual artistic world of Dutch painter Hieronymus Bosch through a multimedia exhibition featuring some of his most famous works. Large-scale projections bring his imaginative creatures, mysterious landscapes and symbolic details to life, offering a closer look at paintings created more than five centuries ago.

Venue: Lumiere-Hall Multimedia Museum; 8 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Andrea Bocelli concert, Nov. 14-15

The programme pays tribute to the music of Italian tenor Andrea Bocelli, featuring some of his best-known songs performed by the Otyrar Sazy Academic Folklore and Ethnographic Orchestra. The repertoire includes Time to Say Goodbye, The Prayer, Vivo per Lei and Besame Mucho, alongside other popular melodies. The concert offers an evening of familiar songs and orchestral arrangements.

Venue: 35 Kaldayakov Street. Tickets are available here.

“Anna Karenina” ballet, Nov.15

Boris Eifman’s ballet brings Leo Tolstoy’s classic novel Anna Karenina to the stage through expressive choreography and dramatic movement. The production explores the complicated relationships, passion and personal struggles of its characters, offering a new interpretation of one of Russian literature’s best-known stories.

Venue: Abay Opera Theater; 110 Kabanbay Batyr Street. Tickets are available here.

“The Duenna” performance, Nov. 14

This adventurous comedy by British playwright Richard Brinsley Sheridan follows a series of romantic intrigues, unexpected twists and amusing misunderstandings. Directed by Alexey Shemes, the production promises a lighthearted theatrical evening filled with humour and lively characters.

Venue: 117 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Kazakhstan-China Freight Traffic Rises 8% in First 10 Months of 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Freight traffic between Kazakhstan and China reached 31.8 million tons in the first 10 months of 2026, an 8% increase compared to the same period last year, when 29.4 million tons were transported, reported Kazakhstan’s national railway company Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ).

Growth was recorded in both directions. From January through October, 12.1 million tons of cargo were transported from China to Kazakhstan, up 9% year on year. Of this volume, 5 million tons passed through the Dostyk border crossing, marking a 13% increase. Another 7.1 million tons were transported through Altynkol, up 6%.

In the opposite direction, Kazakhstan shipped 19.7 million tons of cargo to China, an 8% increase compared to the same period in 2025.

At the border crossings, 13.1 million tons were transported through Dostyk, up 12%, while traffic through Altynkol reached 6.6 million tons, a 1% increase.

The growth in freight traffic reflects ongoing efforts to strengthen transport and logistics links between Kazakhstan and China. Further development of international rail connections is focused on modernizing border infrastructure, increasing the capacity of border crossings and improving logistics processes.

World.title: Tokayev Orders Measures to Curb Corruption in Kazakhstan’s State-Owned Companies
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has ordered the government and oversight bodies to submit proposals to reduce corruption in state-owned companies by Nov. 24, following the detention of senior executives at Samruk-Kazyna Sovereign Wealth Fund and Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the national railway company.

Speaking at an operational meeting of the Security Council on Nov. 13, Tokayev described the detentions as “an extremely serious signal” indicating widespread corruption in state-owned companies.

He stressed that the Constitution is the country’s supreme law and that violations of its provisions would be addressed under the Law and Order principle.

“The Constitution is the Basic Law of our state, the legal passport of the people. Disregarding the Constitution and its fundamental provisions is tantamount to discriminating against the people. Such actions will be suppressed in accordance with the Law and Order principle. No one is allowed to violate the Constitution or even mock this, one could say, sacred document,” Tokayev said.

He also emphasized that officials entrusted with public authority must act decisively to protect national interests.

“All of us entrusted by the people with public authority must demonstrate unwavering commitment to upholding national interests. This is our civic and political duty,” he said.

He noted that Samruk Kazyna manages Kazakhstan’s strategic assets, implements major investment projects and cooperates with leading foreign companies and international financial institutions.

“Behind each such agreement and partnership are numerous years of negotiations, Kazakhstan’s commitments and the trust of the international community in our country,” he said.

State-owned companies continue operations

Tokayev stressed that the detention of executives would not affect the operations of Samruk Kazyna or state-owned companies, including KTZ. All institutions and enterprises under their management continue to operate as usual.

“This serious incident is not a reason for disruptions in the operations of the Fund and state-owned companies. Moreover, I am confident that the fight against corruption should, on the contrary, increase the confidence of investors and creditors in this institution, and its work will become more efficient, transparent and productive,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the recovery of illegally acquired assets, noting that the Prosecutor General’s Office had secured the return of more than 1.3 trillion tenge (US$2.9 billion). The funds were allocated to building 466 social and infrastructure facilities, including medical institutions, water supply systems, schools and sports complexes. Of these, 383 have been completed.

He said the quality of completed facilities should also be assessed, pointing to recurring problems with infrastructure quality, particularly roads.

Corruption statistics and investigations

According to Tokayev, authorities identified 3,168 corruption offenses between 2023 and 2025. Of these, 2,165 were committed by civil servants, while the remaining cases involved other individuals, including employees of the quasi-public sector. The total amount involved exceeded 248 billion tenge (US$550 million).

In the first 10 months of 2026, authorities recorded 751 corruption-related offenses, including 546 committed by civil servants and 205 by other individuals, including employees of quasi-public sector entities.

Tokayev acknowledged that the corruption situation remained challenging and said the authorities would continue to report publicly on the situation and measures being taken to address it. He said all reports of corruption offenses involving officials at different levels would be promptly and thoroughly investigated by the National Security Committee’s Anti-Corruption Service, with the participation of the Prosecutor General’s Office.

“Naturally, there will be no division into ‘our own,’ ‘not quite our own’ and, even more so, ‘outsiders.’ Our Constitution has established the principle of equality of all citizens before the law. We must comply with this requirement,” Tokayev said.

“No one, regardless of their position, achievements or personal connections, should expect exemptions from the law,” he added.

President Tokayev instructed the government and oversight bodies to submit concrete proposals by Nov. 24 to reduce corruption offenses and improve the performance of quasi-public sector companies and their staff.

World.title: IMF, Development Partners Support Early Pension Reform Work in Uzbekistan
World.content:
ASTANA – The International Monetary Fund (IMF), together with the Asian Development Bank (ADB), International Labour Organization (ILO) and World Bank, is working with Uzbekistan’s authorities on an early-stage concept for pension reform, IMF Resident Representative in Uzbekistan Koba Gvenetadze said Nov. 13.

Speaking at a roundtable at the Central Bank of Uzbekistan in Tashkent, Gvenetadze said the reform remains at an early stage, with authorities examining international experience and assessing different approaches to pension system management.
