World.title: Leyla Aliyeva visits joint pavilion of Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Türkiye’s Zero Waste Foundation at COP31, meets with several experts (PHOTO)
World.content:
On November 13, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, and Alena Aliyeva visited the joint pavilion established on the initiative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation and Türkiye’s Zero Waste Foundation on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

While touring the pavilion, Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva were briefed on the stands on display and the projects presented there.

They also visited other pavilions operating at the venue.

The idea of establishing the joint pavilion was first conceived during COP29, held in Baku in 2024. The pavilion organized during that conference was among the most visited.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. The pavilion showcases projects implemented by the Heydar Aliyev Foundation across social, cultural, educational, healthcare, reconstruction and restoration efforts, environmental protection, multiculturalism, and other fields.

It also highlights the activities of both foundations, alongside interactive projects on display.

XXX

Leyla Aliyeva and Alena Aliyeva also visited Uzbekistan’s national pavilion. Built around the concept “A Vineyard: Heritage of the Past, Solutions for the Present, Inspiration for the Future,” the pavilion featured presentations on initiatives and projects in renewable energy, water resource conservation, biodiversity protection, and environmental awareness.

XXX

Subsequently, Leyla Aliyeva held meetings with high-level representatives of several international organizations and environmental experts on the margins of COP31.

During a meeting with Manuel Pulgar-Vidal, WWF Global Leaded for Climate and Energy, the sides highlighted joint projects implemented within the framework of cooperation between IDEA and WWF aimed at protecting the Caucasian leopard and reintroducing goitered gazelles and European bison to their historical habitats in Azerbaijan. They also discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in biodiversity conservation and the restoration of rare animal populations and ecosystems.

Furthermore, Leyla Aliyeva met and exchanged views with several other international experts, scientists, and representatives of nature conservation organizations participating in events organized on the initiative of the IDEA Public Union on the sidelines of COP31.

Discussions addressed the environmental challenges of the Caspian Sea, the impact of climate change on biodiversity, the protection of natural ecosystems, the expansion of scientific research, and the sharing of international best practices.

World.title: Azerbaijan to finish Nations League group stage in first place
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. The Azerbaijan national football team has played its final match in the UEFA Nations League group stage.

Led by head coach Aykhan Abbasov, the team, competing in Group 2 of League D, faced Liechtenstein away from home.

The match ended in a 1–0 victory for Azerbaijan, with Mahir Emreli scoring the decisive goal in the 26th minute.

Azerbaijan thus finished its group-stage campaign in first place with eight points.

The final match in Group 2 will take place on November 16, when Lithuania host Liechtenstein.

World.title: Iranian banks' trade lending grows 94.2% to about $4.92B in seven months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Loans extended by Iranian banks to the trade sector grew by 94.2% year-on-year to 9.41 quadrillion rials (about $4.92 billion) during the first seven months of the current Iranian year (March 21 through October 22, 2026).

According to Trend's calculation, based on statistical data from the Central Bank of Iran, Iranian banks provided 4.85 quadrillion rials (approximately $2.53 billion) in loans to the trade sector during the same period of the previous Iranian year.

According to the statistics, during the first seven months of the current Iranian year, loans worth 8.54 quadrillion rials (roughly $4.46 billion) were provided to the trade sector for working capital.

Furthermore, during the reporting period, loans worth nearly 459 trillion rials (about $240 million) were issued in the trade sector for the establishment of enterprises and other facilities, while 362 trillion rials (approximately $189 million) were provided for enterprise development.

The statistics also show that over the seven-month period, Iranian banks issued loans worth 28.2 trillion rials (roughly $14.7 million) for the purchase of consumer goods in the trade sector, 17.6 trillion rials (about $9.23 million) on a non-repayable basis, and 5.53 trillion rials (approximately $2.89 million) for self-employment.

Additionally, according to the statistics, during the reporting period, Iranian banks issued loans worth 417 billion rials (nearly $218,000) for repairs and 135 billion rials (about $70,500) for home purchases.

During the first seven months of the current Iranian year, banks and financial institutions in Iran issued loans worth 71.5 quadrillion rials (about $37.4 billion) across various sectors. The total value of loans issued during this period increased by 71.7% compared to the same period last year.

For the record, Iran uses the Solar Hijri calendar, also known as the Persian calendar. The country is currently in the year 1405. The Iranian year begins on March 20 or 21. The first six months of the year each have 31 days, the following five months have 30 days, while the final month has 29 days in three out of every four years and 30 days in the fourth year. Consequently, the months of the Iranian calendar begin on the 21st, 22nd or 23rd day of the corresponding Gregorian calendar month.

World.title: Uzbekistan's CO₂ emissions rise 1% to 121.8M tons in 2024 – Eni
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 14. Uzbekistan's carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions increased by 1% in 2024 to 121.8 million metric tons, compared with 120.6 million metric tons a year earlier, according to data published in Italian energy company Eni's World Energy Review 2026.

The review's historical data show that Uzbekistan's CO₂ emissions generally followed an upward trend from 2015 to 2024, rising from 94.4 million metric tons to 121.8 million metric tons.

According to Trend's calculations based on Eni's figures, emissions increased by 27.4 million metric tons, or approximately 29%, over the nine-year period. This corresponds to a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of around 2.9%.

The data also indicate that emissions rose by 8.9% in 2020, from 101.5 million metric tons in 2019 to 110.5 million metric tons. They subsequently increased by 8.1% in 2021 to 119.5 million metric tons, before declining by 2.8% to 116.2 million metric tons in 2022. Emissions then rebounded by 3.8% in 2023, reaching 120.6 million metric tons.

Among the countries covered in the review, Uzbekistan recorded the second-highest CO₂ emissions in Central Asia in 2024, behind Kazakhstan, which reported 243 million metric tons. Turkmenistan followed with 87.9 million metric tons, while Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan recorded 11.9 million and 8.9 million metric tons, respectively.

Uzbekistan accounted for approximately 25.7% of the combined emissions of the five Central Asian countries listed in the review in 2024. Its emissions were also around half the level recorded in Kazakhstan.

Eni's World Energy Review 2026 examines global energy developments using data for 2025. However, the emissions table provides no 2025 figure for Uzbekistan, making 2024 the latest year available for the country.

World.title: Woodside's Mexico oil project 71% complete, first oil targeted in 2028
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Woodside Energy's Trion deepwater oil project in Mexico is 71 percent complete and on budget, with first oil targeted for 2028, according to the company's Capital Markets Day 2026 presentation.

Trion is a 100,000 barrels per day oil development. Woodside said it will provide long-life oil production that diversifies the company's cash flow. The project is expected to contribute about $1.1 billion per year in adjusted operating cash flow in 2028–2032 (Woodside share).

Trion is located in the Perdido Fold Belt of the Gulf of Mexico, about 180 km off the Mexican coastline and 30 km south of the US-Mexico maritime border, in water depths of approximately 2,500 meters. Woodside, the operator, holds a 60% interest, and Mexico's state oil company Pemex holds the remaining 40%. The final investment decision on the project was taken in 2023. Trion is Mexico's first deepwater oil development.

As of the end of the third quarter of 2026, 10 of the planned 24 wells had been drilled and the first subsea tree installed. Fabrication of the floating production unit (FPU) Tláloc has reached about 96% completion, with integration and pre-commissioning underway. Production will be supported by a floating storage and offloading vessel (FSO) with a capacity of 950,000 barrels. Over its life, the project is expected to deliver more than $10 billion in taxes and royalties to Mexico. The field, discovered by Pemex in 2012, holds 3P reserves of around 305 million barrels of oil equivalent.

Woodside Energy, headquartered in Perth, is Australia's largest independent oil and gas company and is listed on the Australian Securities Exchange and the New York Stock Exchange. Its portfolio includes LNG and domestic gas operations in Australia, deepwater oil in the US Gulf of America, the Sangomar oil field in Senegal, and the Trion project under development in Mexico.

World.title: Azerbaijani judoka Gultaj Mammadaliyeva wins bronze at Zagreb Grand Prix
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. Azerbaijani judoka Gultaj Mammadaliyeva has won a bronze medal at the Grand Prix tournament in Zagreb, the capital of Croatia.

Competing in the under-52 kg weight category, Mammadaliyeva defeated Croatia’s Tihea Topolovec and Chinese Taipei’s Pin-Hsien Tseng to reach the quarterfinals.

At this stage, she lost to Hungary’s Róza Györtyás and moved into the repechage round, where she defeated Kosovo’s Fatjona Kasapi. In the bronze medal bout, the Azerbaijani judoka overcame Italy’s Ilaria Finestrone to secure third place.

Another Azerbaijani representative, Nizami Imranov, competing in the under-66 kg category, also came close to winning a medal. He defeated France’s Daki Bouba, Italy’s Matteo Piras, and Morocco’s Abderrahmane Boushita.

However, Imranov lost to Brazil’s Ronaldo Lima in the semifinal. Due to an injury, he was unable to compete in the bronze medal match and finished fifth overall.

Two other Azerbaijani judokas were eliminated in their opening bouts. Turan Bayramov (66 kg) lost to Germany’s Florian Bekeri, while Murad Muradli (60 kg) was defeated by France’s Luka Mkheidze.

The Grand Prix tournament in Zagreb will run until November 15.

World.title: Leyla Aliyeva attends discussions on environmental challenges of Caspian Sea at COP31 (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 13. An event titled “A Sea in Retreat: Climate, Nature and People on the Caspian Frontline” was organized in partnership with the IDEA Public Union and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) on the sidelines of the 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).

Addressing the opening ceremony, Leyla Aliyeva, Vice-President of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, founder and head of the IDEA Public Union, noted that the declining water level of the Caspian Sea threatens the survival of rare species inhabiting the region, including sturgeons and Caspian seals. She underscored the importance of expanding scientific research, enhancing international cooperation, and pursuing joint action to address the sea’s environmental challenges.

Highlighting the projects implemented by the IDEA Public Union in this field, Leyla Aliyeva mentioned that scientific expeditions have been organized to investigate the causes behind the decline in the Caspian seal population, while fingerlings of various fish species have been released into water bodies to replenish fish stocks.

Leyla Aliyeva also highlighted IDEA’s initiatives aimed at cleaning up the Caspian Sea coastline. It was noted that nearly 7,000 volunteers have joined coastal cleanup campaigns organized since 2011, collecting over 120 tons of waste for recycling. Noting that the future of the Caspian Sea depends on decisions made today, she called for protecting its rich nature for future generations.

Stewart Maginnis, IUCN Deputy Director General, and Dario Liguti, Director of the Sustainable Energy Division at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE), also addressed the opening ceremony.

The following panel discussions featured Caspian research expert at the IDEA Public Union Elnur Safarov, representative of the UK’s University of Leeds Simon Goodman, founder and Executive Director of the Great Whale Conservancy Michael Fishbach, as well as representative of the University of Geneva and Chair of the Caspisnet network Alexandre Hedjazi.

Discussions focused on climatic factors driving the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level, biodiversity conservation, adapting marine ecosystems to changing conditions, and strengthening regional collaboration.

The event concluded with the screening of a short documentary produced by the IDEA Public Union highlighting the current environmental situation of the Caspian Sea.

World.title: Rope barriers at parliament round out prickly week for government
World.content:
If the government wanted to signal it was in touch with community concerns, walking through Hollywood-style velvet ropes and gold posts at parliament was probably not the best way to do it.

The ritzy accoutrements, aimed at separating politicians from the media as they arrive at parliament, seem more "let them eat cake" than cozzie living.

It was an image the government could have done without as it closed out a particularly challenging week.

Media barriers

Let's start with the extraordinary scenes of Labor MPs trying to shepherd their colleague, Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan, past waiting media and into parliament.

Journalists have been asking MPs questions at that entrance for decades.

It's not the only way into the building, but it's often the only one media are waiting at.

Colleagues shielded Labor MP Jags Krishnan from the media on Wednesday. (ABC News)

Which makes it all the more extraordinary that when Dr Jags, as he's known, chose to walk through that entrance, MP Terry Healy tried to get between his beleaguered colleague and reporters before fellow MP Pierre Yang tried to pull him through the doorway.

The contribution of Cockburn MP David Scaife, who told reporters to be "ashamed of yourselves", didn't help — although he apologised the following day, saying he had been worried about politicians' safety claiming the entry was blocked by the media.

When the barriers were installed the following day by parliamentary staff, not a single MP who spoke that morning was supportive of them.

The rope barriers were seemingly intended to prevent journalists from getting too close to MPs as they entered the building. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The premier's office subsequently admitted one of its staff had asked two unnamed MPs to "support" Dr Jags on his way into parliament.

"This is now a government with total contempt for transparency," opposition leader Basil Zempilas said.

"They have lost a handle on how to act, both in the chamber, outside the chamber, and with just about everything that they do."

Optics of restricting media

The issue of course isn't really the barriers — which are more of a symbolic than practical obstruction — or whether MPs like the media or not.

It's about the ability for an issue in the public interest — the business dealings and disclosures of Dr Jags — to be fully ventilated, and the appearance which is created when that doesn't happen.

Dr Jags Krishnan in parliament. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

The former GP is being sued in the United States over accusations of failing to pay back a million-dollar loan, which he's vowed to "vigorously defend".

Reporting in other media — which has not been verified by the ABC — has also raised questions about whether Dr Jags complied with the rules by telling parliament about his debts and any gifts he receives.

The opportunity to ask him directly about those issues was lost when he was swept into parliament.

The next day, during an ill-fated bid by the opposition to force an inquiry into the issues, Dr Jags said he was in the final process of selling a network of doctors' surgeries he had built and that "all outstanding matters will be resolved upon settlement".

"I have taken legal advice about my parliamentary declarations and I am confident that these are in order," he added.

Child protection sore point

The other lingering headache for the government is its handling of issues in the child protection system, first brought to light by media reports more than two months ago.

Some progress was made when Cook and Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski met with Dorothy Papertalk, who says the system failed her three grandchildren before they were murdered by their mother.

But those problems do not begin or end in the child protection system, which is why elders and the opposition started questioning what role Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch was playing in improving the lot for First Nations communities.

On Monday the premier denied it had taken Punch months to visit Port Hedland, before his minister admitted later that day it was his first visit since July.

The pair eventually managed to explain Punch's role in listening to Aboriginal communities and providing that information to cabinet, but couldn't really explain what difference that had made.

Don Punch admitted he hadn't been to Port Hedland since July. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

On Thursday he quoted from Pilbara Indigenous leader, Doris Eaton, who wrote that his attendance at an on-country meeting was "greatly appreciated" and a "great example" of collaboration.

But he failed to mention less favourable parts of that letter, including a section which notes her requests from 2024 and 2025 "are yet to be fully addressed or realised" and encouraging him to share her "concerns" with colleagues to instigate "much needed action".

On the backfoot

The government was left on the backfoot this week, forced to defend longstanding issues instead of focusing on anything constructive it was doing.

"I want to be talking about cost of living, health and housing, that's my priorities and that's what it will always be," minister John Carey said on Thursday.

John Carey speaks to journalists outside WA parliament, after the rope barriers were set up. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

And there is plenty to talk about in that space, including concern that the federal government's negative gearing changes may reduce rental supply.

It's yet another potential challenge facing the government at the end of a year which has grown increasingly difficult, after it lost a heartland seat in Secret Harbour to One Nation and struggled to gain support for its university merger proposal.

The summer break presents an opportunity to reset and return with a fresh focus in the new year.

For Labor, that can't come soon enough.

World.title: Litany of missed opportunities in Floreat murder tragedy
World.content:
It was a crime that shocked Perth: a family and domestic violence murder in the heart of Perth's affluent western suburbs.

In what Mark Bombara's daughter, Ariel, would later describe as "planned choices … made to murder, underpinned by a lifetime of power, privilege, control and entitlement", Bombara forced his way into the home of his wife's best friend, Jennifer Petelczyc, in May 2024.

Bombara was looking for his estranged wife, Rowena; instead he found medical receptionist Jennifer, 59, and her 18-year-old daughter, Gretl.

Loading...

"When he realised my mum wasn’t in your home, rather than walking back out of that house he decided time was up, and murdering your whole family would be the next best punishment," Ariel Bombara would tell an inquest into their deaths this week in an devastating disavowal of her father's actions.

Held over five days, the inquest laid bare a cascading series of police errors and missed opportunities to save the lives of the Petelczyc women before they were murdered in cold blood.

The gunman killed Jennifer and Gretl Petelczyc in 2024 in a horrific shooting. (Supplied)

The startling revelations include a two-decades-long failure to review gun licences, four separate pleas to police for help that went unheeded, and multiple Triple Zero (000) calls — made as the murders were unfolding — left on hold.

Triple Zero delays

As the women pleaded for their lives, Gretl twice tried to call emergency services, but both times she waited on the line for more than one minute to be put through to police.

The calls disconnected before she could talk to an officer.

Yet, counter to police policy, no-one called her back.

Ariel Bombara got through to police as she and her mother, Rowena, listened to the murders in real time while on the phone with Jennifer Petelczyc.

Ariel was forced to wait two minutes and 18 seconds for her call to be connected.

When she finally got through and explained the situation, the job was designated a priority two by the call taker.

The two women were killed in their Floreat home. (ABC News: David Weber)

It took five minutes to be upgraded to a priority one.

The first police arrived 11 minutes after the call, just in time to hear the last of five gunshots, with which Mark Bombara took his own life.

Detective Senior Sergeant Matt Edmunds told the court he did not think there was time for officers to intervene and save the women.

Matt Edmunds did not think there was enough time to save the victims when officers arrived. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

Acting State Coroner Sarah Linton agreed, but said if Gretl had spoken to an officer on the phone, she would have at least been reassured help was on the way in her final moments.

The separation

About two months before the murders, police escorted the gunman's estranged wife into the family home to collect her belongings.

Gunman recorded himself during shooting, inquest hears The inquest into the deaths of Jennifer and Gretl Petelcyzc hears new details about the day they died and the gunman's interactions with police weeks before the shooting.

Rowena had left her husband just weeks beforehand, moving out of the home with daughter Ariel.

She and other family members warned the attending officers about Mark Bombara's fragile mental health, with son Isaac telling police there may be firearms in the gun safe or "other locations".

Despite this warning, police officers did not seize the weapons of a suspected domestic violence perpetrator, search the home for unsecured guns or inspect the safe.

If they had, they would have discovered more than 1,000 rounds of illegal ammunition.

The 'nice guy'

Constable Shaun King entered the house first and accepted a cup of tea from Mark Bombara, whose behaviour was the "opposite" of what he was expecting.

"I hate to say it, but he seemed like a nice guy," Constable King said, admitting he had been impressed by Bombara's opulent home with its "million dollar view".

The court heard Mark Bombara manipulated police in the weeks before the shooting. (Supplied)

This had impacted the inexperienced officer's ability to assess Bombara's character, he admitted.

Superintendent Andrew Wilson reviewed body-worn camera footage and said Bombara "groomed" the attending officers into a false sense of security.

"I believe [his behaviour] was manipulative … calculated … in an effort to place seeds of doubt in the attending officers' minds," Superintendent Andrew Wilson said.

Pleas for police help

The day before, Rowena and Ariel had attended Mirrabooka Police Station to make a formal complaint of domestic violence, asking for a police order — issued when police think a person is likely to commit an act of family violence.

Ariel Bombara made several appeals to police about her father. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

They feared for their lives, they told police, recounting a long history of abusive behaviour and noting Mark Bombara had access to firearms.

Questions over police response before Floreat murders The coroner in the Floreat murder-suicide inquest questions why a desperate call to Triple Zero stating someone had been shot in a family violence situation was initially marked as a priority two situation.

They were told the grounds to make a police order were not met.

They tried again. Ariel phoned both the Perth police station and the Family Violence Division, warning her father was increasingly unstable and had access to 13 guns.

Still no police orders were made.

An internal report found officers should have issued a 72-hour police order giving police the power to seize his firearms.

Eight officers were found to have not performed their duty and were subject to internal disciplinary action.

Failure to check weapons

The inquest also revealed Mark Bombara should never have been able to hold a licence for the two Glock handguns he took to the Petelczyc home.

Bombara held a collector's licence on sentimental grounds, despite that no longer being a valid reason to hold guns.

The inquest heard the gunman should not have had the weapons he took to the Floreat home. (ABC News: Julian Robins)

But since no-one was checking the online licence renewal system for about 20 years, his licence was re-issued illegally, six times, from 2005 onwards.

Gun storage issues

Less than 12 months before the murders, police wrote to Bombara with questions about his weapon storage locations.

He said he would get back to them but never did, despite two follow-up letters.

Flaw in WA gun laws revealed at Floreat inquest The man who shot dead a mother and daughter in their Floreat home should not have been able to renew his licence for the murder weapon, a coronial inquest is told.

A computer system upgrade then wiped all records relating to gun storage non-compliance orders.

Police yesterday conceded mistakes had been made.

"WA Police accepts there were important lessons to be learnt from this tragedy," Commissioner Col Blanch said in a statement at the conclusion of the inquest.

"WA Police has been open about the shortcomings identified in the police response leading up to this tragedy."

Col Blanch acknowledged police failures. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

This included "failures in the assessment and management of risk", which had led to 18 recommendations to improve responses to family and domestic violence — of which 14 have been completed, according to the commissioner.

Acting State Coroner Sarah Linton is expected to hand down her recommendations next year.

World.title: Man dies after house fire in Geelong suburb
World.content:
A man has been found dead after a house fire in a Geelong suburb early this morning.

Police said emergency services were called to Southwinds Road, in Armstrong Creek, about 3:10am and found the house fully engulfed in flames.

The man found dead at the scene is yet to be formally identified.

Emergency services at the scene of the house fire. (ABC News)

Police are investigating the cause of the blaze.



After the death of a disabled woman in a fire in the same suburb on Boxing Day in 2017, the government committed to building a new fire station as quickly as possible.



"We are working quickly to find a location for the station and this is an absolute priority for me," Emergency Services Minister James Merlino told the Geelong Advertiser in mid-2018.

"It is unacceptable to see a growing community not as protected as it should be."

Since that commitment, the government purchased land for the station, then sold it off.

A fire truck sits behind temporary fencing in Armstrong Creek, across the road from where a station was meant to be built. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Instead, a fire truck sits behind temporary fencing near the Armstrong Creek land initially bought for the station.



The United Firefighters Union said a series of delays had seen the project repeatedly pushed back.



Anyone who witnessed the fire in Southwinds Road or has dash-cam footage or other information, is urged to contact Crime Stoppers by calling 1800 333 000 or going to www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

World.title: Australian cricket urged to stop 'eating itself' as Sandpapergate rolls on
World.content:
Greg Chappell has urged Australia's past and present cricket stars to end their civil war as the ghosts of Sandpapergate continue to haunt the game.

Usman Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin last week when he claimed the entire Test team that played in Cape Town in 2018 knew of the plot to tamper with the ball.

Cameron Bancroft, who was in charge of using sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball, copped a nine-month ban in the wake of the cheating scandal, while Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for a year and stripped of their leadership roles.

The fallout continues to this very day.

Test skipper Pat Cummins delivered an extraordinary 70-minute press conference in Sydney on Friday where he provided an open floor for journalists to ask whatever they wanted in regards to Sandpapergate 2018 and ball tampering in general, among other hot topics.

The 33-year-old steadfastly rejected claims he had any prior knowledge of the 2018 plot to use sandpaper on the ball in order to gain reverse swing.

He also hit out at Khawaja, saying the accusations were "complete nonsense" and suggested they were "probably defamatory".

Warner returned serve just hours after the press conference, saying he stood by all of Khawaja's claims and wouldn't rest until the full truth came out.

The former Test opener also accused Cummins of throwing Khawaja under the bus with his sandpaper denials.

Usman Khawaja has stood by his comments. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Chappell knows a thing or two about controversy.

In 1981, and with NZ requiring six runs off the final ball to force a draw in a one-day match at the MCG, then-Australia captain Chappell ordered his younger brother Trevor Chappell to bowl the last delivery underarm.

While technically legal at the time, the move caused a massive backlash and forced a rule change, with the incident still brought up to this very day.

"Good luck with that. I think 45 years tells me it will probably be a while before it gets trumped," Chappell replied when asked if 'Sandpapergate' had finally trumped the underarm controversy.

"Mistakes have been made, I think you have to own them.

Cummins faces the music In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

"It would've been a tough time back in 2018 with all of that going on. I don't think you're always ready for these disasters when they happen, but we all make mistakes and they're all human beings.

"They're going to make mistakes, and I think we have to accept that and own those decisions, as I had to do 45 years ago."

Chappell doesn't want the in-fighting in Australian cricket to continue.

"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," Chappell said.

"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket.

"It'll be a distraction, but I think they've all had enough experience that when they walk out on the cricket field there's only one thing they're thinking about."

As for Cummins' claims of having no knowledge of the plan to tamper with the ball?

"We have to believe it," Chappell said.

"Pat's a very honourable man and very talented on the field, but I think he's very talented off the field as well.

"I think from a cricket point of view they just need to move on and focus on what's in front of them."

Khawaja was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands on Saturday, but publishers Pelican said it unfortunately had to be postponed.

AAP

World.title: Former NT administrator opens up about being groomed as a child
World.content:
Hugh Heggie was just 14 years old when an older church youth group leader began grooming him.

The youth group in Victoria, where he grew up, had been a safe place. Then one evening, the leader — a man in his 20s — offered him alcohol and suggested the pair go to the drive-in cinema.

Mr Heggie declined the offer but said the conversation then turned.

"He started talking about men touching boys, or men touching men," he said.

Two days later, the man asked him to go to the drive-in again, and this time he relented and asked his mother for permission.

Now aged 76, Mr Heggie is a former doctor and the former Northern Territory administrator — the NT's equivalent of a state governor — who became a household name during the COVID pandemic as the NT's chief health officer.

More than 60 years after his experience with the youth group leader, he is telling his story publicly for the first time.

Hugh Heggie was the NT's chief health officer during COVID. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

On that day, Mr Heggie said the church leader picked him up and kept offering him alcohol.

If you or anyone you know needs help: Police: Triple Zero (000) if it is an emergency

Kids Helpline: 1800 551 800

Headspace:1800 650 890

ReachOut: au.reachout.com

Bravehearts: 1800 272 831

Lifeline: 13 11 14

1800 Respect National Helpline: 1800 737 732

"I realised he was trying to get me intoxicated, so I pretended to drink," he said.

Halfway through the film, Mr Heggie alleged the man put his hand on his leg.

"When his hand went too far, I got out of the car and said, 'You either take me home now or I will walk home'," he said.

Mr Heggie never returned to the youth group, nor did he report the incident to police or tell his parents.

He said he considered himself lucky to have escaped, and chose to bury what happened, telling no one for decades.

But stories of abuse kept finding their way into his life.

He said family members were sexually assaulted and, as a doctor, other men disclosed their own instances of abuse in the privacy of a consultation room.

As a parent he became hypervigilant, worrying about sending his children to Scouts or friends' homes.

He recalled refusing to let one of his children attend a party in a park.

Hugh Heggie says he never reported what happened to him, but it affected how he acted as a parent. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Other times, dropping my young adult [child] off, I said, 'I'm going to come in and introduce myself to the family' … and I often parked outside so I was there to take her home," he said.

Mr Heggie said he now feels angry about what happened to him.

"I didn't even think about reporting him," he said.

"Because it basically was an attempt, I didn't think about it.

"But yes, it does worry me … particularly because of the possibility there were other young people that he took advantage of."

Clare Leaney says stories like Hugh Heggie's can empower other people to seek justice. (Supplied: National Survivors' Foundation)

Instances of child harm have surged across Australia in the past decade, according to recent research by the University of Sydney.

However, National Survivors Foundation chief executive Clare Leaney said stories like Mr Heggie's were crucial for changing these statistics and empowering people to seek justice.

"Hugh is an example of survivorship that people don't necessarily expect to see," she said.

"Of how survivors [can] build a life that can be both surviving and thriving [despite] the most horrific violence imaginable."

Hugh Heggie swore in Lia Finocchiaro as NT chief minister at Government House in 2024 during his time as the NT administrator. (Supplied: Pema Pakhrin/NT News)

Although more people now speak out, Ms Leaney said gaps in the law remained a barrier.

She said in all states and territories except for Victoria and the ACT, organisations including churches, Scouts and swim clubs could not be held vicariously liable for abuse committed by individuals who were not employees, potentially limiting survivors' avenues for compensation and justice.

Survivors of institutional abuse in Queensland want this loophole closed Survivors of institutional abuse are calling on the state to follow other states in closing a legal loophole stopping victims from seeking justice.

"Justice should not be dependent on a person's employment status," she said.

NT Attorney General Marie-Clare Boothby said the government "will work with national counterparts on a uniform approach to redress and liability" and urged survivors to seek support and justice.

"It takes immense courage to disclose abuse and sexual violence, and I encourage victim-survivors to contact NT Police and to access specialist advice and support."

Mr Heggie is now an ambassador for the National Survivors Foundation, and said he hoped sharing his story would help other survivors feel less alone.

"It's important that we all have an understanding of what occurs, to prevent it," he said.

"We need to provide hope for the next generation … and make sure the next generation of children are safe.

"The metric of that will be whether the numbers of sexual assaults is reduced."

World.title: Police seeking witnesses after violent home invasion in Canberra
World.content:
Investigations are continuing into a violent home invasion in Canberra's inner north suburb of Hackett last month, where a woman holding a child was threatened at knifepoint.

ACT Policing said about 11pm on Monday October 5, three men, armed with a firearm, knife, sword and a baseball bat, forced entry to a home on Harris Place, and demanded money from the woman.

It's alleged one of the men struck her in the head, before the group stole cash and a Mercedes Benz sedan.

Loading YouTube content

Police say the child was unharmed.

They urged anyone who saw suspicious activity in the area on October 5, or who otherwise has information, to contact Crime Stoppers, with the option to share information anonymously.

The men are described as being Polynesian in appearance.

World.title: Melbourne's 'liveable city' reputation questioned after fatal stabbing
World.content:
A HungryPanda delivery rider's fatal stabbing sent shock waves beyond the local community, spreading across China through social media and state media coverage.

Reports of 47-year-old Chinese national Feng Jianming's death last Friday were amplified through WeChat groups and public accounts.

Some dubbed Melbourne as "Little Gotham" — a reference to the fictional, crime-ridden city in Batman comics — while others questioned Melbourne's status as one of the world's most liveable city.

"The world's most liveable city could not protect a delivery rider," read one video post on WeChat.

Delivery rider's death impacts election Some in the Chinese community say the fatal stabbing of a delivery driver is evidence that crime is at "an appalling level".

State media reports have highlighted the hardships experienced by the father-of-two, working far away from home to support his family back in China, and the response from the Chinese consulate in Melbourne.

"[Consul General Fang Xinwen] asked the Premier, Victorian Government and Victoria Police to handle this case fairly in accordance with the law, severely punish the perpetrator, and earnestly safeguard the life and legitimate rights and interests of the Chinese nationals in Victoria," the report said.

This is not the first time Melbourne has been dubbed "Little Gotham" or a "crime capital". The label often resurfaces on social media after serious violent attacks.

Some people have called Melbourne a "crime capital". (ABC News: Jason Fang)

Liveability ranking versus reality

Garrick Yang regularly travels between Shanghai and Melbourne, where he had lived for more than a decade and his parents still do.

Mr Yang said the attack on Mr Feng was "a tragedy" but came as no surprise, following a series of stabbings in recent months.

"When you look at everyday life in Melbourne and see these incidents, you realise how far reality is from [its liveability] reputation," Mr Yang said.

Mr Yang has also been a victim of crime.

In September, his investment property in Heidelberg West was broken into and copper parts were stolen from the hot water system.

He said he gave police the CCTV footage but heard nothing since.

Garrick Yang's property was broken into, with a fence damaged and copper parts stolen from the hot water system. (Supplied: Garrick Yang)

Melbourne has been ranked among the world's top four most liveable cities over the past four years, according to the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU).

It topped the index for a record seven consecutive years from 2011 to 2017.

Melbourne ranked third in the latest index, scoring 95 out of 100 for stability, which is weighted at 25 per cent of the overall score.

The stability category considers factors including petty and violent crime, terrorism and military conflict.

"Those liveability rankings are almost a joke to people like us, who live in China but still have an emotional attachment to Australia," Mr Yang said.

The ABC has approached Victoria Police and the EIU for comment.

'Is Melbourne really this chaotic?'

Sam Huang is a research professor in tourism and services marketing at Edith Cowan University in Perth.

He said while Melbourne remained an attractive city because of its culture and lifestyle, news of Mr Feng's fatal stabbing could risk further damaging its international reputation.

It could have a considerable impact on people's decision to live, study or invest in Melbourne over the next one to two years, he added.

Sam Huang says Melbourne's image could take a hit among prospective students, workers and migrants. (Supplied: Sam Huang)

"Safety is one of the most basic requirements of a liveable city," he said.

"People should not feel their personal safety is threatened when they walk down the street."

For Mr Yang, concerns around safety have gradually eroded his confidence in Melbourne as an investment destination.

He said he already sold two properties and planned to reduce his remaining holdings.

New government policies around property investment had also influenced his decision.

Mr Yang added that his friends in China, who had asked him about visiting Melbourne or sending their kids there to study, were also increasingly worried about safety.

"I think this incident will definitely affect their willingness," he said.

On social media, Chinese citizens with plans to visit Melbourne had been also asking: "Is Melbourne really this chaotic?"

Echo chamber or 'Little Gotham'?

Blake Li, who lives in China's Sichuan province, said he had been following reports about Mr Feng's stabbing among other criminal incidents on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, and Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote.

He said social media could create a misleading impression, so he tried "to cross-check information before accepting it".

Mr Li also questioned whether Melbourne deserved the "Little Gotham" label, arguing that many types of crime also occurred in Chinese cities.

"Robberies, killings and arson can happen in any city," he said.

Victoria's Crime Statistics Agency figures show the state's crime rate peaked in 2025 before dropping 3.8 per cent in the 12 months to June 2026.

Crime rates in the City of Melbourne follow a similar pattern.

However, the City of Melbourne's 2025–26 annual report found only 34 per cent of women and 49 per cent of men surveyed felt safe at night, compared to 35 per cent and 51 per cent in the previous year.

Sharon Kwok says crime statistics and people's sense of safety often differ. (Supplied: Sharon Kwok)

Sharon Kwok, a criminology lecturer at Western Sydney University, said crime statistics and perceptions of safety sometimes differed.

Highly publicised incidents, known as "signal crimes", could have a disproportionate impact because people identified with victims who shared their ethnic background, she said.

"If I'm Chinese and the person who was killed is also Chinese, I might think, 'This could happen to me too.'"

Dr Kwok said proximity also mattered, with people more likely to feel threatened when a crime happened near places they regularly visited.

She said many people in the local Chinese community relied on WeChat for news and information, and followed commentary from key opinion leaders, including Chinese influencers.

"When the same story was repeated by many voices, including friends and family, it could grow in an echo chamber," she said.

World.title: Family-run berry farm looks to AI and automation to ease workforce challenges
World.content:
Western Australia's largest blueberry grower is turning to artificial intelligence and autonomous technology to reduce labour costs and ease the challenge of finding enough workers during the peak harvest period.

Earlier this year, Australia's food producers raised concerns about the federal government's slower visa processing times and limits on working holiday maker numbers, saying the changes could reduce access to seasonal labour.

WA's largest blueberry farm is ramping up production. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Western Berry's blueberry operation is 100 kilometres north of Perth and spans 120 hectares.

This year it will produce just under 1,500 tonnes of blueberries bound for supermarkets across Australia and Asia.

Its owners, the Kwiecien-Fisher family, are in a significant expansion phase and hope to triple production in the coming years.

Derek Fisher and Marek Kwiecien-Fisher at Western Berry. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But producing more fruit will also require more workers, something many horticultural businesses say is becoming increasingly difficult and expensive.

An autonomous foliar sprayer moves through the blueberry plants. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Technology part of the labour solution

The family hopes innovations like driverless tractors, machine harvesting and eventually artificial intelligence will help ease the challenges.

Operations manager Marek Kwiecien-Fisher said the company was trialling autonomous technology as much as it could on the property.

It is using driverless, self-navigating tractors to do foliar spraying of the berries and laser-guided "green on brown" weed control on the ground, and to perform tasks such as hauling berries from the field to the pack house.

A driverless tractor makes its way to the pack house. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"Then in the packing we use a lot of autonomy in photographic packing, grading solutions and autonomous punnetising," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

With autonomous technology now more accessible than ever, farmers across various food industries are determining how self-guided machinery can fit into their businesses, and the balance between people and machines on the farm.

Marek Kwiecien-Fisher says the company is trialling new technology. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Driverless tractors use GPS mapping, sensors and cameras to navigate predetermined routes and can also be operated remotely.

Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said they were an expensive outlay and time consuming when learning how to set up and operate, but he believed they had a firm future on the farm.

Data generated from the pack house is also proving invaluable.

"Even things that we didn't think that we were gaining data on has the ability to show us how we'll operate next year, and what areas we could fill the gaps in, either our production or our supply models or our customer requirements," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

Blueberries are photographed six to nine times before they make their way into these rows, ready to be put into punnets. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said future options for technology use on the property could go as far as humanoid robots pruning plants and AI modelling of future crops.

"If we can teach an AI model where to prune and how to prune, and if that can teach a humanoid robot where to prune and how to prune, you basically get rid of any damage to your drip lines, trellising, your pruning equipment, your plants and it becomes a very precise farming technique," he said.

"The pruning basically sets how much fruit we're going to pick next year, so it's one of the largest indicators of how we can forecast our volumes and our production for the coming season.

"We're [also] looking at autonomous mowing, flower counts and crop health detection systems, so cameras that look at the crop [can] check for poor irrigation."

Western Berry is a family business on a rapid growth trajectory. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Growing in the family

While technology is playing an increasingly important role in the business, Western Berry remains firmly family-run.

Almost 30 years ago Derek Fisher and his wife Barbara wanted space for their young family and purchased what is now one part of the farm.

Derek Fisher says there is strong global demand for Australian blueberries. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

It was a former ostrich property that they initially planted with olives in 2001, but a successful trial of one hectare of blueberries resulted in them changing course and moving into the blueberry industry.

Now their three sons, Adam, Marek and Tom Kwiecien-Fisher, run the business. Adam is in charge of supply chain and packing, Tom oversees the design and construction of new farm areas, and Marek manages operations.

Adam Kwiecien-Fisher manages supply-chain logistics. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

In 2021, the family struck an agreement with global agricultural company United Exports and Oz Varieties, giving them access to the unique OZblu blueberry genetics.

Ripe berries fall off the plant easily, but not before they are ready, which is key for successful machine harvesting.

Tom Kwiecien-Fisher manages the design and construction of new farm areas. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

The property is working with two harvesters. The latest model is battery-operated, solar-powered and controlled via remote control, collecting fruit and stacking trays by itself.

"Eventually, we will be using AI learning to make this machine autonomous so we can press a button and it drives itself," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

The latest model blueberry harvester will eventually move autonomously along the the row of plants. (ABC Mid West and Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

A harvesting machine can pick up to 6 tonnes of blueberries a day at a cost of about 50 cents a kilogram, compared with about $6 a kilogram for hand picking.

He said machinery and autonomous technology service provision was creating a new employment industry within agriculture.

"I think there's a whole new industry into supplying and understanding the technology and the information tech, the IT side of these machines," he said.

"There's a huge opportunity for computer science specialists, people that actually understand how to operate AI, people that understand how to operate those machines."

Quoc Thanh Cao is known as the fastest blueberry picker on the property. (ABC Mid West & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

But Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said at most half of their crop would be machine harvested, and pickers remained a very important asset to the business.

Western Berry employs more than 200 people to pick its crop, making it one of the largest employers in the region.

"We are growing at a rate and expanding at a rate that our full employment numbers are growing faster than tech is replacing jobs, and just because we have tech doesn't mean that workers aren't required," Mr Kwiecien-Fisher said.

The goalkeeper whose challenge resulted in the death of a player in Spain has been banned for 12 matches. FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono was suspended by the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee on Friday after his challenge on Jesus de Miguel resulted in the death of the Tenerife striker last week. Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono not long after the tragic incident. AP Equatorial Guinea international Owono was sent off in the second division clash on November 2 after racing into midfield and colliding with De Miguel while trying to clear an aerial ball. After the collision De Miguel, 30, was placed in intensive care in hospital and the Spanish forward died on November 3.



“The assessment of the conduct under consideration in these proceedings must be based on the facts expressly recorded in the referee’s report, which states that the player was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play’,” said the committee in a statement. Jesús de Miguel died after a cardiac arrest. Instagram/@cdtoficial “The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge. In view of the nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances... the maximum sanction, 12 matches of suspension, is justified.” Spanish police sources last week told AFP an investigation into what happened had been opened under judicial supervision. Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after De Miguel’s death. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club Andorra last week.



“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesus.” Loading FC Andorra coach Carles Manso said on Thursday it would be Owono who decides if and when he returns to football after the tragic incident. Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid president Florentino Perez. The Telegraph, London

World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAviation ‘Extraordinary circumstances’: Flights grounded across US due to communications issues Michael Koziol Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:32am ,first published 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Follow along for our live coverage of the US aviation emergency here. Washington: A ground stop has been issued for all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” after authorities reported serious air traffic control communications issues. The order means flights in the air may land, but those on the ground cannot take off. The shutdown caused chaos at airports, with airlines cancelling more than 1000 flights and delaying nearly 10,000, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. Loading The disruption quickly spread beyond the United States, forcing the cancellation of flights from Canada and Europe. US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day.



US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he said. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” It is the second time since September 11, 2001 that there has been a nationwide ground stop in the US. AP Photo/David Zalubowski The ground stop was issued on Friday afternoon in Washington (about 8.15am Saturday AEDT). The cause of the system failure was not immediately clear. Urging calm, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution, and there was no suggestion at this stage that a cyberattack was to blame.



“There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States,” he said. “This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA.” But Mullin also said nothing could be ruled out at this point. He said he saw no reason to connect Friday’s telecommunications issue with the outage that affected Microsoft systems around the world the previous day. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack at this stage. AP Photo/Alex Brandon “We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that is in the air ... we’re going to get you on the ground. There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones. This isn’t another 9/11.” CNN also reported that two law enforcement officials said preliminary information indicated a cyberattack was not to blame. The FAA has been contacted for further comment.



It is only the third time in US history that a nationwide ground stop has been ordered; the first was during the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and the other was in 2023 when the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system failed. The 2023 outage lasted about 12 hours in total, though departures were able to resume after about 90 minutes. A commuter stands with luggage outside Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Friday afternoon. AP Photo/Tom Brenner From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded airport departure halls and airline desks as departure boards filled with delays and cancellations and aircraft remained parked at gates. “I might cry at some point but not yet,” said Louise Maher, 47, who was still hoping to fly from Newark to London on Friday night despite warnings that her British Airways flight could be delayed by air traffic control restrictions.



Dennis Lennox, a Republican strategist, was on board a plane on the tarmac at MBS International Airport in Michigan when the ground stop was ordered. He was due to fly to Detroit and onwards to Los Angeles. Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: FAA stops all departing flights citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’, Homeland Security secretary denies cyber attack, Microsoft outage connection “We had backed out of the gate and were starting to go through the taxiing process to take off, and we were ordered to return to the gate,” he said. “The initial report was there were radio issues in this area. Within a minute or two, I was able to find out things quicker. We weren’t even given the chance to stay on the plane. We were kicked off the plane and dumped inside the terminal.” Last year, US Congress approved $US12.5 billion ($18.5 billion) to fix the FAA’s ageing communications system, and on Friday the FAA and White House asked Congress for another $US30.1 billion to address other issues.



The FAA has also begun rolling out an artificial intelligence tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) to help manage air traffic across the country. Asked whether Friday’s issues could be AI related, Mullin told a reporter: “We call it SI around here, remember.” The Trump administration has attempted to rename artificial intelligence to superintelligence. Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell told Fox News the ground stop was a sensible measure to “declutter the airspace” and deal with the technical issue. “The ground stop, while a real pain in the neck, is the safest way to go,” he said. United Airlines, one of the main carriers between the US and Australia, said in a post on X that international departures were being managed on a case-by-case basis by the FAA.



The airline operates a number of flights from the US to Australia’s east coast that are due to depart late on Friday night (Los Angeles time). By about 10.30am (AEDT), some international flights had begun departing the US from hubs such as Los Angeles and Washington Dulles, FlightRadar data showed. World.content:
Need to know WorldNorth AmericaAviation Here’s what we know so far about the US flight shutdown, and what it means for travel Chris Zappone and Hannah Hammoud Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:21am ,first published 9:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the ground stop following a system-wide failure involving Air Route Traffic Control Centres. In a post on X, Duffy said: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” View post on X What have the FAA said?

The FAA has attributed the nationwide disruption to “extraordinary circumstances”, but has yet to disclose further details about the incident.



The Department of Homeland Security has also said there is currently no indication that the communications failure was caused by foul play. At this stage, the exact cause of the failure has not been specified. Further updates are expected as the FAA continues to investigate the communications failure. When was the last time this happened? A nationwide ground stop of this scale is an extremely rare occurrence in US aviation history. It is understood to be only the third time such an order has been issued nationwide. The first occurred following the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001, while the second took place in January 2023 after the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system suffered an outage.



Is AI to blame for this? Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: FAA stops all departing flights citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’, Homeland Security secretary denies cyber attack, Microsoft outage connection The communications failure comes just days after the FAA announced plans to begin rolling out an AI system across the US to help air traffic controllers manage traffic and prevent delays, The New York Times has reported. The timing has raised questions. According to the report, the AI technology was first unveiled at Washington DC airports two months ago on the same day a separate communications failure grounded hundreds of flights. That earlier outage was caused by a circuit failure after contractors accidentally cut through a backup fibre line.



University of Sydney aviation professor Rico Merkert said: “It’s really important to have modern infrastructure in this space and without that, you can add as much AI as you like to those systems, but if you don’t have that proper ground infrastructure there, then it’s that’s not functional.” What does this mean for travellers? The ground stop is expected to cause widespread disruption across the US aviation network, with delays and cancellations likely to have knock-on effects throughout the day. The Australian Travel Industry Association CEO Dean Long said it was a developing situation for Australian travellers which will have “knock-on impacts”. For travellers who have booked through an ATIA-accredited travel business, “expect to hear from them or your airline”.



“If you’re travelling in the next 72 hours, that’s our priority.” Planes are parked on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in DFW Airport, Texas. AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez “If you haven’t heard from your travel agent, tour operator or airline yet, get in touch with them.” For those not flying within 72 hours, they should hold off communicating with travel agencies and airlines “so they can look after the travellers who need it most urgently.” “We know this is unsettling for travellers,” Long said. “Our members are there to help, and we are monitoring the situation closely.”



In an update released at 10am AEDT, the FAA said the ground stop remains in place but “as en route facilities recover, flights will be allowed to depart” – with flights being released gradually as air traffic control centres recover. Related Article Updated

Aviation ‘Extraordinary circumstances’: Flights grounded across US due to communications issues For Australian travellers flying to the United States, airports are monitoring the situation and advising passengers to check directly with their airlines. Sydney Airport: All domestic and international flights are operating as normal, with no current impact to airport operations.

All domestic and international flights are operating as normal, with no current impact to airport operations. Melbourne Airport: Passengers booked on morning departures are advised to proceed to the airport as planned until further notice.

Passengers booked on morning departures are advised to proceed to the airport as planned until further notice. Brisbane Airport: American Airlines flight AA008 to Dallas Fort Worth has been delayed by one hour, moving from its scheduled 9.40am departure to 10.40am. The airport has advised passengers to check with their airlines for updates. Sydney Airport said it was monitoring the situation closely, but there was currently no impact to its operations.



“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight,” a spokesperson said. Qantas have advised at this stage there is a limited impact for the airline, but passengers are advised to check for updates through the app – though flight QF4 (New York to Auckland) is expected to be delayed. Most US-bound Qantas flights depart in the afternoon, providing a buffer while the FAA issue is resolved. Meanwhile, US airlines have warned passengers to expect disruptions. United Airlines confirmed that flights already airborne would continue to their destinations, but new domestic departures would remain grounded while the FAA order was in place. United is proactively cancelling flights due to congestion in the nation’s air traffic system, and issuing travel waivers, so customers can change their travel plans.



Delta also has a travel waiver for customers to change their flights. American Airlines also confirmed that aircraft already in the air could continue to their destinations, but warned that disruption to its schedule could continue throughout the day, depending on how long the nationwide ground stop remains in place. Updated WorldNorth AmericaTragedy ‘Miracle on the Mississippi’: Passengers, crew rescued after tanker hits cruise ship in New Orleans Jack Brook and Jeffrey Collins Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:16am ,first published 7:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. New Orleans: A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into the docked American Heritage river cruise paddleboat with 180 people aboard on Friday, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over. Thirty-two people were taken to hospital, but none had critical injuries, Moreno said, calling it “a miracle on the Mississippi”. Loading Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hitting the paddlewheel cruise boat while it appeared to be docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.



Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and several other rescuers rushed to help. The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off it. Emergency personnel and crews work the scene. The Advocate via AP Footage posted to social media showed the cruise ship sideways in the river. The Advocate via AP Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 19-degree water onto nearby ships.



Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and noticed the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water. “It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.” People in lifejackets being dragged from the river. AP Emergency personnel and crews are on the scene. AP The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five storeys high and can hold up to 150 passengers.



The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi. The cruise line said it was working with the Coast Guard and would share more information when possible. View post on X According to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic, the tanker involved in the crash specialises in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, used for road construction and roofing. Ships carrying asphalt and bitumen are often heated well above 120 degrees to prevent the asphalt from solidifying aboard, according to the maritime periodical Marine Insights. It is not immediately clear whether the ship was carrying any materials when the crash occurred.



The 160-metre vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. More to come AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts. A choice must be made: Team Uzzie or Team Pat?
World.content:
Analysis SportBall tampering Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts. A choice must be made: Team Uzzie or Team Pat? Oliver Brown November 14, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Even after more than eight years, “sandpapergate” is the gift that keeps giving, the scandal that leaves an irreparable schism not just within a cricket team but an entire country. As if those events in Cape Town in March 2018 were not lurid enough at the time, with the sight of Cameron Bancroft shoving sandpaper down his trousers a grievous wound to Australia’s sense of itself, Usman Khawaja’s claim that everybody knew about the plot to tamper with the ball has magnified the trauma. Long-time teammates Usman Khawaja with Pat Cummins back in 2018. Getty Images The soap opera has spun so far out of control that professional lip-readers were asked this week to decode a film of Test captain Pat Cummins arguing with his wife Becky on a Sydney street. It is all supremely unedifying, and yet deliciously entertaining. Cummins’ press conference on Friday dialled up the drama, shredding any remaining friendship with Khawaja as he called the retired opener’s accusation of a team conspiracy “100 per cent wrong” and “utter nonsense”.



The unburdening of his pent-up rage lasted 68 minutes and shone a light on his personality as never before. Occasionally too PR-friendly for some tastes, he excoriated Khawaja, telling him: “Friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations.” Has there been a saga like it for raw emotion? In 2018, a disgraced Steve Smith dissolved in front of the cameras and had to be comforted by his father Peter. When an ashen-faced James Sutherland, the then chief executive of Cricket Australia, delivered a statement in Melbourne condemning the players’ behaviour, tensions ran so high that two journalists present had a fight. Loading The difference with Cummins’ performance is that it has been hailed instantly in his homeland as a peace-in-our-time moment. “Outstanding”, “vulnerable”, “credible” were just some of the snap verdicts Down Under. Oh, and “disgustingly handsome”.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Seven takeaways from one of Australian sport’s most memorable press conferences The motivation for these cloying homilies appears to be twofold. First, Cummins is such a gleaming Australian thoroughbred, both a devastating strike bowler and a part-time children’s author advocating the greater use of solar panels, that nothing can be allowed to besmirch his sheen of perfection. Secondly, the idea that he is not telling the truth – that he, and the rest of a brilliant bowling attack, were in on the dastardly scheme from the start – is almost too much for the national psyche to bear. There is evident desperation in Australia to believe Cummins’ version over Khawaja’s. Just look at their respective media appearances this week: where Khawaja received a thorough grilling on the ABC’s 730 current affairs show, Cummins left his audience at Sydney’s Olympic Park in such raptures that he was practically carried out on a sedan chair.



Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, has reopened old wounds. Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts of what happened. And so, the logical extension is that somebody is lying, that a choice must be made as to who to trust. Team Uzzie or Team Pat? The ecstatic notices of the past 24 hours prove Australians are in the captain’s corner, prepared to take his every heartfelt comment at face value and to let the infernal matter rest. All very convenient, very fickle. The problem is the central question – how the bowlers in Cape Town could possibly have been oblivious to the altered ball condition – is left hanging. In 2021, Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement to declare that the first they knew of sandpaper being on the field was when they saw it on the big screen.



“We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo,” they said at the time. “It has gone on too long and it is time to move on.” Loading Except their own teammate seemed not to receive the memo, with Khawaja waiting a further five years to argue in his memoir Sabr, that the Australian dressing room needed to accept collective responsibility for the scam. Promoting the book, he said: “Am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah.” Unsurprisingly, David Warner, Khawaja’s close friend and a man banned for 12 months for his part in it, wasted no time in endorsing this portrayal. And when Cummins contradicted it, he gravely concluded the captain had “thrown Uzzie under the bus”.



The trouble is Khawaja has hardly gone out of his way to present himself as a reliable narrator. He went to pieces under tough interrogation by 730 host Sarah Ferguson, seeking refuge in such vacuous Meghan Markle-isms as “my truth” and “safe space”, before cancelling the rest of his scheduled broadcast appearances. While he is fond of throwing grenades – remember his allegation that he had been treated differently during the last Ashes series as a “coloured cricketer”? – he is not the best at providing concrete proof. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith during the infamous press conference at Newlands in 2018. Getty Images He again pushes the politics of grievance in his book, insisting he lost out to Smith for the Test captaincy on the grounds of race. Even Cummins, once so indulgent of Khawaja that he stopped Australia’s players from spraying champagne so as not to offend a teetotal Muslim, was unimpressed. “If you’re going to say that, you’ve got to have some evidence, and I just don’t think that is the case,” he said. It all leaves Australia’s cricket community in quite the quandary.



You can see their dilemma a mile off: on the one hand, they want to circle the wagons around the golden boy Cummins, and on the other, they are terrified of suggesting any malign motives for distrusting Khawaja. Pat Cummins answered questions for well over an hour. Sam Mooy To cap it all, Warner’s book is due out before long, all but guaranteeing the whole sorry mess will be relitigated once more. For a once great Test team, it is a nightmare without end. For everybody else, it is just about the juiciest Ashes prelude possible. World.content:
Earlier this morning, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop in the US due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.

What caused it?

Telecommunication problems

All Trump administration agencies are citing a telecommunications problem as the reason for halting all departing flights.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the FAA issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he says.

Not terror or a cyberattack

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no foul involved in the ground stop and explicitly said it was not a terrorist attack. “This isn’t another 9/11,” he says.

He, too, blames a telecommunications outage but adds that Trump administration officials do not have a conclusive cause.

Microsoft outage

Mullin also says there is no connection between the nationwide ground stop and the Microsoft outage, which also triggered massive global disruptions yesterday, according to The Washington Post.

The new AI tool

The communications error arrived days after the FAA announced it would begin rolling out an AI toll across the US to help controllers avoid delays, The New York Times reports.

According to that report, the AI tool was initially unveiled in Washington, DC airports two months ago on the same day air traffic communications failures also grounded hundreds of flights.

The incident occurred after a circuit failed when contractors accidentally ripped through a back-up fibre line.

But Mullin also says nothing could be ruled out at this point.

World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby It won’t be the last time the French raid Australia’s top rugby talent Paul Cully November 14, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items.
