The news that Australia’s under-18 captain Justice Taumoepeau is taking his talents to the Top 14 in France for the next three years had a depressingly familiar feel to it. Rugby Australia has done a reasonable job of retaining talent from their junior sides, but not all of those players will kick on, and it’s the few who get away who will come back to hurt them. Australia’s under-18s captain Justice Taumoepeau (being tackled) is off to play domestic rugby in France. Getty Images for Rugby Australia Taumoepeau, a product of the Waratahs system, is in that category and it is a sort of backhanded compliment to Australia that he has been targeted by Pau in France. The club has the reputation as one of the best developers of talent in Europe, with brilliant Test backs Fabien Brau-Boirie and Théo Attissogbe notable graduates from their academy.



Of course, Taumoepeau’s exit comes with the now-standard reassurances that RA will keep in touch and he still wants to play for the Wallabies. But Australia’s claim on the young back-rower has been loosened by his departure and it would be naive to think otherwise. Taumoepeau’s move feels like a kick in the guts because it undermines one of the pillars essential to RA’s bid to revive the Wallabies’ fortunes. France’s Fabien Brau-Boirie, centre, is tackled by Australia’s Ryan Lonergan and Len Ikitau, left, during the Nations Championship international in Brisbane earlier this year. AP Photo/Tertius Pickard Invest in youth and build, they said, and the Wallabies will reap the benefits. Well, that is what RA and NSW did with Taumoepeau, but doing the right thing hasn’t stopped the French from coming in and swooping after years of Australian development.



But, such is the harsher world facing Waratahs coach Michael Cheika as he takes on his second stint in the job. The image of Cheika returning to the Waratahs, flanked by his assistants Stephen Hoiles and Wycliff Palu, prompted some feelgood vibes of better times, like a favourite rock band reforming for another tour. Michael Cheika faces the media for the first time as Waratahs coach last week, flanked by his assistants Stephen Hoiles (left) and Wycliff Palu. James Brickwood There is so much about Cheika’s demeanour and language, not to mention his record, that points to the coach instilling a level of belief among his squad. But, the expectations on Cheika need to come with all manner of caveats.



It would be hard to argue, even risk being labelled a pessimist, that the Waratahs squad Cheika is inheriting is as strong as the one he took over in 2013, never mind the team he refined in the championship year in 2014. There will be a sprinkling of Wallabies, and the return of Angus Bell from his stint in Ulster will strengthen the pack. Young No. 8 Isaac Fonua also showed considerable promise, and Cheika will feel confident Palu can, in time, turn him into another Palu. But last year obvious talents such as Sid Harvey and Jimmy Hendren were up and down with their performances and it is difficult for players of that age to suddenly take a great leap. The return of Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps were designed to infuse the younger players with know-how and a winning mentality, but the Waratahs project feels like one that should be measured in years, not months. Hoiles, as Cheika’s successor, will be the long-term beneficiary.



Related Article Australian rugby Don’t be cranky, be connected: Will Skelton on why French raids can be good for Australian rugby Cheika could make fools of us. Perhaps his shock therapy will work and the Waratahs can challenge for a place in the playoffs next year. That would be a success, never mind the title. But, the reality is the rugby world has shifted since the 2013-2015 period, and a lot of those changes have been hostile to Australian rugby. French clubs view NSW and Queensland as being in the same neighbourhood as Fiji, figuratively as well as literally, and Taumoepeau probably won’t be the last young player to head north. The poaching justifiably infuriates RA, and it is quite the flex for Pau to be able to land Australia’s 18s captain.



But, rightly or wrongly, it does reflect how the balance of power has shifted. When Cheika started at the Waratahs, the Wallabies were No.3 in the world. France was No.4. Today, the Wallabies are No.7 and the French have retained their position, although back-to-back Six Nations titles and a thriving Top 14 suggests they are in a better place than Ireland (No.3). Cheika’s second act at the Waratahs, therefore, will be more challenging than the first. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

The goalkeeper whose challenge resulted in the death of a player in Spain has been banned for 12 matches. FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono was suspended by the Spanish football federation’s disciplinary committee on Friday after his challenge on Jesus de Miguel resulted in the death of the Tenerife striker last week. Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono not long after the tragic incident. AP Equatorial Guinea international Owono was sent off in the second division clash on November 2 after racing into midfield and colliding with De Miguel while trying to clear an aerial ball. After the collision De Miguel, 30, was placed in intensive care in hospital and the Spanish forward died on November 3.



“The assessment of the conduct under consideration in these proceedings must be based on the facts expressly recorded in the referee’s report, which states that the player was sent off for ‘violently striking an opponent in the chest with his leg, using excessive force, while the ball was in play’,” said the committee in a statement. Jesús de Miguel died after a cardiac arrest. Instagram/@cdtoficial “The tragic outcome of the incident, resulting in the death of Jesus de Miguel Alameda, is public knowledge. In view of the nature of the conduct described and the accompanying circumstances... the maximum sanction, 12 matches of suspension, is justified.” Spanish police sources last week told AFP an investigation into what happened had been opened under judicial supervision. Owono said he was enduring the “hardest days of my life” after De Miguel’s death. “These are the hardest days of my life. I struggle to find the words and it is very difficult for me to process anything that has happened,” said Owono in a statement published by his club Andorra last week.



“I feel immense pain over the loss of Jesus. I think of him, of his family, and of all the people who loved him. I know there will be many issues to address, and I will face whatever comes with the utmost respect. But right now, honestly, I cannot think about anything other than Jesus and the pain we are going through. Rest in peace, Jesus.” Loading FC Andorra coach Carles Manso said on Thursday it would be Owono who decides if and when he returns to football after the tragic incident. Last Saturday, Tenerife fans and players gathered at the club’s stadium for a memorial and farewell to De Miguel. His funeral took place last Thursday and around 400 mourners attended, including Spain coach Luis de la Fuente and Real Madrid president Florentino Perez. The Telegraph, London

World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAviation ‘Extraordinary circumstances’: Flights grounded across US due to communications issues Michael Koziol Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:32am ,first published 8:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Follow along for our live coverage of the US aviation emergency here. Washington: A ground stop has been issued for all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety” after authorities reported serious air traffic control communications issues. The order means flights in the air may land, but those on the ground cannot take off. The shutdown caused chaos at airports, with airlines cancelling more than 1000 flights and delaying nearly 10,000, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware. Loading The disruption quickly spread beyond the United States, forcing the cancellation of flights from Canada and Europe. US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day.



US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”. “FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he said. “We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” It is the second time since September 11, 2001 that there has been a nationwide ground stop in the US. AP Photo/David Zalubowski The ground stop was issued on Friday afternoon in Washington (about 8.15am Saturday AEDT). The cause of the system failure was not immediately clear. Urging calm, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House the ground stop was ordered out of an abundance of caution, and there was no suggestion at this stage that a cyberattack was to blame.



“There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States,” he said. “This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA.” But Mullin also said nothing could be ruled out at this point. He said he saw no reason to connect Friday’s telecommunications issue with the outage that affected Microsoft systems around the world the previous day. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyberattack at this stage. AP Photo/Alex Brandon “We are assured that everybody is safe. Everybody that is in the air ... we’re going to get you on the ground. There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones. This isn’t another 9/11.” CNN also reported that two law enforcement officials said preliminary information indicated a cyberattack was not to blame. The FAA has been contacted for further comment.



It is only the third time in US history that a nationwide ground stop has been ordered; the first was during the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, and the other was in 2023 when the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system failed. The 2023 outage lasted about 12 hours in total, though departures were able to resume after about 90 minutes. A commuter stands with luggage outside Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Friday afternoon. AP Photo/Tom Brenner From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded airport departure halls and airline desks as departure boards filled with delays and cancellations and aircraft remained parked at gates. “I might cry at some point but not yet,” said Louise Maher, 47, who was still hoping to fly from Newark to London on Friday night despite warnings that her British Airways flight could be delayed by air traffic control restrictions.



Dennis Lennox, a Republican strategist, was on board a plane on the tarmac at MBS International Airport in Michigan when the ground stop was ordered. He was due to fly to Detroit and onwards to Los Angeles. Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: FAA stops all departing flights citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’, Homeland Security secretary denies cyber attack, Microsoft outage connection “We had backed out of the gate and were starting to go through the taxiing process to take off, and we were ordered to return to the gate,” he said. “The initial report was there were radio issues in this area. Within a minute or two, I was able to find out things quicker. We weren’t even given the chance to stay on the plane. We were kicked off the plane and dumped inside the terminal.” Last year, US Congress approved $US12.5 billion ($18.5 billion) to fix the FAA’s ageing communications system, and on Friday the FAA and White House asked Congress for another $US30.1 billion to address other issues.



The FAA has also begun rolling out an artificial intelligence tool called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) to help manage air traffic across the country. Asked whether Friday’s issues could be AI related, Mullin told a reporter: “We call it SI around here, remember.” The Trump administration has attempted to rename artificial intelligence to superintelligence. Former FAA deputy administrator Daniel Elwell told Fox News the ground stop was a sensible measure to “declutter the airspace” and deal with the technical issue. “The ground stop, while a real pain in the neck, is the safest way to go,” he said. United Airlines, one of the main carriers between the US and Australia, said in a post on X that international departures were being managed on a case-by-case basis by the FAA.



The airline operates a number of flights from the US to Australia’s east coast that are due to depart late on Friday night (Los Angeles time). By about 10.30am (AEDT), some international flights had begun departing the US from hubs such as Los Angeles and Washington Dulles, FlightRadar data showed. World.content:
Need to know WorldNorth AmericaAviation Here’s what we know so far about the US flight shutdown, and what it means for travel Chris Zappone and Hannah Hammoud Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:21am ,first published 9:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued the ground stop following a system-wide failure involving Air Route Traffic Control Centres. In a post on X, Duffy said: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.” View post on X What have the FAA said?

The FAA has attributed the nationwide disruption to “extraordinary circumstances”, but has yet to disclose further details about the incident.



The Department of Homeland Security has also said there is currently no indication that the communications failure was caused by foul play. At this stage, the exact cause of the failure has not been specified. Further updates are expected as the FAA continues to investigate the communications failure. When was the last time this happened? A nationwide ground stop of this scale is an extremely rare occurrence in US aviation history. It is understood to be only the third time such an order has been issued nationwide. The first occurred following the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001, while the second took place in January 2023 after the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system suffered an outage.



Is AI to blame for this? Related Article Live

Aviation US flights grounded LIVE updates: FAA stops all departing flights citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’, Homeland Security secretary denies cyber attack, Microsoft outage connection The communications failure comes just days after the FAA announced plans to begin rolling out an AI system across the US to help air traffic controllers manage traffic and prevent delays, The New York Times has reported. The timing has raised questions. According to the report, the AI technology was first unveiled at Washington DC airports two months ago on the same day a separate communications failure grounded hundreds of flights. That earlier outage was caused by a circuit failure after contractors accidentally cut through a backup fibre line.



University of Sydney aviation professor Rico Merkert said: “It’s really important to have modern infrastructure in this space and without that, you can add as much AI as you like to those systems, but if you don’t have that proper ground infrastructure there, then it’s that’s not functional.” What does this mean for travellers? The ground stop is expected to cause widespread disruption across the US aviation network, with delays and cancellations likely to have knock-on effects throughout the day. The Australian Travel Industry Association CEO Dean Long said it was a developing situation for Australian travellers which will have “knock-on impacts”. For travellers who have booked through an ATIA-accredited travel business, “expect to hear from them or your airline”.



“If you’re travelling in the next 72 hours, that’s our priority.” Planes are parked on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in DFW Airport, Texas. AP Photo/Tony Gutierrez “If you haven’t heard from your travel agent, tour operator or airline yet, get in touch with them.” For those not flying within 72 hours, they should hold off communicating with travel agencies and airlines “so they can look after the travellers who need it most urgently.” “We know this is unsettling for travellers,” Long said. “Our members are there to help, and we are monitoring the situation closely.”



In an update released at 10am AEDT, the FAA said the ground stop remains in place but “as en route facilities recover, flights will be allowed to depart” – with flights being released gradually as air traffic control centres recover. Related Article Updated

Aviation ‘Extraordinary circumstances’: Flights grounded across US due to communications issues For Australian travellers flying to the United States, airports are monitoring the situation and advising passengers to check directly with their airlines. Sydney Airport: All domestic and international flights are operating as normal, with no current impact to airport operations.

All domestic and international flights are operating as normal, with no current impact to airport operations. Melbourne Airport: Passengers booked on morning departures are advised to proceed to the airport as planned until further notice.

Passengers booked on morning departures are advised to proceed to the airport as planned until further notice. Brisbane Airport: American Airlines flight AA008 to Dallas Fort Worth has been delayed by one hour, moving from its scheduled 9.40am departure to 10.40am. The airport has advised passengers to check with their airlines for updates. Sydney Airport said it was monitoring the situation closely, but there was currently no impact to its operations.



“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight,” a spokesperson said. Qantas have advised at this stage there is a limited impact for the airline, but passengers are advised to check for updates through the app – though flight QF4 (New York to Auckland) is expected to be delayed. Most US-bound Qantas flights depart in the afternoon, providing a buffer while the FAA issue is resolved. Meanwhile, US airlines have warned passengers to expect disruptions. United Airlines confirmed that flights already airborne would continue to their destinations, but new domestic departures would remain grounded while the FAA order was in place. United is proactively cancelling flights due to congestion in the nation’s air traffic system, and issuing travel waivers, so customers can change their travel plans.



Delta also has a travel waiver for customers to change their flights. American Airlines also confirmed that aircraft already in the air could continue to their destinations, but warned that disruption to its schedule could continue throughout the day, depending on how long the nationwide ground stop remains in place. Updated WorldNorth AmericaTragedy ‘Miracle on the Mississippi’: Passengers, crew rescued after tanker hits cruise ship in New Orleans Jack Brook and Jeffrey Collins Updated November 14, 2026 — 10:16am ,first published 7:48am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. New Orleans: A tanker in New Orleans that apparently lost its steering slammed into the docked American Heritage river cruise paddleboat with 180 people aboard on Friday, New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno said. All aboard survived after the crash prompted a massive rescue operation for passengers and crew who plunged into the Mississippi River as the ship took on water and began to topple over. Thirty-two people were taken to hospital, but none had critical injuries, Moreno said, calling it “a miracle on the Mississippi”. Loading Video from the scene showed the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker hitting the paddlewheel cruise boat while it appeared to be docked as metal and glass crashed and crunched.



Tugboat operators, nearby workers, police and several other rescuers rushed to help. The boat started listing within minutes and flipped while emergency workers were still trying to get everyone off it. Emergency personnel and crews work the scene. The Advocate via AP Footage posted to social media showed the cruise ship sideways in the river. The Advocate via AP Dozens of people on board and at least two police officers were dragged from the 19-degree water onto nearby ships.



Devon Flanagan was at his job nearby at the Port of New Orleans when workers rushed down the dock. He got out of his truck and noticed the American Heritage on its side and passengers in the water. “It was just chaos,” he said. “You had all types of ships, like other barges and other companies down there trying to help out, which also was a little convoluted because you had people still in the water.” People in lifejackets being dragged from the river. AP Emergency personnel and crews are on the scene. AP The cruise ship was built in 2015 and operated by American Cruise Lines. It is five storeys high and can hold up to 150 passengers.



The American Heritage was finishing an eight-day cruise to several Mississippi River destinations in Louisiana and Mississippi. The cruise line said it was working with the Coast Guard and would share more information when possible. View post on X According to the live shipping tracker MarineTraffic, the tanker involved in the crash specialises in carrying large quantities of asphalt and bitumen, used for road construction and roofing. Ships carrying asphalt and bitumen are often heated well above 120 degrees to prevent the asphalt from solidifying aboard, according to the maritime periodical Marine Insights. It is not immediately clear whether the ship was carrying any materials when the crash occurred.



The 160-metre vessel had a final destination in New Orleans, according to MarineTraffic, and was sailing under a flag for the Marshall Islands. More to come AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts. A choice must be made: Team Uzzie or Team Pat?
World.content:
Analysis SportBall tampering Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts. A choice must be made: Team Uzzie or Team Pat? Oliver Brown November 14, 2026 — 9:50am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Even after more than eight years, “sandpapergate” is the gift that keeps giving, the scandal that leaves an irreparable schism not just within a cricket team but an entire country. As if those events in Cape Town in March 2018 were not lurid enough at the time, with the sight of Cameron Bancroft shoving sandpaper down his trousers a grievous wound to Australia’s sense of itself, Usman Khawaja’s claim that everybody knew about the plot to tamper with the ball has magnified the trauma. Long-time teammates Usman Khawaja with Pat Cummins back in 2018. Getty Images The soap opera has spun so far out of control that professional lip-readers were asked this week to decode a film of Test captain Pat Cummins arguing with his wife Becky on a Sydney street. It is all supremely unedifying, and yet deliciously entertaining. Cummins’ press conference on Friday dialled up the drama, shredding any remaining friendship with Khawaja as he called the retired opener’s accusation of a team conspiracy “100 per cent wrong” and “utter nonsense”.



The unburdening of his pent-up rage lasted 68 minutes and shone a light on his personality as never before. Occasionally too PR-friendly for some tastes, he excoriated Khawaja, telling him: “Friends aren’t casual with each other’s lives and reputations.” Has there been a saga like it for raw emotion? In 2018, a disgraced Steve Smith dissolved in front of the cameras and had to be comforted by his father Peter. When an ashen-faced James Sutherland, the then chief executive of Cricket Australia, delivered a statement in Melbourne condemning the players’ behaviour, tensions ran so high that two journalists present had a fight. Loading The difference with Cummins’ performance is that it has been hailed instantly in his homeland as a peace-in-our-time moment. “Outstanding”, “vulnerable”, “credible” were just some of the snap verdicts Down Under. Oh, and “disgustingly handsome”.



Editor's pick Analysis

Australian cricket Seven takeaways from one of Australian sport’s most memorable press conferences The motivation for these cloying homilies appears to be twofold. First, Cummins is such a gleaming Australian thoroughbred, both a devastating strike bowler and a part-time children’s author advocating the greater use of solar panels, that nothing can be allowed to besmirch his sheen of perfection. Secondly, the idea that he is not telling the truth – that he, and the rest of a brilliant bowling attack, were in on the dastardly scheme from the start – is almost too much for the national psyche to bear. There is evident desperation in Australia to believe Cummins’ version over Khawaja’s. Just look at their respective media appearances this week: where Khawaja received a thorough grilling on the ABC’s 730 current affairs show, Cummins left his audience at Sydney’s Olympic Park in such raptures that he was practically carried out on a sedan chair.



Usman Khawaja’s memoir, Sabr, has reopened old wounds. Two men, two diametrically opposite accounts of what happened. And so, the logical extension is that somebody is lying, that a choice must be made as to who to trust. Team Uzzie or Team Pat? The ecstatic notices of the past 24 hours prove Australians are in the captain’s corner, prepared to take his every heartfelt comment at face value and to let the infernal matter rest. All very convenient, very fickle. The problem is the central question – how the bowlers in Cape Town could possibly have been oblivious to the altered ball condition – is left hanging. In 2021, Cummins, Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc and Nathan Lyon issued a joint statement to declare that the first they knew of sandpaper being on the field was when they saw it on the big screen.



“We respectfully request an end to the rumour-mongering and innuendo,” they said at the time. “It has gone on too long and it is time to move on.” Loading Except their own teammate seemed not to receive the memo, with Khawaja waiting a further five years to argue in his memoir Sabr, that the Australian dressing room needed to accept collective responsibility for the scam. Promoting the book, he said: “Am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah.” Unsurprisingly, David Warner, Khawaja’s close friend and a man banned for 12 months for his part in it, wasted no time in endorsing this portrayal. And when Cummins contradicted it, he gravely concluded the captain had “thrown Uzzie under the bus”.



The trouble is Khawaja has hardly gone out of his way to present himself as a reliable narrator. He went to pieces under tough interrogation by 730 host Sarah Ferguson, seeking refuge in such vacuous Meghan Markle-isms as “my truth” and “safe space”, before cancelling the rest of his scheduled broadcast appearances. While he is fond of throwing grenades – remember his allegation that he had been treated differently during the last Ashes series as a “coloured cricketer”? – he is not the best at providing concrete proof. Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith during the infamous press conference at Newlands in 2018. Getty Images He again pushes the politics of grievance in his book, insisting he lost out to Smith for the Test captaincy on the grounds of race. Even Cummins, once so indulgent of Khawaja that he stopped Australia’s players from spraying champagne so as not to offend a teetotal Muslim, was unimpressed. “If you’re going to say that, you’ve got to have some evidence, and I just don’t think that is the case,” he said. It all leaves Australia’s cricket community in quite the quandary.



You can see their dilemma a mile off: on the one hand, they want to circle the wagons around the golden boy Cummins, and on the other, they are terrified of suggesting any malign motives for distrusting Khawaja. Pat Cummins answered questions for well over an hour. Sam Mooy To cap it all, Warner’s book is due out before long, all but guaranteeing the whole sorry mess will be relitigated once more. For a once great Test team, it is a nightmare without end. For everybody else, it is just about the juiciest Ashes prelude possible. World.title: US flights grounded LIVE updates: FAA stops all departing flights citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’, Homeland Security secretary denies cyber attack, Microsoft outage connection
World.content:
Earlier this morning, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop in the US due to “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”.

What caused it?

Telecommunication problems

All Trump administration agencies are citing a telecommunications problem as the reason for halting all departing flights.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy says the FAA issued the nationwide ground stop “following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centres”.

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue,” he says.

Not terror or a cyberattack

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin stressed there was no foul involved in the ground stop and explicitly said it was not a terrorist attack. “This isn’t another 9/11,” he says.

He, too, blames a telecommunications outage but adds that Trump administration officials do not have a conclusive cause.

Microsoft outage

Mullin also says there is no connection between the nationwide ground stop and the Microsoft outage, which also triggered massive global disruptions yesterday, according to The Washington Post.

The new AI tool

The communications error arrived days after the FAA announced it would begin rolling out an AI toll across the US to help controllers avoid delays, The New York Times reports.

According to that report, the AI tool was initially unveiled in Washington, DC airports two months ago on the same day air traffic communications failures also grounded hundreds of flights.

The incident occurred after a circuit failed when contractors accidentally ripped through a back-up fibre line.

But Mullin also says nothing could be ruled out at this point.

World.title: It won’t be the last time the French raid Australia’s top rugby talent
World.content:
Analysis SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby It won’t be the last time the French raid Australia’s top rugby talent Paul Cully November 14, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The news that Australia’s under-18 captain Justice Taumoepeau is taking his talents to the Top 14 in France for the next three years had a depressingly familiar feel to it. Rugby Australia has done a reasonable job of retaining talent from their junior sides, but not all of those players will kick on, and it’s the few who get away who will come back to hurt them. Australia’s under-18s captain Justice Taumoepeau (being tackled) is off to play domestic rugby in France. Getty Images for Rugby Australia Taumoepeau, a product of the Waratahs system, is in that category and it is a sort of backhanded compliment to Australia that he has been targeted by Pau in France. The club has the reputation as one of the best developers of talent in Europe, with brilliant Test backs Fabien Brau-Boirie and Théo Attissogbe notable graduates from their academy.



Of course, Taumoepeau’s exit comes with the now-standard reassurances that RA will keep in touch and he still wants to play for the Wallabies. But Australia’s claim on the young back-rower has been loosened by his departure and it would be naive to think otherwise. Taumoepeau’s move feels like a kick in the guts because it undermines one of the pillars essential to RA’s bid to revive the Wallabies’ fortunes. France’s Fabien Brau-Boirie, centre, is tackled by Australia’s Ryan Lonergan and Len Ikitau, left, during the Nations Championship international in Brisbane earlier this year. AP Photo/Tertius Pickard Invest in youth and build, they said, and the Wallabies will reap the benefits. Well, that is what RA and NSW did with Taumoepeau, but doing the right thing hasn’t stopped the French from coming in and swooping after years of Australian development.



But, such is the harsher world facing Waratahs coach Michael Cheika as he takes on his second stint in the job. The image of Cheika returning to the Waratahs, flanked by his assistants Stephen Hoiles and Wycliff Palu, prompted some feelgood vibes of better times, like a favourite rock band reforming for another tour. Michael Cheika faces the media for the first time as Waratahs coach last week, flanked by his assistants Stephen Hoiles (left) and Wycliff Palu. James Brickwood There is so much about Cheika’s demeanour and language, not to mention his record, that points to the coach instilling a level of belief among his squad. But, the expectations on Cheika need to come with all manner of caveats.



It would be hard to argue, even risk being labelled a pessimist, that the Waratahs squad Cheika is inheriting is as strong as the one he took over in 2013, never mind the team he refined in the championship year in 2014. There will be a sprinkling of Wallabies, and the return of Angus Bell from his stint in Ulster will strengthen the pack. Young No. 8 Isaac Fonua also showed considerable promise, and Cheika will feel confident Palu can, in time, turn him into another Palu. But last year obvious talents such as Sid Harvey and Jimmy Hendren were up and down with their performances and it is difficult for players of that age to suddenly take a great leap. The return of Bernard Foley and Nick Phipps were designed to infuse the younger players with know-how and a winning mentality, but the Waratahs project feels like one that should be measured in years, not months. Hoiles, as Cheika’s successor, will be the long-term beneficiary.



Related Article Australian rugby Don’t be cranky, be connected: Will Skelton on why French raids can be good for Australian rugby Cheika could make fools of us. Perhaps his shock therapy will work and the Waratahs can challenge for a place in the playoffs next year. That would be a success, never mind the title. But, the reality is the rugby world has shifted since the 2013-2015 period, and a lot of those changes have been hostile to Australian rugby. French clubs view NSW and Queensland as being in the same neighbourhood as Fiji, figuratively as well as literally, and Taumoepeau probably won’t be the last young player to head north. The poaching justifiably infuriates RA, and it is quite the flex for Pau to be able to land Australia’s 18s captain.



But, rightly or wrongly, it does reflect how the balance of power has shifted. When Cheika started at the Waratahs, the Wallabies were No.3 in the world. France was No.4. Today, the Wallabies are No.7 and the French have retained their position, although back-to-back Six Nations titles and a thriving Top 14 suggests they are in a better place than Ireland (No.3). Cheika’s second act at the Waratahs, therefore, will be more challenging than the first. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: RNZ chief executive Paul Thompson announces early departure from organisation
World.content:
RNZ CEO Paul Thompson is to leave the organisation on Monday, six weeks early, after controversy over a financial blowout at the public broadcaster.

Thompson, RNZ's CEO for 13 years and a former president of the global Public Media Alliance, was due to leave on December 31.

In a statement this morning, Thompson said he felt it was best for himself, his family and RNZ to leave.

Thompson made a bombshell announcement on Monday that RNZ was facing a shock $12 million loss and will axe 58 jobs - around one in six staff.

It has seen questions raised about whether his position was tenable and protests planned by staff unions.

The broadcaster's chief financial officer Hilary Parker resigned unexpectedly in October.

The $11.8m loss is more than 25 times the $470,000 RNZ had expected to lose over the year to June.

RNZ has commissioned an independent review of how it got its finances wrong.

RNZ chairman Brent Impey - who was appointed to the Board of Directors in 2024 and became chair in July - said Thompson had responded to a difficult situation "with courage and integrity".

"As I said on Tuesday, I have considerable empathy for him as a chief executive who was provided with inaccurate financial information. He has responded to a difficult situation with courage and integrity.

"We wish him all the best."

Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Media and Communications Minister Paul Goldsmith said it "was the right thing to do".

His office said there was no indication of him stepping in over RNZ's governance decisions at this stage.

Associate Finance Minister David Seymour, a shareholding minister in RNZ, also welcomed the decision.

"I hope the board will reflect carefully on this recent period and make their next appointments very carefully.

"The chief executive is responsible for the performance of the company, and RNZ has fallen well short of what taxpayers have a right to expect.

"The people who suffer most from that underperformance are the hard-working staff and the public who fund it."

Earlier this week Thompson was questioned by Checkpoint's Lisa Owen if he should quit early but pushed back saying, the government had reduced RNZ's funding.

"We thought we were addressing that. We weren't."

In a statement to staff today, Thompson said it had been a privilege to lead RNZ.

"The last few weeks have, of course, been difficult. As Chief Executive and Editor-in-Chief I take responsibility for the financial issues we are dealing with. It is a sad note to end on. I will contribute to the independent review to help ensure RNZ robustly examines what went wrong and identifies improvements."

He said he was proud of work to modernize the organisation, "including leading on trust, diversifying and growing audiences and content, improving journalism and connecting with more New Zealanders than ever before".

He said public media played a vital role and urged staff to keep up "the great and important work".

World.title: West Auckland mall evacuated after battery fire
World.content:
A lithium battery fire has prompted evacuations at a west Auckland shopping mall.

Fire and Emergency says it was called to the NorthWest Shopping Centre about 11.30am on Saturday after smoke was seen in the area.

A lithium-ion battery had caught fire inside a shop, a FENZ spokesperson said.

Six crews attended the fire. Supplied

Six fire crews supported by aerial units were at the scene at its peak. Most had since left and the fire had been extinguished.

The building was being ventilated, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Wellington police raid nets coins, cars, copper, cannabis and more
World.content:
The seizure of cash, gold, guns and luxury cars was "a long time coming", police say, following a raid in the capital.

Police in Wellington on Saturday said after a year-long investigation they spent two days searching two properties, uncovering a "huge haul", including gamma-hydroxybutyrate, cannabis, a kilogram of methamphetamine "in distinctive wrapping" worth about $105,000, and "space vape" liquid.

They also took more than $100,000 in cash, $50,000 in gold coins, two guns, a "large recycling bin full of copper" and nine classic cars, including a limousine, a Chevrolet Bel Air and a Plymouth Savoy.

Items seized in a raid by Wellington police, November 2026. Police / supplied

Items seized in a raid by Wellington police, November 2026. Police / supplied

Two men were arrested, aged 53 and 32, and face more than 20 drug- and firearm-related charges between them. Police said more were likely.

"One of the men has been supplying a wide range of illicit drugs from his property for many years, benefitting off the addiction of others," Detective Senior Sergeant Lee Underhill said.

"It may have been a long time coming, but we are pleased to have taken these drugs and firearms out of the community, as well as seizing millions of dollars' worth of assets that I believe are the profits from his illegal enterprise."

Items seized in a raid by Wellington police, November 2026. Police / supplied

She said 3D-printed firearms were a growing problem.

"The view from the top of the hill might have been worth a million dollars, but the cost of alleged criminal activity could prove considerably higher."

Items seized in a raid by Wellington police, November 2026. Police / supplied

Detective Sergeant Sam Buckley said there had been a noticeable increase in criminals hiding their proceeds "through the purchase of virtual assets, shares and precious metals".

World.title: Wheels up: Air NZ to launch flights between Hamilton and Queenstown in 2027
World.content:
Direct flights will run between Hamilton and Queenstown for the first time from next June.

Air New Zealand says three return flights a week will run on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays using an Airbus A320 with 171 seats.

The flights will come just in time for the busy winter season, the airline says.

Hamilton Airport says the flights will meet strong demand from residents, support tourism flows between the two regions and strengthen Hamilton's role as a gateway to the central North Island.

The year-round service will allow travellers to reach Queenstown without having to fly direct from Auckland or catch connecting flights via Wellington or Christchurch.

Hamilton Airport chief executive Mark Morgan says the new service will further increase the airport's growing passenger base, with a record 530,000 passengers travelling through Hamilton last year. It will offer about 53,300 seats annually across both directions.

"It's a significant milestone for Hamilton Airport but also a great vote of confidence in the wider region," Morgan said.

"This decision by Air New Zealand responds to a long-standing desire for better connections between the two regions. It will reduce the need for international visitors to backtrack through Auckland, leaving more time to explore the central North Island.

"There is a great opportunity to develop inbound tourism and new touring itineraries linking Queenstown with places like Hamilton Gardens, Hobbiton, Waitomo, Rotorua and Taupo. We'll work with Air New Zealand and tourism partners to develop that opportunity over time," he said.

The new service will use existing airport infrastructure and will not require further investment. Hamilton Airport already accommodates Airbus A320 jet services to Christchurch and can coordinate terminal operations, security screening and staffing for the new flights.

"Three services a week is a great place to start," Morgan said of the route's future. "We'll work together to promote the service and build demand throughout the year."

Local support would be key to attracting more airlines and building more routes out of Hamilton, he said.

World.title: Whangārei man arrested after 15-hour standoff with police while up a tree
World.content:
A Whangārei man has been arrested after a 15-hour standoff with police where he refused to come down from a tree.

Whangārei Area Commander Inspector Maria Nordstrom said at about 10:30am on Friday, a 40-year-old man who was a person of interest with an active arrest warrant fled from police after being spotted on Wairau Drive in Tikipunga.

The man allegedly fled on foot, swimming across a small river onto nearby farmland.

The police Eagle helicopter found him in a tree in bushland at about 12pm.

After nearly 12 hours, at about 1:40am on Saturday, the man came down from the tree and was taken into police custody.

He was expected to appear at the Whangārei District Court on Saturday in relation to the arrest warrant.

World.title: COP31 hears 1.5°C overshoot not an option for Pacific
World.content:
The President of the Marshall Islands says the global response to the threat of overshoot of the Paris Agreement's goal must be overwhelming or the world we know, is over.

A new UN report says global warming beyond 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels is now inevitable and the world must limit the "overshoot" as much as possibly before reversing it.

Pacific leaders are joining other world leaders in in Antalya, Türkiye for the COP31 climate summit.

The UN report acknowledges that the international community has made progress on climate change.

But it said global action to cut greenhouse gas emissions have not been fast enough to avoid global warming crossing 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels in the next few years.

Marshall Islands President Dr Hilda Heine described to delegates at the UN climate summit what an overshoot means in the Pacific.

"We are watching eco-systems die, and we are feeling temperatures rise. Every fraction of a degree we warm brings a catastrophe," she said.

"Overshoot must be kept as small and short as possible and be rapidly reverse. We are fallen short of the emission reductions needed to stay under 1.5."

The President of the Marshall Islands says the global response to the threat of overshoot of the Paris Agreement's goal must be overwhelming or the world we know, is over. Chewy Lin/Office of the President, Republic of the Marshall Islands

President Heine also told delegates that every new oil well drilled, every piece of coal extracted is a threat to her country's future.

She said the discovery of new fossil fuels resources is not something to celebrate, but something to fear.

"Fossil fuel interest are also the root cause of delayed action, blocking a road to a healthier, safer world. Yet even as fossil fuels supplies fail and economies falter, and the financial case for renewal is clear, we still see trillions in fossil subsidies."

The Marshall president said the Pacific is charting a course to a future - free from fossil fuels dependency.

She wasn't the only Pacific leader to speak about a 1.5 overshoot.

Palau's President, Surangel Whipps Jr said this COP31 must turn the tide as the 1.5 goal is slips away.

"For the Pacific, this is not an abstract target, it is an existential threat to our food, our economies and sovereignty. States must honour their international obligations, noting the International Court of Justice clear finding that breaching climate obligations is an internationally wrongful act, carrying state responsibility."

The President of the Federated States of Micronesia Wesley Simina also addressed delegates at the gathering.

President Simina reaffirmed that climate change remains the single greatest threat to the security, livelihoods and well-being of Pacific peoples.

He said the 1.5 threshold is of fundamental importance for the future of island states.

"Our reefs are more than a eco-system, they protect our shores, sustain our fisheries, feed our families and carry the stories and traditions of our communities. Climate change threatens our tuna stocks, likewise threatening our livelihoods and economy."

President Simina said for Pacific peoples, the ocean is inseparable from their identity, culture and security.

World.title: Have I made an investing mistake? Ask Susan
World.content:
I am a single, mid-30s female. About a month-and-a-half ago, I started a new permanent job with a significant pay cut.

I also invested a significant amount (about 30 percent) of my life savings ($200,000-plus) in managed funds, with about 50 percent in balanced, 25 percent in growth and 25 percent in global share funds (high risk). I felt like I had done my research when taking out these investments and that I wouldn't need access to the funds within the next three years.

I had been planning to transfer more money into these investments each payday, but since opening these investments, the value has now dropped. This is causing me a lot of anxiety and fear that I might lose a lot of money that I worked hard for, and can't afford to lose.

Added to this is the large component tech stocks have in the US share markets, and political and global economic uncertainty.

I have stopped contributing to my investment funds and am too scared to look at the balances. I know that you cannot time the market - it's about time in the market.

I feel like I overestimated my risk appetite, but I also know that it's too late to change my funds to lower risk funds, as I would be realising a loss. Plus, if you are going to change the fund type, you should only do it once.

I also have KiwiSaver, which is high growth. I have seen the balance of this fluctuate over time (eg during Covid and with the recent oil crisis), but this hasn't caused me the anxiety and fear like my new investment funds have.

Are you able to please provide any advice or reassurance (or otherwise!) for my situation? I thought I might restart my contributions or take out some short term PIEs, after the OCR announcement, and elections here and the US, but I am feeling anxious that I will make another poor decision.

I don't think you've made as poor a decision as you think you have. Everything you've done actually looks fine to me and it sounds like you just need to keep going.

Koura founder Rupert Carlyon agrees with me and says you seem quite switched on, although you are suffering normal anxieties.

"She has done her risk assessment properly and has made it clear that she will not be taking any money out for at least three years, which is good.

"One thing worth thinking about is whether she will be withdrawing everything in three years or only a part of it. If it is all in three years, then she might want to think about whether the global share allocation is appropriate.

"Over the next few years, she can expect some material ups and downs. She has already been through this with her KiwiSaver and her managed funds will not be different at all.

"If she is truly invested for the long term - longer than the three years, in my view - she might want to take advantage of the falling prices and invest in the markets while they are down."

Carlyon is correct that, if you are investing when prices are down, you have an opportunity to benefit from the recovery, when it comes. Provided your strategy is still appropriate for your goals and risk profile, I would stick with your plans, if I were you.

I am in my 80s. I have no living relatives, so I sold my house and have been spending most of the money I received from the sale on things I couldn't afford before.

I am now living comfortably in a flat. I have a reasonable amount left, after ticking off all the things on my 'bucket list'. What I'd like to know is whether or not I should donate to my favourite charities now, so I can see the good results, or leave the bequests until I die.

Should I require rest home care in the future, can any monies I've donated be clawed back?

I asked the Ministry of Social Development about this. General group manager of service delivery Shannon Soughtton said, when someone applied for the rest home subsidy, a range of factors were assessed, including income and assets.

"This assessment is complex and is done on a case-by-case basis, looking at the individual person or couple's circumstances. However, all donations, including to charities, are assessed under the gifting rules for residential care subsidy asset testing.

"We won't count up to $8500 of assets gifted each year in the last five years, from when the subsidy application is made. This is a total of $42,500 gifted in the last five years.

"In terms of gifted assets from longer than five years ago, we won't count up to $27,000 a year of assets that are gifted or donated.

"Everyone's situation is different and we strongly encourage people to get in touch with us, if they want to understand how donations may affect their eligibility for the residential care subsidy."

Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

World.title: Flag football takes flight as young Aussie athletes compete in China
World.content:
A team of high school athletes has travelled from the Gold Coast to China to compete against some of the world's best NFL flag football players.

The fast-emerging sport is a non-contact take on the United States's most beloved game and looks a bit like OzTag.

Teams of five run plays to pass a football down the field in the hope of scoring touchdowns, pulling flags from the belt of their opponents to stop play.

Khodi Fabian, 15, had spent most of her life excelling at Australian sports, including touch football, before putting on the flag belt.

Khodi plays the role of wide receiver, catching long balls down the field thrown by the quarterback.

"I never thought I'd get into NFL. My life has been all touch," she said.

Despite that, the teen didn't shy away from the new sport, and represented Queensland in a competition earlier this year.

Coco Gillett (left) and Khodi Fabian say playing touch football has opened the door to competing in a future Olympic Games. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Kodhi is among 10 Palm Beach-Currumbin State High School students competing in this weekend's NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championship in Shanghai.

The team is the only Australian side invited to play in the competition.

"It's really fun to do something different, especially since it's a new sport. It's exciting to play," Khodi said.

Rapid growth on way to Olympics

In flag football, teammates work together to pull flags from the belt of their opposition to stop play. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

Flag football will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles in 2028, generating rapid growth in participation since the move was announced in 2023.

The fast-approaching showcase has prompted major investment by the NFL in Australia, headquartered on the Gold Coast.

A 2022 pilot of 10 local schools helped the sport gather steam, before it was expanded to 750 schools across Australia with free flag kits announced by NFL commissioner Roger Goodell in April.

"There's over 20 million people playing in a very short period of time. By the time we get to [Brisbane] 2032 that number will be exponentially higher," Mr Goodell said.

Bindy McCormack says flag football presents huge career opportunities and professional pathways for her students. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Teacher Bindy McCormack agreed the growth had been rapid.

After first seeing the game three years ago during state championships on the Gold Coast, Ms McCormack said she was hooked.

"We took a team to compete and we'd never played before, we just learnt on the run," the coach said.

"We ended up winning and there were lots of selectors, lots of talk about the opportunities moving forward, so I think that locked me in to embed it within the school."

Fun keeps girls playing sport

A team of 10 Gold Coast students are the only Australians competing at the NFL Flag Asia Pacific Championships in Shanghai. (ABC Gold Coast: Emily Dobson)

NFL Australia and New Zealand general manager Charlotte Offord said the league was footing the bill for the team of 10 plus two coaches to travel and compete in the one-day international event.

She said the investment aimed to break down barriers for women in sport and create more pathways for young people, regardless of the outcome of the China championship.

"There's US colleges for young athletes to go and play flag now," Ms Offord said.

"We've recently announced we'll launch a professional flag league in the next five years … where people will be paid to play in the US."

Charlotte Offord says footing the bill for the trip is an investment by NFL Flag in the future of the game domestically. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

Coco Gillett, 13, plays centre for the team heading abroad and said she had been "gobsmacked" to get a call-up to compete internationally.

Despite the difference to her usual sports, Coco said the culture of the game had helped her enjoy playing flag.

"All coming together and scoring and having fun with your friends … there's lots of celebrating," she said.

Unlike some of her teammates, Coco will be too young to qualify for the LA Games in 2028, something she said would drive her to keep her sights set on the big leagues.

"The Olympics would be great … I just want to try and get better each year and progress," Coco said.

World.title: Tears for Pochettino as Man Utd turn to former Spurs boss
World.content:
Tears filled Mauricio Pochettino's eyes as he discussed quitting the US national team for his dream job with Manchester United.

"A decision that in some parts, it's a very sad decision, in other parts, we are professional and we need also to try to find the next step, to try and make your dreams come true," he said.

Just three months after the US Soccer Federation announced his contract to lead the Americans through to the 2030 World Cup, Pochettino said he will depart next week for Old Trafford.

The Argentine will try to revive the 20-time English champions, who sit in the relegation zone after 10 games of the Premier League season.

"They know that there's not too many opportunities [that] can happen in your career like a side of Manchester United and, of course, when that arrives, it's difficult to turn down," Pochettino said during an emotional news conference at the US team training camp.

He signed a two-and-a-half-year contract and will take over on November 18 ahead of a crucial Premier League match against Liverpool at Anfield four days later, becoming United's eighth permanent coach or manager since Alex Ferguson retired in 2013.

Pochettino choked up at a news conference, speaking while seated between USSF president Cindy Parlow Cone and chief executive JT Batson.

"One of the most difficult decision in our career," he said, crying and rubbing his hands as Cone put a supportive hand on his back.

He did not want to speak about the state of United.

Mauricio Pochettino has coached from the visitors dug out at Old Trafford in the Premier League. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

The English club said the 54-year-old was "renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players".

It said he had "consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues".

Pochettino's appointment came one day after Michael Carrick was fired for overseeing United's worst league start in 40 years.

Manchester United sits in 18th place in the Premier League.

Pochettino and his assistants will remain with the US for the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday.

The former Spurs coach took over the US team in 2024 and led the co-host Americans to the round of 16 at this year's World Cup.

The USSF is likely to inquire about Pep Guardiola's interest and also could consider elevating Under-23 coach Steve Cherundolo, a former national team defender.

The Americans' next game with the full player pool after Tuesday is likely to be in late March, so the US could take its time with its search.

Going into his final two games, Pochettino led the US to 21 wins, 12 losses and two draws — counting a penalty shootout win over Costa Rica as a draw. He was the first long-term US coach not to win any titles since Steve Sampson from 1995-98.

Pochettino said he told his US players and staff of his decision in a meeting on Thursday.

"I want to say thank you because they were very supportive and they really understand the situation," Pochettino said.

"And they know us, how committed we are for the next two games."

Mauricio Pochettino will lead the USA in two more matches against Haiti this international window. (Getty Images: Press Association/PA Images)

After coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea in the Premier League, Espanyol in Spain and winning the French title with Paris Saint-Germain, Pochettino takes a job that has proved to be too big for a succession of managers since Ferguson led the team to a record 13 Premier League titles and two Champions League crowns during a near 27-year tenure.

United has not won the league since Ferguson's last season in 2013 and has been overtaken by rivals Manchester City, Liverpool, Chelsea and Arsenal.

Champions League-winning coaches Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho failed to meet United's expectations, while David Moyes, Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, Erik ten Hag and Carrick also came up short.

Despite winning the French league with PSG in 2022, arguably Pochettino's greatest achievement was turning Tottenham into a serial title contender in the Premier League and also leading the club to the Champions League final in 2019.

He has never won a major trophy in England, most recently losing the final of the English League Cup with Chelsea in 2024.

It is not known how much Pochettino will earn at United, as typically European soccer teams do not disclose the salaries of coaches and players.

United has spent huge sums on coaches and executives over the past 13 years and paid well in excess of $100 million in severance payments alone.

AP

World.title: McKeown returns, Pallister stars at Swim GP
World.content:
Lani Pallister produced the race of the evening and Kaylee McKeown made a successful return in the opening session of the inaugural Swim GP.

This is McKeown's return to competition after the backstroke star pulled out of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games because of glandular fever.

She won the 50m backstroke skins event, beating Iona Anderson in the last round on Friday night at the Melbourne Sports and Aquatic Centre.

Asked if she was having fun immediately after the backstroke skins, a breathless McKeown groaned "no".

Pallister won the 400m freestyle in 3 minutes 53.73 seconds, just two seconds off her personal best.

At the start of next month, the Australian distance freestyle ace will compete at the world short-course championships in Beijing.

Lani Pallister of team KingTide was superb, as ever. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Wahoo team leads on 105 points, 11 ahead of Kraken, with McKeown's Tsunami team next on 77 and Pallister's King Tide scoring 63 and with work to do in Saturday's final session.

Swim GP format Traditional swimming competitions are no longer enough, as Swimming Australia continues to explore alternative formats with the Swim GP in Melbourne, and the return of the International Swimming League in London this December.

Kyle Chalmers is captaining the Kraken team, but he is not competing in the made-for-TV novelty event.

On doctor's orders the 28-year-old is in the midst of a six-week break from swimming after the latest MRI scan on his troublesome back.

Six weeks is manageable, especially with three Olympics under his belt and all the faith that experience brings.

But an injury tweak at the Swim GP could turn that into 10 weeks, with next year's national trials looming large, and the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away.

"Earlier, when I was going through surgeries, I'd always try to force myself back in the pool and set myself back further — taking more anti-inflammatory tablets or getting a cortisone injection as a quick fix," he told AAP.

"But my doctor has advised me to have six weeks of no swimming and it's very important to take that seriously, so I don't push that six weeks out to 10 weeks.

"Then I'm really behind the eight ball of where I need to be."

Kyle Chalmers is resting his back for this event. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

After qualifying for the Paris Olympics two years ago, Chalmers revealed he had needed four epidural injections into his spine. That is as brutal as it sounds and he'd prefer not to go through it again.

"It would have been up there as one of the worst experiences for an athlete," he said.

"At some point you have to step back and say 'I am a human being first, I'm not just a racehorse that needs to be jabbed'.

"I don't want the quick fix, I need the long-term solution so I can run around in the backyard with my daughter — hopefully also future children."

Chalmers also noted that he usually takes time out of the water around this time of year.

He calls this enforced lay-off a small road bump.

But Chalmers was keen to be in Melbourne and lead the Kraken team, calling the Swim GP a great opportunity for the sport.

"I know I could race here and it could be fine, but does it put me back a little bit further in my rehab, and trying to get my body right for what matters most?" he said.

"That's why it's still cool to be able to be here and be part of the team."

Fellow Olympic gold medallist Mollie O'Callaghan also pulled out of the event as she manages a skin infection.

Swim GP is a points-based competition in a 25m pool, with no official times recorded and a variety of relay and individual race formats.

World.title: Wallabies ring changes ahead of Scotland Test
World.content:
Carter Gordon is back at five-eighth to steer the creaking ship as the Wallabies seek to urgently get back on course against Scotland at Murrayfield in the Nations Championship.

After the calamitous 45-22 thrashing by England at Twickenham, the Wallabies have made three changes, with Declan Meredith paying the price for a woeful outing against England.

Gordon is recalled just two months after breaking his leg against Argentina, with Ben Donaldson remaining as cover on the bench.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has been shifted from the left wing to inside centre alongside Len Ikitau as coach Les Kiss changes the midfield partnership for the sixth successive Test.

Star flanker Rob Valetini returns as the starting number 6 after the two-time John Eales Medal winner started from the bench last time out, in a familiar back-row partnership with skipper Harry Wilson and current player-of-the-year Fraser McReight.

With Tom Hooper and Brandan Paenga-Amosa making welcome comebacks on the bench after injury, Kiss wants to see a big response from his team who've suffered three heavy defeats on the bounce.

"We've had a good week of training but after falling short of our own expectations last week it's vital we transfer our hard work onto the field for the 80 minutes on Sunday," Kiss said.

"Playing Scotland on their home turf is a massive Test and we're all determined to make our supporters proud by elevating our game to the level it needs to be."

The Wallabies were well beaten by England at Twickenham. (Getty Images: RFU/Dan Mullan )

Winger Harry Potter is also back at the venue of his Test debut, with Suaalii back in midfield to replace the injured Isaac Henry. He'll be partnering with Ikitau for the 18th time at Test level.

Western Force skipper Jeremy Williams shifts back to lock alongside Josh Canham after the experiment of playing him in the back row against England didn't pay dividends.

Lachlan Shaw will play his first Test in Europe as the lock cover, while Hooper should be a valuable addition in the back row after his recent shoulder injury.

Scotland, meanwhile, have made two changes from their team that faded so badly against New Zealand last weekend, with Blair Kinghorn and record try-scorer Darcy Graham taking up positions in the back three.

Australia-born players Sione Tuipulotu, captaining the side at centre, and number 8 Jack Dempsey, will both start for the Scots, who were well beaten by the All Blacks 21-43 last time out.

Former Australian under 20s star Tuipulotu played a big part in Scotland's win over the Wallabies at Murrayfield two years ago.

Former Waratah's player Dempsey played 14 times for the Wallabies, most recently in 2019.

World.title: Socceroos crush Qatar in Doha demolition
World.content:
The Socceroos have enjoyed one of their most emphatic outings under Tony Popovic, outclassing woeful Asian Cup holders Qatar 3-0 with a statement win in front of the champions' home fans in Doha.

Goals from Riley McGree, Tete Yengi and Nestory Irankunda in a dominant first-half display put the one-sided friendly to bed by the break on Friday (Saturday AEDT) with the help of dreadful defending from the back-to-back continental champions.

The fare did get totally disjointed after the break amid a bewildering raft of personnel changes, as subs Eli Adams, Sam Klein, Kasey Bos and Diesel Herrington all earned their Socceroos debuts, but Australia remained in complete control with the hosts only firing their first tame shot after 72 minutes.

"The win was what we wanted and we set the game up with a very good first-half," Popovic told Paramount+.

"We won some balls high up the pitch, which is always encouraging, in difficult conditions. A lot of the boys have come from Europe where it's a lot cooler, so we were tested physically to be that aggressive."

Relieved that they won't have to travel to Amman for their second match next Tuesday (Wednesday AEDT) and that Asian Cup finalists Jordan will come to Doha to face them, Popovic's men seemed relaxed and confident from the start.

It certainly helped when in the fifth minute, new Qatar goalkeeper Mahmoud Abunada had a complete brain fade, attempting a short pass to his central defenders only to deliver it straight to a grateful Riley McGree, who slotted home left-footed into an unguarded net.

It was the Middlesbrough creator's second international goal, a gift four years after his first.

McGree, who missed the World Cup through injury, showed what the Socceroos had missed as he ran the midfield show early on, also firing over narrowly with a 17th minute volley.

Nestory Irankunda scored the Socceroos' third. (Getty Images: Mohamed Farag)

With Julen Lopetegui's hosts looking strangely lethargic and toothless, it was no surprise when another aimless clearance from Abunada resulted in Connor Metcalfe pouncing to put Yengi in the clear to finish neatly just after the half-hour.

Irankunda had a ball on the left flank tormenting the Qatari defence and another neat bit of midfield thieving and distribution from Metcalfe enabled him to free the Sporting Lisbon star to smash home his eighth international goal five minutes before the break.

It was the first time in five years the Socceroos had scored three in an overseas international, and it could have been six at the break, such was their dominance.

Popovic rang the changes in abundance after half time, conceding: "We lost a bit of cohesion and fluency, but we got a lot of debuts as well, so special moment for them."

Brotherly love was the order of the day. Kusini Yengi replaced Tete at the break, while on 65 minutes, Bos joined his absent older sibling Jordy as a full-fledged Socceroo before Diesel replaced Lucas Herrington, who'd had an armchair ride all match, in the final 10 minutes.

Popovic, while looking frustrated on the bench that his side hadn't kicked on with more goals, couldn't complain at a fine night's work after 14 Australian shots on goal were answered by just three from Qatar, and not one on target except for an offside goal in the 88th minute.

The Socceroos can now face Jordan with confidence, perhaps just a little miffed they won't be back in the Middle East in January for the Asian Cup now that it's been rescheduled to December 2027 in Saudi Arabia because of the regional conflict.

World.title: Spectacular try helps England to Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup glory
World.content:
England is Wheelchair Rugby League World champion for a third time after triumphing in a fiery, exhilarating final against France in Wollongong.

A spectacular try on the cusp of half-time proved pivotal for the English, with superstar Jack Brown rolling half the length of the pitch to collect a perfectly weighted Rob Hawkins kick and put his side ahead.

England kept the advantage for most of a hotly contested second half before surging clear late to triumph 50-38 and prompt a rousing rendition of the English sporting anthem Three Lions.

Earlier, Australia's Wheelaroos finished their campaign on a high, beating Ireland 70-24 in the third-place play-off.

Brown's superb effort came after a topsy-turvy first-half between wheelchair rugby league's two great powers, who have now combined for all five World Cup titles to date.

England raced to a 10-0 lead within the first 10 minutes, but was pegged back quickly, with French livewire Leo Hivernat scoring a try and providing a brilliant no-look pass to set up Damien Dore.

Tempers flared in the first period when England's Mason Billington shoved Hivernat to the ground, prompting a mid-court coming-together between the two teams.

Being a non-disabled player in elite wheelchair sport Leading out Australia at this month's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup will be a dream come true for Bayley McKenna, the Wheelaroos first non-disabled skipper.

A flurry of quick points followed for the French, but England eventually regained its composure, with Hawkins levelling things up in the right corner before setting up Brown in the half's dying moments.

France's Dany Denuwelaere crossed for a second-half hat-trick, but England proved too strong, with Brown scoring twice to complete his treble and Joe Coyd finishing with four tries.

Wheelaroos finish campaign on a high

Still licking their wounds from the 86-18 loss to England in Tuesday's semifinal, the Wheelaroos were out to finish their campaign on a high against an Irish side ranked one place ahead of them in the world rankings.

And Australia raced out of the blocks in the evening's curtain raiser, with Cory Cannane crossing within a minute and Toby Popple completing a quickfire double to have the tournament hosts 16-0 ahead after just seven minutes of play.

Ireland's Cian Horgan proceeded to hit back barely 60 seconds later, but his four-pointer would prove to be Australia's only concession in a dominant first half.

Wheelaroos captain Bayley McKenna was a surprise omission from coach Brett Clark's starting five, but returned early on to score his ninth try of the competition as the Australians reached the break with a 36-point advantage.

Ireland's Oran Spain, forced to rely on the kindness of an Irish tourist to replace a wheelchair broken on the eve of the tournament, suffered a heavy first-period fall but returned after half-time to score his side's second try in an improved showing from his side.

However, McKenna continued to influence the game, providing a deft assist for Daniel Anstey before tumbling over for two late tries to complete both his hat-trick and Australia's 70-24 victory.

Anstey also finished with a treble as the Wheelaroos secured a third-place finish, their equal, second-best finish in tournament history.

World.title: Australia's next fast bowling star blows England away on ODI debut
World.content:
Mahli Beardman has stamped his reputation as the next big thing in Australian cricket by slicing his way through England during a memorable ODI debut in Perth.

On a day when Australian cricket was still knee-deep dealing with the ghosts of Sandpapergate, Beardman snared 6–24 as England was skittled for 131 in 33.4 overs at Perth Stadium.

Australia chased the runs down with ease, led by captain Mitch Marsh's explosive 50 from 30 balls at the top of the order.

The 21-year-old Beardman was nearly unplayable at times, with England collapsing from 2–38 to 7–60 on the back of Beardman's burst.

It marked just the second time an Australian has produced a five-wicket haul in their ODI debut, following on from Tony Dodemaide's haul of 5–21 against Sri Lanka at the WACA Ground in 1988.

Only some late handy runs from Gus Atkinson (29 not out off 32 balls) and Will Jacks (25) ensured England made it to triple figures, with the visitors 8–65 at one stage.

"It all happened very quickly," Beardman told Fox Cricket when asked about his big haul.

"It's just a great privilege and honour to be able to represent my country. And to go out and take a few wickets as well is the cherry on top.

"Harry Brook was a nice wicket to get off the mark. Anytime you get your first one it's a weight off your shoulders, so that was awesome."

The right-arm paceman snared his first ODI wicket in his second over when he found the edge of England captain Brook (1).

Hitting speeds of up to 145.4 kilometres per hour, Beardman was able to entice 200-game milestone man Joe Root (17 off 36 balls) to drive on the up to gift wicketkeeper Josh Inglis his third catch of the innings.

And Beardman was on a hat-trick when he collected the scalp of Jordan Cox at the start of his fourth over — again with another pearler of a delivery that caught the edge.

Sam Curran's attempted pull off Beardman's bouncer gave Adam Zampa a catch on the boundary rope and Beardman his fourth wicket.

And Beardman's five-wicket haul was complete when Liam Dawson was caught at gully, giving the West Australian figures of 5–13 off 4.4 overs at that point.

Spencer Johnson (3–42) ensured the party continued by jumping high in the air to pull off a one-handed catch off his own bowling to send Jamie Overton packing.

Atkinson and Jofra Archer (11) struck a series of boundaries in a 29-run last-wicket stand before Beardman completed the demolition job by having Archer caught at gully.

Beardman's figures were the fourth best by a debutant in ODI world cricket, with Charlie Cassell's effort of 7–21 for Scotland against Oman in 2024 still the best.

Marsh's early burst made sure the result was never in doubt for Australia, despite Travis Head being bowled for a golden duck by Gus Atkinson.

Marsh hit a series of enormous sixes in a thrilling but brief knock, before Cooper Connolly (27), Matt Renshaw (26*) and Josh Inglis (23*) helped steer Australia home in just the 24th over.
